Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 16, verse 1–4:

(p-324) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Tafsir (exegesis) of Surat an-Nahl

This surah was called "the Surah of Blessings" because of what Allah enumerates in it of His blessings upon His servants. It is Meccan, except for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you punish, then punish with the like of that with which you were punished﴾ [an-Nahl: 126], the verse which was revealed in Medina concerning the mutilation of Hamza, may Allah be pleased with him, and the slain of Uhud; and except for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And be patient, and your patience is not but by Allah﴾ [an-Nahl: 127]; and except for His saying: ﴿Then indeed your Lord, for those who emigrated﴾ [an-Nahl: 110], the verse; as for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who emigrated for Allah after they had been wronged﴾ [an-Nahl: 41], it is Meccan, concerning the emigration to Abyssinia.

His saying, mighty and majestic is He:

﴿The command of Allah has come, so do not seek to hasten it. Exalted is He above what they associate.﴾ ﴿He sends down the angels with the Spirit, by His command, upon whom He wills of His servants: "Warn that there is no god but Me, so fear Me."﴾ ﴿He created the heavens and the earth in truth. Exalted is He above what they associate.﴾ ﴿He created man from a drop of semen, and then he is an open adversary.﴾

It has been narrated that when Jibril, peace be upon him, recited in the recitation of the revelation: ﴿The command of Allah has come﴾, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) leapt up standing, and when he said: ﴿so do not seek to hasten it﴾, he calmed down. As for His saying: ﴿the command of Allah﴾, most of the exegetes said concerning it: it means the Resurrection, and in it is a threat for the disbelievers. (p-325) It was also said: what is meant is the victory of Muhammad (ﷺ). It was said: what is meant is the punishment of the disbelievers of Mecca by the killing of Muhammad, peace be upon him, by them and his dominance over them; Naqqash mentioned something similar from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father. It was also said: what is meant is the obligations of Allah and His rulings upon His servants and His law for them; this is the saying of ad-Dahhak. But this is far-fetched because of His saying: ﴿so do not seek to hasten it﴾, for we know of no hastening except three: two of them are for the disbelievers, in the Resurrection and in the punishment, and the third is for the believers, in victory and the manifestation of Islam. His saying "has come" (atā), according to this view, is an announcement of a coming that will come, and this is valid by way of emphasis: when the report is true, one emphasizes the future by expressing it in the form of the past, i.e., as if, because of its clarity and the certainty of it, it has already occurred; and this is fitting in the report of Allah, blessed and exalted, because of the truthfulness of its occurrence.

Some people said: "atā" means "qaruba" (has drawn near), and this is similar to what I said. In my view, speaking this way is permissible only for one who knows the indicator of emphasis and understands the figurative usage; but if the addressee does not understand the indicator, then it is not permissible to put the past in place of the future, because that corrupts the report and makes it false. It is permitted in the conditional only because the indicator is clear, with "an" (that). Whoever said: "the command is the Resurrection" said: His saying: ﴿so do not seek to hasten it﴾ is a rebuttal of those who say: ﴿Hasten to us our portion﴾ [Sad: 16] and similar, of the punishment; or addressed to the believers who were impatient for victory, according to the reading of one who reads with the ta' (t) — and this is the reading of the majority — addressed to the believers; or addressed to the disbelievers, meaning: say to them: ﴿so do not seek to hasten it﴾. Sa'id ibn Jubayr read with the ya' (y), referring to the absent polytheists. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "tushrikun" with ta' from above; all the rest read with ya'. At-Tabari preferred the reading with ta' from above in both places. Abu Hatim said: "yushrikun" with ya' from below in this and the one after it was read by al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn Nisah, al-Hasan, and Abu Raja'; 'Isa read the first with ta' from above and the second with ya' from below; and both with ta' from above were read by Abu al-'Aliya, Talha, al-A'mash, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman, Yahya ibn Wathhab, and al-Jahdari; and al-Asma'i narrated from Nafi' the ta' in the first.

His saying: ﴿subhanahu wa ta'ala﴾ means: as a declaration of His transcendence. At-Tabari narrated from Ibn Jurayj who said: When ﴿The command of Allah has come, so do not seek to hasten it﴾ was revealed, some men of the disbelievers said: "This one claims that the command of Allah has come; so let us refrain from what we are upon until we see." When they saw nothing, they returned, and then ﴿The reckoning of the people has drawn near, while they are in heedlessness, turning away﴾ [al-Anbiya': 1] was revealed, so they said the like of that; then they returned, and ﴿And if We delay the punishment from them until a counted nation, they will surely say: what holds it back?﴾ [Hud: 8] — the verse was revealed. Abu Bakr ibn Hafs said: When ﴿The command of Allah has come﴾ was revealed, they raised their heads, so ﴿so do not seek to hasten it﴾ was revealed. At-Tabari narrated from Abu Sadiq that he read: "O My servants, the command of Allah has come, so do not seek to hasten it." And "subhanahu" is in the accusative as a verbal noun, i.e., as a declaration of His transcendence.

Nafi', 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read "yunazzilu al-malaikata" with ya' and a doubled zay; at-Tabari preferred it because of the multiplicity it conveys. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read with a single zay, kasra, and a sukun on the nun. Ibn Abi 'Abla read with nun for majesty and a doubled zay. Qatada read with nun and a single zay with sukun on the nun. In this and the one before it there is much irregularity. Abu Bakr narrated from 'Asim "tanazzala" with a damma on the ta', fath on the nun and zay, doubled, and raising "al-malaikatu" as an unnamed agent; this is the reading of al-A'mash. al-Jahdari read with ya' damma, sukun on the nun, and fath on the zay. al-Hasan, Abu al-'Aliya, 'Asim, al-Jahdari, and al-A'raj read with fath on the ta' and raising "al-malaikatu" as the subject; al-Mufaddal narrated it from 'Asim. And "al-malaikata" here is Jibril, peace be upon him.

The interpreters differed concerning "al-Ruh" (the Spirit). Mujahid said: the Spirit is prophethood. Ibn 'Abbas said: revelation. Qatada said: with mercy and revelation. ar-Rabi' ibn Anas said: every word of Allah is a spirit, and from it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We have revealed to you a spirit from Our command﴾ [ash-Shura: 52]. Ibn Jurayj said: the Spirit is a being having a form like the form of the children of Adam; he never descended except that he was with Jibril, and they are many, and they are angels. This is a weak view, for no chain supports it. az-Zajjaj said: the Spirit is that by which hearts live, from Allah's guidance to them.

Abu Muhammad, the Qadi, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is a good view, and it seems the expression is by way of analogy and comparison: that this which He commanded the prophets to warn people of, namely the call to monotheism, is, by comparison with the commands regarding actions and acts of worship, like the spirit to the body. Do you not see His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Is one who was dead and We gave him life and made for him a light﴾ [al-An'am: 122]? And "min" (of) in this verse, on this interpretation which we have assumed, is partitive; and on the other views it is explanatory of the genus. The "min" in His saying: ﴿upon whom He wills﴾ is for the prophets. The "an" (that) is in the position of the genitive as an apposition to "al-Ruh," and it may be in the position of the accusative by dropping the preposition, on the reckoning of "bi-an andharu" (that they warn), and it may be interpretive, in the sense of "i.e." Al-A'mash read "li-yundhiru" (so that they warn). Warning is fitting here even though the wording contains no explicit fear, inasmuch as those who were to be warned were disbelievers in the divinity; so within the command to them there is a place of fear, and within the announcement of the oneness there is a prohibition of what they were upon and a threat.

Then He, exalted is He, mentioned what is said to the prophets by revelation in meaning, and did not mention it in its exact wording, for if He had mentioned it in wording he would have said: "that there is no god but Allah." But He mentioned it in its meaning; and this is common in all sayings when they are reported: they may be reported in their exact wording, or reported in meaning only.

His saying, exalted is He: "He created the heavens and the earth" is a sign calling attention to the power of Allah, exalted is He. His saying "in truth" means: with what is due and fitting; for these indicate attributes that make it right for the one to whom they belong to create, originate, and restore: they are life, knowledge, power, and effective will, unlike their partners, to whom none of the attributes of lordship are fitting. Al-A'mash read with an added fa': "fa-ta'ala."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He created man from a drop of semen﴾: "man" is meant as the genus, and He took for him the two extremes so that the distance between them might appear to him through the power of Allah. It was narrated that the verse was revealed concerning the saying of Ubayy ibn Khalaf: "Who will give life to bones when they are decayed?" His saying "adversary" (khasim) may mean the disbelievers who dispute about Allah and argue about His oneness and His law; this was mentioned by Ibn Salam from al-Hasan al-Basri; and it may (p-328) mean something more general than this, on the ground that the verse enumerates the blessing of intellect and speech upon mankind; and it appears that when this is established in the disputation of the disbelievers, a threat of some kind is added to the lesson.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 16, verse 1–4:

(p-324) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Tafsir (exegesis) of Surat an-Nahl

This surah was called "the Surah of Blessings" because of what Allah enumerates in it of His blessings upon His servants. It is Meccan, except for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you punish, then punish with the like of that with which you were punished﴾ [an-Nahl: 126], the verse which was revealed in Medina concerning the mutilation of Hamza, may Allah be pleased with him, and the slain of Uhud; and except for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And be patient, and your patience is not but by Allah﴾ [an-Nahl: 127]; and except for His saying: ﴿Then indeed your Lord, for those who emigrated﴾ [an-Nahl: 110], the verse; as for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who emigrated for Allah after they had been wronged﴾ [an-Nahl: 41], it is Meccan, concerning the emigration to Abyssinia.

His saying, mighty and majestic is He:

﴿The command of Allah has come, so do not seek to hasten it. Exalted is He above what they associate.﴾ ﴿He sends down the angels with the Spirit, by His command, upon whom He wills of His servants: "Warn that there is no god but Me, so fear Me."﴾ ﴿He created the heavens and the earth in truth. Exalted is He above what they associate.﴾ ﴿He created man from a drop of semen, and then he is an open adversary.﴾

It has been narrated that when Jibril, peace be upon him, recited in the recitation of the revelation: ﴿The command of Allah has come﴾, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) leapt up standing, and when he said: ﴿so do not seek to hasten it﴾, he calmed down. As for His saying: ﴿the command of Allah﴾, most of the exegetes said concerning it: it means the Resurrection, and in it is a threat for the disbelievers. (p-325) It was also said: what is meant is the victory of Muhammad (ﷺ). It was said: what is meant is the punishment of the disbelievers of Mecca by the killing of Muhammad, peace be upon him, by them and his dominance over them; Naqqash mentioned something similar from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father. It was also said: what is meant is the obligations of Allah and His rulings upon His servants and His law for them; this is the saying of ad-Dahhak. But this is far-fetched because of His saying: ﴿so do not seek to hasten it﴾, for we know of no hastening except three: two of them are for the disbelievers, in the Resurrection and in the punishment, and the third is for the believers, in victory and the manifestation of Islam. His saying "has come" (atā), according to this view, is an announcement of a coming that will come, and this is valid by way of emphasis: when the report is true, one emphasizes the future by expressing it in the form of the past, i.e., as if, because of its clarity and the certainty of it, it has already occurred; and this is fitting in the report of Allah, blessed and exalted, because of the truthfulness of its occurrence.

Some people said: "atā" means "qaruba" (has drawn near), and this is similar to what I said. In my view, speaking this way is permissible only for one who knows the indicator of emphasis and understands the figurative usage; but if the addressee does not understand the indicator, then it is not permissible to put the past in place of the future, because that corrupts the report and makes it false. It is permitted in the conditional only because the indicator is clear, with "an" (that). Whoever said: "the command is the Resurrection" said: His saying: ﴿so do not seek to hasten it﴾ is a rebuttal of those who say: ﴿Hasten to us our portion﴾ [Sad: 16] and similar, of the punishment; or addressed to the believers who were impatient for victory, according to the reading of one who reads with the ta' (t) — and this is the reading of the majority — addressed to the believers; or addressed to the disbelievers, meaning: say to them: ﴿so do not seek to hasten it﴾. Sa'id ibn Jubayr read with the ya' (y), referring to the absent polytheists. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "tushrikun" with ta' from above; all the rest read with ya'. At-Tabari preferred the reading with ta' from above in both places. Abu Hatim said: "yushrikun" with ya' from below in this and the one after it was read by al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn Nisah, al-Hasan, and Abu Raja'; 'Isa read the first with ta' from above and the second with ya' from below; and both with ta' from above were read by Abu al-'Aliya, Talha, al-A'mash, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman, Yahya ibn Wathhab, and al-Jahdari; and al-Asma'i narrated from Nafi' the ta' in the first.

His saying: ﴿subhanahu wa ta'ala﴾ means: as a declaration of His transcendence. At-Tabari narrated from Ibn Jurayj who said: When ﴿The command of Allah has come, so do not seek to hasten it﴾ was revealed, some men of the disbelievers said: "This one claims that the command of Allah has come; so let us refrain from what we are upon until we see." When they saw nothing, they returned, and then ﴿The reckoning of the people has drawn near, while they are in heedlessness, turning away﴾ [al-Anbiya': 1] was revealed, so they said the like of that; then they returned, and ﴿And if We delay the punishment from them until a counted nation, they will surely say: what holds it back?﴾ [Hud: 8] — the verse was revealed. Abu Bakr ibn Hafs said: When ﴿The command of Allah has come﴾ was revealed, they raised their heads, so ﴿so do not seek to hasten it﴾ was revealed. At-Tabari narrated from Abu Sadiq that he read: "O My servants, the command of Allah has come, so do not seek to hasten it." And "subhanahu" is in the accusative as a verbal noun, i.e., as a declaration of His transcendence.

Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read with a single zay, kasra, and a sukun on the nun. Ibn Abi 'Abla read with nun for majesty and a doubled zay. Qatada read with nun and a single zay with sukun on the nun. In this and the one before it there is much irregularity. Abu Bakr narrated from 'Asim "tanazzala" with a damma on the ta', fath on the nun and zay, doubled, and raising "al-malaikatu" as an unnamed agent; this is the reading of al-A'mash. al-Jahdari read with ya' damma, sukun on the nun, and fath on the zay. al-Hasan, Abu al-'Aliya, 'Asim, al-Jahdari, and al-A'raj read with fath on the ta' and raising "al-malaikatu" as the subject; al-Mufaddal narrated it from 'Asim. And "al-malaikata" here is Jibril, peace be upon him.

Qatada said: with mercy and revelation. ar-Rabi' ibn Anas said: every word of Allah is a spirit, and from it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We have revealed to you a spirit from Our command﴾ [ash-Shura: 52]. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 16, verses 5–9:

His saying, mighty and majestic is He:

﴿And the cattle He created for you; in them is warmth and benefits, and from them you eat.﴾ ﴿And for you in them is beauty when you bring them home at evening and when you send them forth to pasture.﴾ ﴿And they carry your loads to a land you could not reach except with great hardship to yourselves. Indeed, your Lord is Kind and Merciful.﴾ ﴿And horses, mules, and donkeys, for you to ride and as adornment. And He creates what you do not know.﴾ ﴿And upon Allah is the direction of the way, and there is deviant [of it]. And if He had willed, He would have guided you all.﴾

"Al-an'am" (cattle): camels, cows, and sheep. It is most commonly said "ni'am" and "an'am" for camels, and it is used as a collective noun; it is not said of sheep in the singular. Its being in the accusative is either by coordination with "al-insan" (man), or by an implied verb, and the latter is the more likely.

"Al-difʾ" (warmth): heating and the removal of cold by means of coverings. Al-Nahhas reported from al-Umawi that he said: "Al-difʾ, in the language of some people, is the breeding of camels." Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "The offspring of every thing." The first meaning is the correct one. Al-Zuhri and Abu Ja'far recited it as "diffun," with the fa' vowelled with a damma, shadda, and tanwin.

"Al-manafi'" (benefits): their milk and what is made from it, their fats, their tilling (with them) and drawing water by them, and other things. Then he mentioned "eating," which is from all of them.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And for you in them is beauty﴾ means in appearance. ﴿When you bring them home﴾ means when you return them at the time of evening to their dwellings, so they come back full-bellied with udders filled. "Tuslihun" (you send them forth) means you take them out in the morning to pasture. You say "sarahtu al-sa'ima" (I sent forth the grazing animal) when you let it go to graze, so it "sarahat" (grazed); like "raja'tuhu" (I returned it), "raja'a" (it returned). This beauty belongs to its owner and to those who love him, and to those who envy him. This meaning is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Wealth and children are the adornment of the life of this world﴾ [al-Kahf: 46]. 'Ikrimah and al-Dahhak recited: "Hina ma turihun wa hinan tuslihun" (when you bring them home and at times you send them forth), and a group recited: "Hinan turihun" (at times you bring them home).

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

These readings are weak, and I suspect them to be a copyist's error (tashif).

"Al-athqal" (loads): goods and belongings. It is said that what is meant here is bodies, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the earth brings forth its burdens﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 2], i.e., the children of Adam. The wording allows both meanings. Al-Naqqash said: From this, mankind and jinn are called "al-thaqalan" (the two burdens). His saying: ﴿To a land﴾ means to whatever land you head toward, according to the varying purposes of people. 'Ikrimah, Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: What is meant is Makkah, and in the verse, on this view, there is an exhortation to Hajj.

"Al-shiqq" (hardship): difficulty. From it is the saying of the poet:

"And one with camels who herds them, who is for him, weary and persistent in their hardship."

That is: from their hardship. It is said of it: "shiqq" and "shaqq," meaning hardship. Abu Ja'far al-Qari', 'Amr ibn Maymun, Ibn Arqam, Mujahid, and al-A'raj recited "bi-shaqqi" with a fatha on the shin; and it is related from Nafi' and Abu 'Amr. Al-Farra' held that the meaning of ﴿bi-shiqqi al-anfus﴾ is "by the loss of half of them," as if they had melted from fatigue and weariness, just as one says to a man: "You cannot do such-and-such except by the loss of most of your self and a piece of your liver," and similar figurative expressions. Those who vowelled the shin with a fatha held it to be a verbal noun of "shaqqa yashuqqu." Then Allah made obligatory His kindness and mercy in these blessings, which removed hardships and lifted burdens.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And horses, mules, and donkeys﴾ is a coordination, i.e., and He created the horses. Ibn Abi 'Abla recited "wal-khayla wal-bighala wal-hamira" with ḍamma on all of them. Horses were called "khayl" because of their proud gait (ikhtiyal fi al-mishya), as a Bedouin explained to Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala'. His saying "wa-zinatan" is in the accusative by an implied verb whose estimate is "and We made it an adornment." Abu 'Iyad recited "li-tarkabuha zinatan" without the waw, and the accusative then is a circumstantial state (hal) from the pronoun in "tarkabuha." His saying: ﴿And He creates what you do not know﴾ is a general lesson in the accusative: the creatures of Allah, from animals and other things, are not encompassed in knowledge by any human; rather, what is hidden from him is greater than what is known. It has been reported that Allah created a thousand kinds of animals, four hundred of them on land, and scattered their like in the sea, and added two hundred there which are not on land.

Whoever specified something in the interpretation of this verse, such as the saying of one who said: "the moth of clothes" and other things, does so only by way of example, not that what he mentioned is the intended meaning in itself. Al-Tabari said: ﴿What you do not know﴾ is what Allah has prepared in Paradise for its people and in Hell for its people, which no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived. Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, and those who followed his position, used this verse as an argument for disliking, or prohibiting according to the difference of opinion on this matter, the eating of the flesh of horses, mules, and donkeys. Al-Tabari reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: Ibn Jubayr said: Ibn 'Abbas was asked about the flesh of horses, mules, and donkeys, and he disliked it, arguing from this verse, and said: "Allah made the cattle for eating and these for riding." Al-Hakam ibn 'Uyayna used to say: horses, mules, and donkeys are forbidden in the Book of Allah, the Exalted, and he cited this verse as proof. This argument is not considered binding by a group of scholars, who said: Allah, mighty and majestic, mentioned the greatness of the benefits of cattle, and mentioned the greatness of the benefits of these and their most important aspects; and that does not necessitate that what was mentioned for these does not include these. Al-Tabari said: In their consensus on the permissibility of riding what is mentioned for eating, there is evidence for the permissibility of eating what is mentioned for riding.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

On this there is room for debate. The flesh of horses is lawful according to many scholars, and the permissibility of eating it is supported by the hadith of Asma' bint Abi Bakr, may Allah be pleased with them both, and the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah: "We used to eat horses in the time of the Prophet ﷺ." Mules and donkeys are disliked according to the majority, and this is the verified position of Malik, may Allah have mercy on him. The argument of those who attached horses to mules and donkeys in disliking is analogy, since they resemble each other and differ from cattle in that they do not chew the cud, they have hooves, they have no multiple stomachs, and they interbreed, as mules are between horses and donkeys. This is from the perspective of reasoning; as for the perspective of the law, they are mentioned together in this verse, and zakat is dropped for them.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And upon Allah is the direction of the way﴾ the verse. This is also among the most excellent blessings of Allah, blessed and exalted is He: that is, upon Allah is the straightening and clarifying of the path of guidance, and that is by setting up proofs and sending messengers; and this is the view of the commentators. It is possible that the meaning is: whoever takes the straight path, upon Allah is His mercy, His bounty, and His way, and to Him is his destination. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿This is a straight path﴾ [Al 'Imran: 51], and the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "And evil is not attributed to You," i.e., it does not lead to Your mercy. "A direct path" means clear, straight, and near; from it is the saying of the rajiz poet: "So he turned away from the way of the direct path."

The "al" in "al-sabil" (the way) is for a specific reference, namely the way of the Law, and it is not for the genus; had it been for the genus, there would not be any deviant in it.

His saying: ﴿And there is deviant [of it]﴾ means the ways of the Jews, the Christians, and others such as the idol-worshippers. The pronoun in "minha" refers to the ways implied by the meaning of the verse, as if He had said: "And among the ways is a deviant one." It is returned to them although they were not previously mentioned, because the word "al-sabil" implies them in meaning. It is also possible that the pronoun in "minha" refers to the way of the Law previously mentioned, and "min" is partitive, and the meaning is the sects of error from the community of Muhammad ﷺ, as if He had said: "And among the offshoots of the road on this way and its branches is a deviant one."

His saying: ﴿And if He had willed, He would have guided you all﴾ means: He would have created guidance in the hearts of all of you, and none would have gone astray. Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is: if He had willed, He would have presented to you a sign that compels you to faith and guidance.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is an evil statement belonging to the people of innovation who hold that Allah does not create the actions of servants. Al-Zajjaj did not intend it, and he fell into it, may Allah have mercy on him, without intent. In the codex of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud it reads: "wa-minkum ja'ir" (and among you is a deviant one), and 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, recited: "wa-minkum ja'ir." And "al-sabil" is used both as masculine and feminine.

You say "sarahtu al-sa'ima" (I sent forth the grazing animal) when you let it go to graze, so it "sarahat" (grazed); like "raja'tuhu" (I returned it), "raja'a" (it returned). This beauty belongs to its owner and to those who love him, and to those who envy him. This meaning is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Wealth and children are the adornment of the life of this world﴾ [al-Kahf: 46]. 'Ikrimah and al-Dahhak recited: "Hina ma turihun wa hinan tuslihun" (when you bring them home and at times you send them forth), and a group recited: "Hinan turihun" (at times you bring them home).

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

These readings are weak, and I suspect them to be a copyist's error (tashif).

"Al-athqal" (loads): goods and belongings. It is said that what is meant here is bodies, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the earth brings forth its burdens﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 2], i.e., the children of Adam. The wording allows both meanings. Al-Naqqash said: From this, mankind and jinn are called "al-thaqalan" (the two burdens). His saying: ﴿To a land﴾ means to whatever land you head toward, according to the varying purposes of people. 'Ikrimah, Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: What is meant is Makkah, and in the verse, on this view, there is an exhortation to Hajj.

"Al-shiqq" (hardship): difficulty. From it is the saying of the poet:

"And one with camels who herds them, who is for him, weary and persistent in their hardship."

That is: from their hardship. It is said of it: "shiqq" and "shaqq," meaning hardship. Abu Ja'far al-Qari', 'Amr ibn Maymun, Ibn Arqam, Mujahid, and al-A'raj recited "bi-shaqqi" with a fatha on the shin; and it is related from Nafi' and Abu 'Amr. Al-Farra' held that the meaning of ﴿bi-shiqqi al-anfus﴾ is "by the loss of half of them," as if they had melted from fatigue and weariness, just as one says to a man: "You cannot do such-and-such except by the loss of most of your self and a piece of your liver," and similar figurative expressions. Those who vowelled the shin with a fatha held it to be a verbal noun of "shaqqa yashuqqu." Then Allah made obligatory His kindness and mercy in these blessings, which removed hardships and lifted burdens.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And horses, mules, and donkeys﴾ is a coordination, i.e., and He created the horses. Ibn Abi 'Abla recited "wal-khayla wal-bighala wal-hamira" with ḍamma on all of them. Horses were called "khayl" because of their proud gait (ikhtiyal fi al-mishya), as a Bedouin explained to Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala'. His saying "wa-zinatan" is in the accusative by an implied verb whose estimate is "and We made it an adornment." Abu 'Iyad recited "li-tarkabuha zinatan" without the waw, and the accusative then is a circumstantial state (hal) from the pronoun in "tarkabuha." His saying: ﴿And He creates what you do not know﴾ is a general lesson in the accusative: the creatures of Allah, from animals and other things, are not encompassed in knowledge by any human; rather, what is hidden from him is greater than what is known. It has been reported that Allah created a thousand kinds of animals, four hundred of them on land, and scattered their like in the sea, and added two hundred there which are not on land.

Whoever specified something in the interpretation of this verse, such as the saying of one who said: "the moth of clothes" and other things, does so only by way of example, not that what he mentioned is the intended meaning in itself. Al-Tabari said: ﴿What you do not know﴾ is what Allah has prepared in Paradise for its people and in Hell for its people, which no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived. Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, and those who followed his position, used this verse as an argument for disliking, or prohibiting according to the difference of opinion on this matter, the eating of the flesh of horses, mules, and donkeys. Al-Tabari reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: Ibn Jubayr said: Ibn 'Abbas was asked about the flesh of horses, mules, and donkeys, and he disliked it, arguing from this verse, and said: "Allah made the cattle for eating and these for riding." Al-Hakam ibn 'Uyayna used to say: horses, mules, and donkeys are forbidden in the Book of Allah, the Exalted, and he cited this verse as proof. This argument is not considered binding by a group of scholars, who said: Allah, mighty and majestic, mentioned the greatness of the benefits of cattle, and mentioned the greatness of the benefits of these and their most important aspects; and that does not necessitate that what was mentioned for these does not include these. Al-Tabari said: In their consensus on the permissibility of riding what is mentioned for eating, there is evidence for the permissibility of eating what is mentioned for riding.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

On this there is room for debate. The flesh of horses is lawful according to many scholars, and the permissibility of eating it is supported by the hadith of Asma' bint Abi Bakr, may Allah be pleased with them both, and the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah: "We used to eat horses in the time of the Prophet ﷺ." Mules and donkeys are disliked according to the majority, and this is the verified position of Malik, may Allah have mercy on him. The argument of those who attached horses to mules and donkeys in disliking is analogy, since they resemble each other and differ from cattle in that they do not chew the cud, they have hooves, they have no multiple stomachs, and they interbreed, as mules are between horses and donkeys. This is from the perspective of reasoning; as for the perspective of the law, they are mentioned together in this verse, and zakat is dropped for them.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And upon Allah is the direction of the way﴾ the verse. This is also among the most excellent blessings of Allah, blessed and exalted is He: that is, upon Allah is the straightening and clarifying of the path of guidance, and that is by setting up proofs and sending messengers; and this is the view of the commentators. It is possible that the meaning is: whoever takes the straight path, upon Allah is His mercy, His bounty, and His way, and to Him is his destination. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿This is a straight path﴾ [Al 'Imran: 51], and the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "And evil is not attributed to You," i.e., it does not lead to Your mercy. "A direct path" means clear, straight, and near; from it is the saying of the rajiz poet: "So he turned away from the way of the direct path."

The "al" in "al-sabil" (the way) is for a specific reference, namely the way of the Law, and it is not for the genus; had it been for the genus, there would not be any deviant in it.

His saying: ﴿And there is deviant [of it]﴾ means the ways of the Jews, the Christians, and others such as the idol-worshippers. The pronoun in "minha" refers to the ways implied by the meaning of the verse, as if He had said: "And among the ways is a deviant one." It is returned to them although they were not previously mentioned, because the word "al-sabil" implies them in meaning. It is also possible that the pronoun in "minha" refers to the way of the Law previously mentioned, and "min" is partitive, and the meaning is the sects of error from the community of Muhammad ﷺ, as if He had said: "And among the offshoots of the road on this way and its branches is a deviant one."

His saying: ﴿And if He had willed, He would have guided you all﴾ means: He would have created guidance in the hearts of all of you, and none would have gone astray. Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is: if He had willed, He would have presented to you a sign that compels you to faith and guidance.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is an evil statement belonging to the people of innovation who hold that Allah does not create the actions of servants. Al-Zajjaj did not intend it, and he fell into it, may Allah have mercy on him, without intent. In the codex of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud it reads: "wa-minkum ja'ir" (and among you is a deviant one), and 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, recited: "wa-minkum ja'ir." And "al-sabil" is used both as masculine and feminine.

﴿He is the One who sent down water from the sky for you; from it is drink, and from it are trees in which you pasture your livestock.﴾ ﴿With it He causes to grow for you crops, olives, date palms, grapes, and every kind of fruit. Indeed, in that is a sign for a people who give thought.﴾ ﴿He subjected for you the night and the day, the sun and the moon, and the stars are subjected by His command. Indeed, in that are signs for a people who use reason.﴾

This is an enumeration of the blessing of Allah in the rain. His saying ﴿and from it are trees﴾ means: from it they come into being gradually [p. 333], since it waters the earth and thereby the trees grow from this watering. This is a figurative usage (tajawwuz), as the poet said:

"The humps of camels in its clouds"

And as another poet called the herbage "sky" in his saying:

"When the sky descends upon the land of a people, / we graze it, even if they are angry."

Abu Ishaq said: Everything that grows on the earth is called shajar (tree). ʿIkrima said: "Do not eat the price of the shajar, for it is forbidden (musht), meaning the pasture (kala)."

The word tusimun means: you pasture your livestock. Its sawm (grazing) is from ra'y (pasturing), and you send them out to graze. Livestock are called al-sa'ima (free-grazing). The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "On free-grazing sheep there is zakat." It is said: "asama al-rajul mashiyatahu isamatan" when he released his livestock to graze, and "sawwamaha" also, and then they grazed. From this is the saying of al-A'sha:

"The people walked with the tent-poles to the weakened (camels), / and the one pasturing his herd was weary of where to drive them."

And from it is the saying of another:

"Like the son of Bazi'a, or like another resembling him— / woe to you, son of the one who pastures camels!"

That is: the one who tends camels. Those who interpret the text explained "tusimun" as "tarʿawn" (you pasture).

Al-Jumhur (the majority of readers) read "yunbitu" with the letter ya', meaning: Allah causes to grow. It is said: "nabata al-shajaru" and "anbatahu Allah" (Allah caused it to grow). It is also said: "anbata al-shajaru" with the same meaning as "nabata." Al-Asmaʿi used to reject this and would accuse Zuhayr's ode in which it says:

"Until, when the herbage had sprouted..."

Abu Bakr, from ʿAsim, read "nunbitu" with the nun of majesty (nun al-ʿazama). Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, specifically mentioned these four because they are the noblest of what grows and the most comprehensive in benefits. Then He generalized by saying ﴿and every kind of fruit﴾ [an-Nahl: 69]. Then He referred the matter to reflection on the variations of plants and trees, which is a place of lesson in their colors, the consistency of their creation, and the harmony of their subtle forms. Glory be to the Creator, the Mighty.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He subjected for you the night and the day...﴾, the verse. Al-Jumhur read "sakhkhara" as governing all that was mentioned [p. 335], and read "musakhkharat" in the accusative as an emphatic circumstantial clause (al-hal al-muʾakkada, a qualifying state that reinforces the main statement), as in the saying of Allah: ﴿He is the truth, confirming...﴾ [Fatir: 31], and as the poet said:

"I am the son of Dara, my lineage known through her."

And similar to this. Ibn ʿAmir read "wa-al-shamsu wa-al-qamaru wa-al-nujumu musakhkharatun" with the nominative for all of it. Hafs, from ʿAsim, read "wa-al-nujumu musakhkharatun" in the nominative and put the preceding items in the accusative. The meaning of this verse is that these created things are subjected in an order by which human benefit continues: from the night, tranquility and livelihood, and other things from the day. As for the benefits of the sun and the moon, they are too many to count. As for the stars, they are guidance. For this reason they are counted among the blessings bestowed upon the children of Adam. Among the blessing of them is their light at times. Al-Zajjaj said: and by them one knows the number of years and the calculation.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

"In this there is room for consideration."

Ibn Masʿud, al-Aʿmash, and Talha ibn Musarrif read "wa-al-riyahu musakhkharatun" in place of "wa-al-nujumi." Then He said: ﴿Indeed, in that are signs...﴾ in the plural because of the greatness of the matter, since each of the things mentioned is a sign in itself, not sharing with the other. He said in the previous verse: "la-ayatin" (a sign) because one single thing encompasses those four, namely vegetation. Likewise in the mention of what He created in variety by its diversity. Also, it has the meaning of "ayat" (signs), with the singular used to mean the plural.

(p. 336) The words of the Exalted: ﴿And what He has created for you on the earth, of varying colors. Indeed, in that is a sign for a people who are mindful.﴾ ﴿And it is He who subjected the sea, that you may eat from it fresh meat and extract from it ornaments which you wear. And you see the ships plowing through it, and that you may seek of His bounty, and perhaps you will be grateful.﴾ ﴿And He cast into the earth firmly set mountains, lest it should shake with you, and rivers and roads, that you may be guided.﴾

(p. 336) ﴿And what He has created for you on the earth﴾ means: He scattered and spread out. The word "dhurriyya" (offspring) derives from this root according to one of the opinions on its etymology. His words "ālwānuhu" (its colors) mean its kinds, as you say: "These are varieties of fruit and of food." Since these scattered things on the earth are of different kinds, they are counted among the blessings, and the benefit derived from them appears in many ways. That benefit does not appear merely from their being colored red, yellow, and otherwise. It is possible that the reference to the differences of colors, red and yellow, is intended, but the first is clearer.

His exalted words: ﴿And it is He who subjected the sea﴾ and so on, are an enumeration of Allah's blessings. The subjection of the sea is the enabling of humans to dispose of it and its being made submissive for riding, for transporting provisions, and for other purposes.

"Al-baḥr" (the sea) is abundant water, whether salty or fresh; all of it is called a sea. Here "al-baḥr" is a generic noun. If that is so, then from it comes the eating of fresh meat, and from it comes the extraction of ornaments. The eating of meat occurs from both its salty and its fresh water, while the extraction of ornaments, as far as is known, comes only from salt water. Among what is known of this are pearls, coral, mother-of-pearl, and sea wool. Pearls are sometimes found in fresh water, but they are rarely worn; rather, they are used for medicine. It is also said that there is a sea-type in emerald. The poet al-Hudhalī was faulted for his statement describing a pearl:

"So she brought it from a pearl of Lataymiyya,
upon whose face the water of the Euphrates surges."

He made it from sweet water.

The eminent judge Abū Muḥammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

Consider his saying "yamūju" (surges): he described its luster and its watery quality, comparing it to the water of the Euphrates, and did not aim at the point for which he was faulted.

"Al-laḥm al-ṭarī" (fresh meat) is fish. "Al-ḥilya" (ornament) is what is worn. "Al-fulk" (ships) here is a plural. "Mawākhir" is the plural of "mākhira." "Al-makhr" in the language is the sound that comes from the blowing of the wind on something that is cut through, or that accompanies water in general. From this it follows that "al-makhr" can be from the wind, and can be from a ship and the like. In this verse it refers to ships. It is said of clouds, "banātu makhr" (daughters of the makhr), by way of comparison, because in their movement there is that sound which comes from the wind, and the water in the clouds and their motion resembles the state of the sea. However, al-Zajjāj said: "Banāt al-baḥr" (daughters of the sea) are white clouds with no water in them. Some linguists said: "Al-makhr" in Arabic speech means cutting; it is said "makhara al-māʾ al-arḍ" (the water cut through the earth). Thus it is clear that the word can be applied to ships as "mawākhir." Others said: "Mawākhir" means it moves forward and back with one wind. These statements are not an explanation of the word itself; rather, they meant that the ships are "mawākhir" in these states, so they specified these states, because they are the place of the enumerated blessings. The mere fact that a ship cuts through water is not a blessing in itself; the blessing lies in its cutting through in these states, in trade, in travel on it, and in what Allah grants through it of profits and favors. Al-Ṭabarī said: "Al-makhr" in the language is the sound of the blowing of the wind, and he did not restrict it to being in water. He said that among its uses is the saying of Wāṣil, the client of Abū ʿUyayna: "If one of you wants to urinate, let him take the makhr of the wind," meaning: let him observe its sound among bodies, from where it blows, so that he avoids facing it, lest it return his urine upon him.

His saying: ﴿and that you may seek﴾ (wa-li-tabtaghū) is conjoined to His saying "to eat" (ta'kulū). This is the mention of a blessing that has countless details. It includes riding the sea for trade and for seeking profits. These are three causes of the subjection of the sea.

His exalted words: ﴿And He cast into the earth﴾ and so on. The interpreters said: "Alqā" (cast) means "khalaqa" (created) and "ja'ala" (made).

The eminent judge Abū Muḥammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

In my view it is more specific than "khalaqa" and "ja'ala." This is because "alqā" implies that Allah brought the mountains into existence not from the earth, but by His power and invention. This view is supported by what is narrated in the stories from al-Ḥasan, from Qays ibn ʿIbād, that when Allah created the earth, it began to shake, so the angels said: "This will not let anyone remain upon its back." **Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 16, verses 16–21:**

Allah the Mighty and Majestic says:

﴿And landmarks; and by the star they are guided.﴾ ﴿Is He who creates like one who does not create? Will you not then be mindful?﴾ ﴿And if you tried to count the favour of Allah, you could not enumerate it. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ ﴿And Allah knows what you conceal and what you declare.﴾ ﴿And those whom they invoke besides Allah create nothing, while they themselves are created.﴾ ﴿They are dead, not living, and they do not know when they will be resurrected.﴾

"عَلاماتٍ" (ʿalāmāt, landmarks) is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning: He made these things so that you may take heed by them. "وعلامات" means a lesson and an indication in every course of travel, for one is guided by mountains, rivers and roads. People differed over the meaning of "وَعَلامَاتٍ." In my view the most evident meaning is what I have mentioned. Ibn al-Kalbi said: the landmarks are the mountains. Ibrahim al-Nakhaʿi and Mujahid said: the landmarks are the stars; some of them are called landmarks, and by some of them one is guided. Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: the landmarks are the markers of roads by day, and the stars are the guidance by night.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The correct view, when we take the statement as not dependent on what precedes it, is that the word is general and includes this and other things, for everything that indicates something and by which it is known is an ʿalāma (sign). The best of the sayings mentioned is the saying of Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, because it is general in meaning, so reflect on it. My father, may Allah have mercy on him, narrated to me that he heard some of the people of knowledge in the East say: In the Indian Ocean, which runs from Yemen to India, there are long, thin fish resembling snakes in their colours, movement and twisting, and they are called ʿalāmāt, because they are a sign of arrival at the land of India and an indication of safety and reaching India, given the length and difficulty of that sea. Some people said that these are what Allah intended in this verse. My father, may Allah be pleased with him, said: I am among those who have witnessed and seen those signs in the aforementioned sea, and a large number of them related to me.

The majority of readers read "وَبِالنَّجْمِ" (wa-bi-l-najm, "and by the star") as a noun of genus (ism jins). Yahya ibn Wathhab read "وَبِالنَّجْمِ" with a damma on the nūn and sukūn on the jīm, as a lightening of its damma. Al-Hasan read it with the damma, as a plural, like saqf / suqf and rahn / ruhun. It is possible that it means the stars, with the wāw dropped.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

In my view this is a weak explanation.

Al-Farraʾ said: what is meant is the Pole Star (al-Jady) and the two Guards (al-Farqadan). Others said: what is meant is the Pole that does not move. Others said something other than this, and some said it is a noun of genus. This last is the correct view.

Then Allah established for them the distinction between one who creates things and originates them and one who has no power over any of that. He expressed the idols with "مَن" (man, "one who") for two reasons. The first is that the verse includes a refutation of everyone who worshipped other than Allah, and groups have worshipped those who are referred to by "مَن." The second is that the expression, in regard to the idols, follows the belief of the disbelievers that they have influence and actions. Then He rebuked them with His saying: ﴿Will you not then be mindful?﴾

Allah's saying: ﴿And if you tried to count the favour of Allah, you could not enumerate it﴾ means: if you attempted to count it, number by number, so that nothing of it would be left out, you would not be able to do so, and it would not be possible for you to enumerate it, for it is in every moment of your conditions. "النعمة" (al-niʿma, "the favour") here is singular, but intended as a plural. Given the inability to count the favours of Allah, Blessed and Exalted, it follows that the one who gives thanks for them falls short of some of them. Therefore the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, meaning: for your shortcoming in giving thanks for all of them. Al-Tabari took this approach. It is objected to him that the favour of Allah, in the servant's saying "All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds," with its conditions of intention and obedience, equals all the favours; but where is its saying with its conditions? The address "﴿And if you tried to count the favour of Allah, you could not enumerate it﴾" is general to all people.

His saying: ﴿And Allah knows what you conceal and what you declare﴾ is connected to what precedes it, meaning: Indeed Allah is Forgiving of your shortcoming in giving thanks for what you cannot count of the favours of Allah, and Allah Exalted knows your secret and your open speech, which relieves you of the obligation to thank for every single favour. This is according to the reading of the one who reads "تُسِرُّونَ" (tusirrūna, "you conceal") with the tāʾ, addressing the believers. The majority of readers read "تُسِرُّونَ" with the tāʾ at the beginning, and "وَتُعْلِنُونَ" (tuʿlinūna, "and you declare") and "تَدْعُونَ" (tadʿūna, "you invoke") likewise; this is the reading of al-Aʿraj, Shayba, Abu Jaʿfar and Mujahid, with the meaning: Say, O Muhammad, to the disbelievers. ʿĀṣim read "تُسِرُّونَ" and "تُعْلِنُونَ" with the tāʾ at the beginning, and "يَدْعُونَ" (yadʿūna, "they invoke") with the yāʾ at the beginning, referring to the disbelievers in the third person; this is the reading of al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan. Hubayra narrated from Hafs from ʿĀṣim that all of these are with the yāʾ, in the third person for the disbelievers. It is narrated from al-Kisāʾi and Abu Bakr from ʿĀṣim that all of these are with the tāʾ at the beginning. Al-Aʿmash and the companions of ʿAbd Allah read: "يَعْلَمُ الَّذِي تُبْدُونَ وَمَا تَكْتُمُونَ" (yaʿlamu alladhī tubdūna wa-mā taktumūn) and "تَدْعُونَ" with the tāʾ at the beginning in all three. Talha read: "مَا تُخْفُونَ وَمَا تُعْلِنُونَ" (mā tukhfūna wa-mā tuʿlinūn) and "تَدْعُونَ" with the tāʾ at the beginning in all three. "يَدْعُونَ" (yadʿūna) means they call upon it as a god. He expressed the idols with "الَّذِينَ" (alladhīna, "those who") according to what we have already mentioned, that this includes the idols, those worshipped besides Allah, and others.

Allah's saying: ﴿They create nothing, while they themselves are created﴾ is the most comprehensive expression concerning their state with respect to lordship (rubūbiyya). Muhammad al-Yamani read: "وَالَّذِينَ يُدْعَوْنَ" (wa-alladhīna yudʿawna) with a damma on the yāʾ and a fatḥa on the ʿayn, in the passive voice, with the subject unnamed.

"أمْوَاتٌ" (amwāt, "dead") is meant to refer to those who are invoked besides Allah. It is in the nominative as the predicate of an implied inchoative subject, its estimate being: They are dead. It is also permissible that it be a predicate of "وَالَّذِينَ" (alladhīna), following a predicate in the phrase "لا يَخْلُقُونَ" (they create nothing). He described them with death figuratively; what is meant is that they never accepted life and were never characterised by it. According to the reading of the one who reads "وَالَّذِينَ يَدْعُونَ" with the yāʾ, referring to the disbelievers in the third person, it is permissible that by "الأمْوَات" (the dead) are meant the disbelievers whose pronoun is in "يَدْعُونَ." He likened them to the dead, not the living, in that they are astray and not guided. On this view, His saying ﴿and they do not know when they will be resurrected﴾ fits them. The resurrection (al-baʿth) here is the gathering from the graves. "أيَّانَ" (ayyāna, "when") is an adverb of time, indeclinable. Abu ʿAbd al-Rahman al-Sulami read "إيَّانَ" with a kasra on the hamza; both the fatḥa and the kasra in it are dialectal variants (lughatān).

A group said: ﴿and they do not know﴾, that is, the disbelievers, ﴿when they will be resurrected﴾; the two pronouns refer to them. Another group said: ﴿and they do not know﴾, that is, the idols, when the disbelievers will be resurrected. It is also possible that the two pronouns refer to the idols, as in the idiom: "I roused the sleeper from his sleep" when you awaken him, and "the archer launched his arrow" (baʿatha al-rāmī sahmahu). It is as if He described them with the utmost inertness: even if you sought to move them by movement, they would not perceive it. According to the interpretation of the one who takes the two pronouns as referring to the disbelievers, the speech should be understood as a warning, meaning: the disbelievers do not know when they will be raised to punishment. Had this meaning been expressed alone, describing them as not knowing when they will be resurrected would have had no particular point, for the angels, the prophets and the righteous are likewise ignorant of the time of resurrection. Some commentators mentioned that His saying ﴿when they will be resurrected﴾ is an adverbial complement of His saying: ﴿Your God is one God﴾ [al-Nahl: 22], and that the speech is complete at "﴿and they do not know﴾"; then He informed about the Day of Resurrection that God is one in it, and in this there is a threat.

Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: the landmarks are the markers of roads by day, and the stars are the guidance by night.

The best of the sayings mentioned is the saying of Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, because it is general in meaning, so reflect on it. My father, may Allah have mercy on him, narrated to me that he heard some of the people of knowledge in the East say: In the Indian Ocean, which runs from Yemen to India, there are long, thin fish resembling snakes in their colours, movement and twisting, and they are called ʿalāmāt, because they are a sign of arrival at the land of India and an indication of safety and reaching India, given the length and difficulty of that sea. Some people said that these are what Allah intended in this verse. My father, may Allah be pleased with him, said: I am among those who have witnessed and seen those signs in the aforementioned sea, and a large number of them related to me.

In my view this is a weak explanation.

Hubayra narrated from Hafs from ʿĀṣim that all of these are with the yāʾ, in the third person for the disbelievers. It is narrated from al-Kisāʾi and Abu Bakr from ʿĀṣim that all of these are with the tāʾ at the beginning. Al-Aʿmash and the companions of ʿAbd Allah read: "يَعْلَمُ الَّذِي تُبْدُونَ وَمَا تَكْتُمُونَ" (yaʿlamu alladhī tubdūna wa-mā taktumūn) and "تَدْعُونَ" with the tāʾ at the beginning in all three. The resurrection (al-baʿth) here is the gathering from the graves. "أيَّانَ" (ayyāna, "when") is an adverb of time, indeclinable. Abu ʿAbd al-Rahman al-Sulami read "إيَّانَ" with a kasra on the hamza; both the fatḥa and the kasra in it are dialectal variants (lughatān).

A group said: ﴿and they do not know﴾, that is, the disbelievers, ﴿when they will be resurrected﴾; the two pronouns refer to them. Another group said: ﴿and they do not know﴾, that is, the idols, when the disbelievers will be resurrected. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 16, verses 22–25:

The Most High said:

﴿Your God is one God. As for those who do not believe in the Hereafter, their hearts are denying, and they are arrogant.﴾ ﴿Undoubtedly, Allah knows what they conceal and what they reveal. Indeed, He does not love the arrogant.﴾ ﴿And when it is said to them, "What has your Lord sent down?" they say, "Tales of the ancients."﴾ ﴿That they may bear their burdens in full on the Day of Resurrection, and some of the burdens of those whom they mislead without knowledge. Unquestionably, evil is what they bear.﴾

Since the description of the idols has preceded, the true report of God's oneness has come. This is an address to all people, informing them that Allah, the Exalted, is one in a complete oneness, which needs no addition to complete it. Then He informed of the denial in the hearts of the disbelievers, that they believe in the divinity of other things, and that they are arrogant in refusing to abandon their belief in them and in discarding the way of their fathers in worshipping them. He described them as not believing in the Hereafter, because it is the strongest level of disbelief, namely combining denial of Allah, blessed and exalted is He, with denial of the Resurrection. This is because whoever truly believes in the Resurrection cannot possibly deny Allah, blessed and exalted is He.

As for His saying, ﴿Undoubtedly (lā jarama)﴾: a group of linguists rendered its meaning as "there is no doubt (lā budda)" and "there is no escape (lā maḥāla)." Another group said its meaning is "it is true that (ḥaqqa anna) Allah…" The position of Sibawayh is that "lā" is a negation of what preceded in the speech, and "jarama" means "it was required" or "it was due," and the position of al-Zajjaj is similar to this. However, according to both of their positions, "lā" is inseparable from "jarama"; the one does not part from the other. There are dialectal variants of "jarama," whose mention has already passed in the surah of Hud. Abu 'Ubayda recited:

"Fazara has surely incurred (it)"

and he said its meaning is: "it is due upon them and required that they be angry." According to the position of Sibawayh, "anna" is the agent governed by "jarama." The majority read "anna" with a fatḥa (opening vowel). 'Isa al-Thaqafi read "inna" with a kasra on the alif, as a new sentence (qaṭ'). Yahya ibn Sallam and al-Naqqash said: what is meant here by "what they conceal" is their consultation in the Dar al-Nadwa (the assembly house of Quraysh) about killing the Prophet (ﷺ). His saying, ﴿Indeed, He does not love the arrogant﴾, is general, covering both disbelievers and believers, each of whom takes his share of it. In a hadith: "He will not enter Paradise who has in his heart the weight of a mustard seed of arrogance," and in it: "Arrogance is rejecting the truth and looking down upon people." It is narrated from al-Hasan ibn 'Ali that he used to sit with the poor, speak with them, and then recite: ﴿Indeed, He does not love the arrogant﴾. It is also reported in a hadith: "Whoever of the believers prostrates to Allah one prostration, he has been cleared of arrogance."

As for His saying, ﴿And when it is said to them, "What has your Lord sent down?"﴾ and the rest of the verse: the pronoun in "lahum" refers to the disbelievers of Makkah. It is said that the occasion of the revelation was that al-Nadr ibn al-Harith travelled from Makkah to al-Hira and elsewhere, then came back to Makkah. He had acquired books of history, "Kalila wa Dimna" and the accounts of Isfandiyar and Rustam, and he used to say: "Muhammad only narrates the tales of the ancients, and my narration is more beautiful than his." As for His saying, "mā dhā" (what): it may be that "mā" is an interrogative and "dhā" means "alladhī" (which), and in "anzala" there is a returning pronoun. It may also be that "mā" and "dhā" are a single compound noun, as if he had said: "What thing?" Their saying, "tales of the ancients," is not an answer to the first question, because they did not mean that something was sent down, nor that something was completed as a revelation. Rather, they began the report by saying that this is the tales of the ancients. The actual answer to the question is the saying of the believers in the verse that follows: "good (khayran)." Their saying, "tales of the ancients," is only an answer in meaning. As for the answer to the question according to its wording, it is not so.

The lām in His saying, ﴿that they may bear﴾ (li-yaḥmilū), may be lām al-'āqiba (the lām of consequence), because they did not intend by their saying "tales of the ancients" that they would bear burdens. It may also be the pure lām of kay (purpose), meaning: He decreed this. It may also be the lām al-amr (the lām of command), meaning a binding decree upon them, and the humiliation that necessitates it for them. "Al-awzār" means the burdens. His saying, ﴿and some of﴾ (wa min), the "min" is for partition. This is because this misleading chief bears the full burden of his own sin, and he bears a burden of the sins of every misleader through him, and the burdens of those others are not diminished. His saying, ﴿without knowledge﴾ may mean the misleader himself, i.e., he misled without a proof that stood before him. It may also mean: without knowledge on the part of the imitators whom they mislead. Then Allah, the Exalted, began the report of the evil of what they bear for the Hereafter. Al-Tabari and others transmitted, in explanation of this verse, a hadith whose text is: "Whoever calls to misguidance and is followed, he bears a like burden of those who follow him, without their burdens being diminished in the least; and whoever calls to guidance and is followed, he has a like reward of their rewards, without their rewards being diminished in the least." The word "sā'a" (how evil) is a verb whose subject is "mā," and it does not need a complement (ṣila) here.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 16, verse 26–27:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Those before them had already schemed, so God came at their structures from their foundations, and the roof fell down upon them from above, and the punishment came upon them from where they did not perceive.﴾ ﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection He will disgrace them and say: "Where are My partners, for whose sake you used to oppose [the believers]?" Those who were given knowledge will say: "Indeed, disgrace and misfortune today are upon the disbelievers."﴾

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, and others among the exegetes said: the reference in ﴿those before them﴾ is to Nimrod, who built the tower (al-sarh) to ascend into the heaven, as he supposed. When he exceeded in his arrogance and in its height toward the sky, two farsakh according to what al-Naqqash related, God sent a wind against it and it demolished it, and its roof fell upon him and upon his followers. It was also said that Jibril, peace be upon him, demolished it with his wing and cast its top into the sea, and those who were below it were crushed. Another group said: what is meant by ﴿those before them﴾ is every disbeliever among the earlier nations who schemed and upon whom a punishment from God the Exalted descended. According to this view, His saying ﴿God came at their structures from their foundations﴾ up to the end of the verse is an illustration and a comparison, meaning: their situation is like the situation of one who was dealt with in this way. Another group said: what is meant by His saying ﴿the roof fell down upon them from above﴾ is: the punishment came to them from the direction of the sky.

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This tends toward riddle-like speech.

The meaning of His saying ﴿from above them﴾ is to remove the possibility of ambiguity in His saying ﴿the roof fell down upon them﴾, for you say: "His building collapsed upon so-and-so" when he was not beneath it, just as you say: "his goods were spoiled for him." And His saying "from above them" makes it necessary that they were beneath it.

His saying "God came" means: the command of God and His authority came. The majority recited "bunyanahum" (their structure), a group recited "binyatahum," Ja'far ibn Muhammad recited "baniyyatahum," and al-Dahhak recited "buyutahum" (their houses). The majority recited "al-saqf" (the roof) with a sukun on the qaf, a group recited it with a damma on it, which is a dialect form of it, al-A'raj recited with a damma on the sin and the qaf, and Mujahid recited with a damma on the sin and a sukun on the qaf.

His saying ﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection﴾ and the verse: in the preceding verse God mentioned the state of these schemers in this world; in this verse He mentions their state in the Hereafter. His saying "yukhzihim" (He will disgrace them) is a term encompassing all the calamities that descend upon them, and that returns to their being made to enter the Fire. This is similar to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Our Lord, indeed whoever You cause to enter the Fire, You have disgraced him﴾ [Al 'Imran: 192]. His saying ﴿Where are My partners﴾ is a rebuke to them, and He attributed them to Himself in addressing the disbelievers, meaning: according to your claim and your assertion. Abu 'Ali said: this is like what He said, Exalted is He, quoting: ﴿Taste it, indeed you are the mighty, the noble﴾ [al-Dukhan: 49], and like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O magician, call upon your Lord for us﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 49].

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Attributions are arranged, both in meaning and in what is spoken, by the subtlest of connections, and this is abundant in their speech. Among it is the saying of the poet:

When I say "lead me," he says, swearing by Allah an oath, "so that he may make you independent of me, this vessel of yours, all of it."

Here he attributed the vessel to the one who pours from it. The reading of al-Bazzi from Ibn Kathir was "shurakaya" with shortening of the "shuraka'" and fath on the ya; the majority recited with the long vowel and fath on the ya after the hamza; and a group recited with the long vowel and a sakin ya.

His saying "tushaqqun" (you oppose) means: you fight and dispute, i.e., you are in a split while the truth is in another split. The majority recited "tushaqqun" with fath on the nun; Nafi' alone recited it with kasra on it, and it is related from al-Hasan with a difference. Abu Hatim considered this reading weak, and the discussion of its like has already passed in al-Hijr regarding "tubashshirun." A group recited "tushaqqunni" with the nun doubled and kasra on it followed by a ya. As for ﴿those who were given knowledge﴾, they are, according to some exegetes, the angels; Yahya ibn Sallam said: they are the believers, and this address from them is on the Day of Resurrection.

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The correct view is that it encompasses everyone whom God has given knowledge of this, from all who attend the place of standing, angel, human, and others. The rest of the verse is clear.

(p-347) His Majesty said:

﴿Those whose souls the angels take while they are wronging themselves. Then they will offer submission, [saying], "We did not do any evil." Yes! Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what you used to do.﴾ ﴿So enter the gates of Hell, to abide therein; and wretched is the abode of the arrogant.﴾ ﴿And it will be said to those who feared Allah, "What has your Lord sent down?" They will say, "Good." For those who do good in this world is good, and the home of the Hereafter is better. And excellent is the home of the righteous.﴾

"Those" (alladhīna) is a description (na't) of "the disbelievers" according to the view of most of the commentators. It is also possible that "those" is in the nominative as a new subject (mubtada'), separate from what precedes it, and its predicate is in His words, ﴿then they offered submission﴾, with the fa' inserted into the predicate, and this kind of construction does occur. "The angels" (al-malā'ika) means those who take their souls. His words ﴿wronging themselves﴾ are a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). "Submission" (al-salam) here means surrender (al-istislām): that is, they threw down their hands and said, "We did not do any evil," so the verb "they said" (qālū) is omitted because the context indicates it. Al-Ḥasan said: "These are stages: at times they acknowledge against themselves, as He said: ﴿And they will testify against themselves that they were disbelievers﴾ [al-An'am: 130], and at times they deny, as in this verse." Their words ﴿We did not do any evil﴾ may carry two possible meanings: first, that they lied and intended the lie as a means of protecting themselves, similar to their saying: ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ [al-An'am: 23]; and second, that they reported about themselves that they did not do any evil, reporting their own assumption about themselves, which is itself false. The fitting reply to them in both cases is "Yes" (balā), that is, it is said to them, "Yes." His words ﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what you used to do﴾ are a warning and a threat. The apparent meaning of the verse is that it is general to all disbelievers. Their offering of submission is the opposite of their earlier opposition. Ikrima said: It was revealed concerning a group of people from Makkah who believed in their hearts but did not emigrate; the disbelievers of Makkah took them out forcibly to Badr, and they were killed there, so this verse was revealed concerning them.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 16, verses 31–32:**

Allah the Mighty and Majestic says:

﴿Gardens of Eden, which they will enter, beneath which rivers flow; for them therein is whatever they wish. Thus does Allah reward the God-fearing.﴾ ﴿Those whom the angels take in death while they are pure, saying: "Peace be upon you. Enter the Garden for what you used to do."﴾

It is possible that "jannatu" (gardens) is in the nominative as the predicate (khabar) of an implied subject (mubtada', the subject of a nominal sentence), with the sense: "They are the Gardens of Eden." It is possible that it is nominative by the phrase ﴿And excellent is the abode of the God-fearing: Gardens of Eden﴾. It is possible that the sense is: "For them are Gardens of Eden." It is also possible that "jannatu" is the subject, and its predicate is "yadkhulunaha" (they enter it). Zayd ibn Thabit and Abu 'Abd al-Rahman read "jannata" in the accusative, which is like the phrase "Zayd, I struck him." The majority of people read "yadkhulunaha." Isma'il reported from Nafi' the reading "yudkhalunaha" (with a damma on the ya and a fatha on the kha'), but this is not authentically from Nafi'. It is also related from Abu Ja'far and Shayba ibn Nisah. The phrase ﴿beneath which rivers flow﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). The rest of the verse is clear.

The majority read "tatawaffahum" with a ta' (feminine prefix). Al-A'mash and Hamza read "yatawaffahum" with a ya' from below. In the Mushaf (codex) of Ibn Mas'ud, it is "tawaffahum" with a single ta' in both places. "Tayyibina" (pure) is an expression for the goodness of their condition and their readiness for death. This is in contrast to what was said of the disbelievers: ﴿wronging themselves﴾. The tayyib is one with nothing impure in him. From this is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿You are pure, so enter it, abiding therein﴾ [al-Zumar: 73]. The angels' words ﴿Peace be upon you﴾ are a glad tiding from Allah the Exalted. There are authentic hadiths on this which would take long to mention. His words ﴿for what you used to do﴾ mean: for what was in your deeds of your earning. This is figurative. He linked their entry into the Garden to their deeds, inasmuch as deeds were made a sign for the servant's entry into the Garden. This is challenged by the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "No one enters the Garden by his deed." They said: "Not even you, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Not even I, unless Allah covers me with His grace and mercy." This verse, by interpretation (ta'wil), returns to the meaning of the hadith, and from mercy and covering is that Allah enables the servant to good deeds. The purpose of the hadith is to deny that it is obligatory upon Allah the Exalted by reason, as a group of the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school) maintained.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 16, verses 33–35**

The words of the Most High:

﴿Do they only wait for the angels to come to them, or for the command of your Lord to come? So did those before them do, and Allah did not wrong them, but they were wronging themselves.﴾ ﴿So the evil consequences of what they had done befell them, and what they used to mock encompassed them.﴾ ﴿And those who associated others with Allah said: "If Allah had willed, we would not have worshipped anything besides Him, neither we nor our fathers, nor would we have forbidden anything besides Him." So did those before them do. Is there upon the messengers anything but clear notification?﴾

"Yanzurun" (﴿يَنْظُرُونَ﴾) means "yantazirun" (they wait). When "nazara" refers to sight with the eye, the Arabs use it with "ila" (to). When it is not followed by "ila", it means "intazara" (to wait), as Imru' al-Qays said:

*"Indeed, if you two look upon me for a while, from time to time, you would benefit me at Lada Umm Jundub."*

From this is the words of the Most High, quoting others: ﴿Wait for us, that we may borrow from your light﴾ [al-Hadid: 13]. It has also come, irregularly, that "nazarat" is used in the sense of seeing without "ila", as in the poet's words:

*"Dazzling in beauty and grace, they look (at us) as the gazelles look at the arak trees."*

The majority of readers recited "ta'tiyahum" (﴿تَأْتِيَهُمُ﴾) with a "ta" at the beginning. Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited "ya'tiyahum" (﴿يَأْتِيَهُمُ﴾) with a "ya", and this is the reading of Yahya ibn Wathhab, Talha, and al-A'mash. The meaning of the statement is that the angels come to seize their souls while they are wronging themselves. His words ﴿or the command of your Lord comes﴾ are a threat that includes the establishment of the Hour or the punishment of this world.

Then the Most High mentioned that this was the practice of their predecessors among the nations, meaning that they were punished. That was not an injustice, because that punishment was not placed in other than its proper place. Rather, they wronged themselves by placing their disbelief in the direction of Allah, the Most High, and by inclining to idols and images; this is placing a thing in other than its proper place. "They wronged themselves" means they harmed themselves by their own action, even if they did not intend to wrong or harm them.

The words of the Most High ﴿So the evil consequences of what they had done befell them﴾ mean: the recompense for that in this world and in the Hereafter. "Haqa" (﴿وَحاقَ﴾) means "nazala" (to descend) and "ahata" (to encompass). Here there is an omitted element indicated by the apparent meaning of the statement; its estimate is: the recompense of what they used to mock.

The words of the Most High ﴿And those who associated others with Allah said﴾ through to the end of the verse constitute a dispute from the disbelievers. This is because most disbelievers believe in the existence of Allah, the Most High, and that He is their Creator and Provider. If the people of this verse were of this category, it is as though they said: "O Muhammad, we are under Allah's sight in our worship of idols and in taking them so that they may benefit and bring us near to Allah in nearness. If Allah disliked our action, He would have changed it long ago, either by destroying us or by guiding us." Among the disbelievers there was a group who did not believe in the existence of Allah. If the people of this verse were of this category, it is as though they took an argument against the Prophet, peace be upon him, from his own words, meaning: "The Lord whom you affirm, O Muhammad, and who is as you describe Him, knows and is able. There is no doubt that He knows our situation, and if He disliked it He would have changed it."

The response to these two groups is that Allah, the Most High, forbids disbelief, yet He may have willed it for some people. He set up the proofs, sent the messengers, and facilitated for each one what had been decreed upon him. This dispute, between whichever of the two categories I have supposed, (p-352) contains no mockery. However, Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj said that this statement is in the manner of mockery. Abu Ishaq, and Allah knows best, went to the view that the group who do not say that it is a sin, and then established the argument from the position of their opponent, are as though they were mocking in that. This is pure dispute, and the response to it is as we have mentioned.

The words of the Most High ﴿So is there upon the messengers anything but clear notification?﴾ point to what we have mentioned.

His words "wa la harramna" (﴿وَلا حَرَّمْنا﴾) mean the bahira, the sa'iba, the wasila, and other things that they forbade. Allah, blessed and exalted is He, informed that this tendency had been preceded by the earlier disbelievers in adopting it. It is as though He said: the matter is not as they supposed, that when Allah wills disbelief He does not command its abandonment. Rather, Allah has set up proofs for His servants and sent messengers as warners, and upon them there is nothing but notification.
