**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 16, verses 33–35**

The words of the Most High:

﴿Do they only wait for the angels to come to them, or for the command of your Lord to come? So did those before them do, and Allah did not wrong them, but they were wronging themselves.﴾ ﴿So the evil consequences of what they had done befell them, and what they used to mock encompassed them.﴾ ﴿And those who associated others with Allah said: "If Allah had willed, we would not have worshipped anything besides Him, neither we nor our fathers, nor would we have forbidden anything besides Him." So did those before them do. Is there upon the messengers anything but clear notification?﴾

"Yanzurun" (﴿يَنْظُرُونَ﴾) means "yantazirun" (they wait). When "nazara" refers to sight with the eye, the Arabs use it with "ila" (to). When it is not followed by "ila", it means "intazara" (to wait), as Imru' al-Qays said:

*"Indeed, if you two look upon me for a while, from time to time, you would benefit me at Lada Umm Jundub."*

From this is the words of the Most High, quoting others: ﴿Wait for us, that we may borrow from your light﴾ [al-Hadid: 13]. It has also come, irregularly, that "nazarat" is used in the sense of seeing without "ila", as in the poet's words:

*"Dazzling in beauty and grace, they look (at us) as the gazelles look at the arak trees."*

The majority of readers recited "ta'tiyahum" (﴿تَأْتِيَهُمُ﴾) with a "ta" at the beginning. Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited "ya'tiyahum" (﴿يَأْتِيَهُمُ﴾) with a "ya", and this is the reading of Yahya ibn Wathhab, Talha, and al-A'mash. The meaning of the statement is that the angels come to seize their souls while they are wronging themselves. His words ﴿or the command of your Lord comes﴾ are a threat that includes the establishment of the Hour or the punishment of this world.

That was not an injustice, because that punishment was not placed in other than its proper place. Rather, they wronged themselves by placing their disbelief in the direction of Allah, the Most High, and by inclining to idols and images; this is placing a thing in other than its proper place. "They wronged themselves" means they harmed themselves by their own action, even if they did not intend to wrong or harm them.

"Haqa" (﴿وَحاقَ﴾) means "nazala" (to descend) and "ahata" (to encompass). Here there is an omitted element indicated by the apparent meaning of the statement; its estimate is: the recompense of what they used to mock.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 16, verse 36–38:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿And We certainly sent into every community a messenger, [saying]: "Worship Allah and avoid the taghut (false deities)." Then among them were those whom Allah guided, and among them were those upon whom error was justly decreed. So travel through the earth and observe how was the end of the deniers.﴾ ﴿If you are eager for their guidance, indeed Allah does not guide those He leads astray, and for them there will be no helpers.﴾ ﴿And they swore by Allah with the utmost of their oaths: "Allah will not raise up those who die." Yes, it is a promise binding upon Him, but most people do not know.﴾

When His saying, ﴿Then is there upon the messengers except the clear conveyance?﴾ [al-Nahl: 35], pointed to establishing the proof, as we have mentioned, this verse came in between to explain that He sent the messengers commanding His worship and the avoidance of worshipping other than Him. The "taghut" (transgressor, i.e. false object of worship) in the language is everything worshipped besides Allah, whether a human being who consents to that, or a stone, or a piece of wood. Then He informed that among them were those who took heed, and Allah guided them and they looked with their insight, and among them were those who turned away and disbelieved, so error was decreed upon them, and it leads to the Fire inevitably, and among them were those whom it led to the punishment of Allah in this world. Then He referred them, for knowledge of this, to seeking in the earth, and to surveying the nations, and to standing upon the ends of the disbelieving deniers.

As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿If you are eager﴾, the verse. Al-ḥirṣ (eagerness) is the most intense desire for a thing. This is a consolation to the Prophet (ﷺ), meaning: your eagerness does not benefit, for these are matters that are decreed.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, al-Hasan, al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Mujahid, Shibl, Muzahim al-Khurasani, Abu Raja' al-'Utaridi, and Ibn Sirin read: "lā yuhdā" with a damma on the yā' and a fatḥa on the dāl. ʿĀṣim, Ḥamza, and al-Kisā'ī read: "lā yahdī" with a fatḥa on the yā' and a kasra on the dāl (p-353), and this is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn al-Musayyab, and a group. This has two meanings: that Allah does not guide the one whom He has decreed to be led astray; and the other meaning is that the Arabs say "yahdī al-rajul" in the sense of "ihtadā" (he became guided), related by al-Farra', and in the Qur'an: ﴿lā yahiddī illā an yuhdā﴾ [Yunus: 35]. Abu 'Ali and others made it mean "yahtadī". A group read with a fatḥa on the yā' and kasras on the hā' and dāl, and a group read "yuhdī" with a damma on the yā' and a kasra on the dāl, and this reading is weak. In the Codex of Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "fa-inna Allāha lā hādiya liman aḍall", and Abu Hatim related it as: "fa-innahu lā hādiya liman aḍall". Abu 'Ali said: "The pronoun referring back to the subject of 'inna' is implied in 'yuḍill' in every reading except the reading 'yahdī' with a fatḥa on the yā' and a kasra on the dāl, meaning: Allah guides; the referring pronoun is implied in 'yahdī'." As for His saying, ﴿and for them there are no helpers﴾, it is a pronoun in the sense of "min" (the plural form of the subject). The Arabs say: "ḥaraṣa yaḥraṣu" and "ḥaraṣa yaḥriṣu", and the kasra in the future is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz. al-Hasan, Ibrahim, and Abu Haywa read with a fatḥa on the rā' in His saying "ḥaraṣa", and Ibrahim read: "wa-in taḥraṣ" with an added wāw.

The pronoun in His saying "wa-aqsamū" refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh. It is mentioned that a man from among the Muslims was a neighbour of a man from among the polytheists, and in his speech he said: "No, by Him whom I hope for after death." The disbeliever said to him: "Will He resurrect after death?" He said: "Yes." So the disbeliever swore, exerting himself in his oath, that Allah does not resurrect anyone after death, and the verse was revealed on account of that. "Jahd" is a verbal noun, and its meaning is: with the utmost of their effort. Then Allah, Exalted, responded to them with His saying "Yes," thereby affirming the resurrection. His saying, ﴿a promise upon Him, binding﴾, are two emphatic verbal nouns. al-Dahhak read: "Yes, a promise upon Him, a truth" with the nominative on the two verbal nouns (p-354). Most people in this verse are the disbelievers who deny the resurrection. The resurrection from graves is something the intellect permits, and the report of the Sharia established it through the tongue of all the prophets. Some of the Shi'a said: the reference in this verse is to 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, and that Allah will resurrect him in this world; and this is the doctrine of the return (raj'a). Their saying is false, a fabrication against Allah and a lie, which Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and others refuted.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 16, verses 39–40:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿That He may make clear to them that about which they differ, and that those who disbelieved may know that they were liars.﴾ ﴿Indeed, Our word to a thing when We intend it is only that We say to it, "Be," and it is.﴾

The lam in His saying "liyubayyina" (that He may make clear) is connected to what is implied in His saying "bala" (yes), because the implied meaning is: "Yes, He resurrects in order to make clear." It was also said that it is connected to His saying: ﴿And We certainly sent into every nation a messenger﴾ [al-Nahl: 36]. The first is more correct in meaning, because by it the lying of the disbelievers in denying resurrection can be understood.

As for His saying: ﴿Indeed, Our word﴾ and the rest of the verse: "innama" (indeed/only) in the speech of the Arabs is for emphasis and for confirming the restriction to what is mentioned. It may, along with this, be exclusive (restrictive) when the context indicates that meaning, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah is but one God﴾ [al-Nisa: 171]. As for the saying of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him: "Indeed, usury is only in credit (nasi'ah)," and the saying of the Arabs: "Indeed, the brave man is only 'Antarah," only the meaning of emphasis remains in them. "Innama" in this verse is for restriction (exclusivity). The principle of discussion regarding this verse is that we say: the will and the command, which are two of the eternal attributes of Allah, may He be blessed and exalted, are both eternal and without beginning. What is in the wording of this verse of the meaning of futurity and beginning (istiqbal and istinaf) returns only to the willed thing, not to the will, because the willed things that are brought into existence when they are commanded to "Be" are a beginning and a futurity, not in the will to that, nor in the command to it, since those two are eternal. Because of the willed thing, He expressed it with "idha" (when) and "naqulu" (We say). Now we return to these words and clarify the aspect of each one individually: As for His saying "li-shay'" (to a thing), it admits of two aspects. One of them: the things that are willed and to which it is said "Be" are known to exist in all of them over the length of time and by the decree of Allah, exalted is He; so when their existence is certain, it is permissible to call them "things" while they are in a state of non-existence. The second aspect: His saying "li-shay'" is a reminder to us of the examples you look into, i.e., every thing you take from existing things, its path is that it is willed and it is said to it "Be," and it is; and that thing taken from the existents serves as an example of what comes later of matters and what came before. By this we are freed from calling the non-existent a "thing." His saying "idha aradnahu" (when We intend it) is placed in the position of "willed," but He used these resumptive expressions according to the fact that existents come and appear one thing after another, as if He said: "when what is willed from it appears." On this aspect goes His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah will see your deed and His Messenger﴾, and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And that Allah may know those who believe﴾ [Al 'Imran: 140], and similar to these, whose meaning is: what Allah, exalted is He, saw and knew in all of eternity will occur from you. His saying: ﴿an naqula﴾ (that We say) takes the position of a verbal noun, as if He said: "Our saying," but "an" with the verb gives a futurity that is not in the verbal noun in most of its usage, and it may come in places where time is not considered, as in this verse, and as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And among His signs is that the heaven and the earth stand by His command﴾ [al-Rum: 25], and other than that. His saying "lahu" (to it): most people hold that the thing is that which is addressed as if it were present, and that Allah, may He be blessed and exalted, said in eternity to all that He created: "Be," with the condition of time and attribute. Al-Zajjaj said: "lahu" means "for its sake" (min ajlihi), and this can be understood to refer to the first meaning. Some people held that His saying "an naqula" is metaphorical, as you say: "He spoke with his head and so he raised it," and "He spoke with his hand and so he struck so-and-so." Abu Mansur rejected this approach and held that the first is the first. The majority read "fayakunu" with a raised nun (damma), while Ibn 'Amir and al-Kisa'i read it here and in Ya-Sin with a fatha on it; this is the reading of Ibn Muhaysin.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The first is further away in terms of the sequence (ta'qib) that accompanies the fa' in most of its usages, so consider it.

In this brief discussion there is what allows one to perceive the essentials of this issue, but the requirement of brevity prevented expanding on the objections and their answers. The purpose of this verse is to inform those who deny resurrection of how insignificant its matter is before Allah, exalted is He, and how near it is to His power; there is no lord other than Him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 16, verses 39–40:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿That He may make clear to them that about which they differ, and that those who disbelieved may know that they were liars.﴾ ﴿Indeed, Our word to a thing when We intend it is only that We say to it, "Be," and it is.﴾

The lam in His saying "liyubayyina" (that He may make clear) is connected to what is implied in His saying "bala" (yes), because the implied meaning is: "Yes, He resurrects in order to make clear." It was also said that it is connected to His saying: ﴿And We certainly sent into every nation a messenger﴾ [al-Nahl: 36]. The first is more correct in meaning, because by it the lying of the disbelievers in denying resurrection can be understood.

As for His saying: ﴿Indeed, Our word﴾ and the rest of the verse: "innama" (indeed/only) in the speech of the Arabs is for emphasis and for confirming the restriction to what is mentioned. It may, along with this, be exclusive (restrictive) when the context indicates that meaning, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah is but one God﴾ [al-Nisa: 171]. As for the saying of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him: "Indeed, usury is only in credit (nasi'ah)," and the saying of the Arabs: "Indeed, the brave man is only 'Antarah," only the meaning of emphasis remains in them. "Innama" in this verse is for restriction (exclusivity). The principle of discussion regarding this verse is that we say: the will and the command, which are two of the eternal attributes of Allah, may He be blessed and exalted, are both eternal and without beginning. What is in the wording of this verse of the meaning of futurity and beginning (istiqbal and istinaf) returns only to the willed thing, not to the will, because the willed things that are brought into existence when they are commanded to "Be" are a beginning and a futurity, not in the will to that, nor in the command to it, since those two are eternal. Because of the willed thing, He expressed it with "idha" (when) and "naqulu" (We say). Now we return to these words and clarify the aspect of each one individually: As for His saying "li-shay'" (to a thing), it admits of two aspects. One of them: the things that are willed and to which it is said "Be" are known to exist in all of them over the length of time and by the decree of Allah, exalted is He; so when their existence is certain, it is permissible to call them "things" while they are in a state of non-existence. The second aspect: His saying "li-shay'" is a reminder to us of the examples you look into, i.e., every thing you take from existing things, its path is that it is willed and it is said to it "Be," and it is; and that thing taken from the existents serves as an example of what comes later of matters and what came before. By this we are freed from calling the non-existent a "thing." His saying "idha aradnahu" (when We intend it) is placed in the position of "willed," but He used these resumptive expressions according to the fact that existents come and appear one thing after another, as if He said: "when what is willed from it appears." On this aspect goes His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah will see your deed and His Messenger﴾, and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And that Allah may know those who believe﴾ [Al 'Imran: 140], and similar to these, whose meaning is: what Allah, exalted is He, saw and knew in all of eternity will occur from you. His saying: ﴿an naqula﴾ (that We say) takes the position of a verbal noun, as if He said: "Our saying," but "an" with the verb gives a futurity that is not in the verbal noun in most of its usage, and it may come in places where time is not considered, as in this verse, and as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And among His signs is that the heaven and the earth stand by His command﴾ [al-Rum: 25], and other than that. His saying "lahu" (to it): most people hold that the thing is that which is addressed as if it were present, and that Allah, may He be blessed and exalted, said in eternity to all that He created: "Be," with the condition of time and attribute. Al-Zajjaj said: "lahu" means "for its sake" (min ajlihi), and this can be understood to refer to the first meaning. Some people held that His saying "an naqula" is metaphorical, as you say: "He spoke with his head and so he raised it," and "He spoke with his hand and so he struck so-and-so." Abu Mansur rejected this approach and held that the first is the first. The majority read "fayakunu" with a raised nun (damma), while Ibn 'Amir and al-Kisa'i read it here and in Ya-Sin with a fatha on it; this is the reading of Ibn Muhaysin.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The first is further away in terms of the sequence (ta'qib) that accompanies the fa' in most of its usages, so consider it.

In this brief discussion there is what allows one to perceive the essentials of this issue, but the requirement of brevity prevented expanding on the objections and their answers. The purpose of this verse is to inform those who deny resurrection of how insignificant its matter is before Allah, exalted is He, and how near it is to His power; there is no lord other than Him.

[p. 357]

The Exalted said: ﴿And those who emigrated for God's sake after they had been wronged – We will surely settle them in this world in a good place. And the reward of the Hereafter is greater, if only they knew.﴾ ﴿Those who were patient and put their trust in their Lord.﴾ ﴿We did not send before you except men to whom We revealed. So ask the People of the Reminder, if you do not know,﴾ ﴿with clear proofs and scriptures. And We have sent down to you the Reminder, that you may explain to people what has been sent down to them, and that perhaps they will reflect.﴾

When God Most High mentioned the disbelievers of Makkah, who swore that God would not raise up anyone who dies, and their statement was refuted, He mentioned the believers of Makkah who were contemporary with them. They are those who emigrated to the land of Abyssinia (al-Habasha). This is the view of the majority (al-Jumhur), and it is the correct view regarding the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) of this verse, because the emigration to Madinah had not yet taken place at the time this verse was revealed. A group said that the occasion of the verse was Abu Jandal ibn Suhayl ibn 'Amr, but this is weak, because the affair of Abu Jandal occurred while the Prophet (ﷺ) was in Madinah. Another group said: it was revealed concerning 'Ammar, Suhayb, Khabbab and their companions, who were harmed in Makkah and left it. In any case, the verse, in its meaning, encompasses every person who emigrated, both earlier and later.

The majority read "linubawwi'annahum" (we will surely settle them). Ibn Mas'ud, Na'im ibn Maysara, al-Rabi' ibn Khuthaym, and the Commander of the Faithful 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him, read "linuthwiyannahum." Both words have the same meaning in one place, namely establishing (al-taqrir). A group said: "al-hasanah" (the good place) is a promise of a noble spot, which the unseen revealed to be Madinah, and to it the phrase "hasanah" refers. Another group said: "al-hasanah" is the lasting good mention (lisan al-sidq) left for them throughout the ages. In the phrase "linubawwi'annahum" or "linuthwiyannahum," on this interpretation, there is a great deal of metaphorical extension (tajawwuz) and a distant metaphor (isti'arah). This is on the basis that "al-hasanah" is the life and the abode, and that the apparent verb is the governing element for it. Abu al-Fath said: he put it in the accusative on the meaning "We will treat them well in that, with good treatment," and "hasanah" was placed in the position of "ihsanan" (good treatment). A group held that "al-hasanah" is general, covering every praiseworthy matter that a human being attains. On this interpretation the aforementioned metaphor is concealed. This view includes what is reported from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, that he would give wealth at the time of distribution to a man from among the emigrants and say to him: "Take what God has promised you in this world, and the reward of the Hereafter is greater," and then he would recite this verse. This view also includes victory over the enemy, the conquest of lands, and every hope that the emigrants attained. "The reward of the Hereafter" here refers to Paradise. The pronoun in "ya'lamun" (they know) refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh. The response of "law" (if) is elided and omitted, and the object of "ya'lamun" is likewise omitted. There is scrutiny regarding this.

The Exalted's words ﴿Those who were patient﴾ are a description of the emigrants whom God promised. Patience (al-sabr) comprises restraint from desires, endurance of hardships for the sake of God Most High, and trust in God (al-tawakkul) with its detailed levels. Among those who trust there is one who excessively relies on this, and that is permissible and good, as long as it does not go to the extreme of causing destruction. And there is one who is moderate: he strives well and trusts, and this is in line with the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Tie it and trust [in God]." And there is one who falls short, and there is no benefit in his shortcoming, for he only has what has been decreed for him.

The Exalted's words ﴿We did not send before you﴾ and so on, are a response to the disbelievers of Quraysh, who considered it unlikely that a human being could be a messenger from God Most High. So God informed them, addressing Muhammad (ﷺ), that He had sent to the nations only men, and had not sent an angel or anything other than that. "Rijalan" (men) is in the accusative governed by "arsalna" (We sent), and "illa" (except) is affirmative. The majority read "yuha" (is revealed) with a damma on the yā' and a fatha on the ḥā'. A group read it with a damma on the yā' and a kasra on the ḥā'. 'Asim, by the transmission of Hafs alone, read "nuhi" with a nūn and a kasra on the ḥā'. This is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, Talhah ibn Musarrif, and Abu 'Abd al-Rahman. Then the Exalted said: "fas'alu" (so ask), that is, say to them: ask. And "ahl al-dhikr" (the People of the Reminder) here means the Jews and Christians, as stated by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and al-Hasan. Al-A'mash and Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah said that what is meant is those among them who embraced Islam. Abu Ja'far and Ibn Zayd said: "ahl al-dhikr" means the people of the Qur'an. Both of these views are weak, because there is no proof against the disbelievers in the report of believers about what was mentioned, since they would deny these fabrications. Al-Zajjaj said: "ahl al-dhikr" is general, covering everyone who is ascribed to knowledge.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

The most apparent of all of this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, that "ahl al-dhikr" here means the rabbis (ahbar) of the Jews and Christians who did not embrace Islam. In this particular case, they only inform that the messengers were human beings, and their reports are a proof against these people, for they have always confirmed them (the messengers), and they are not accused of testimony against us, because they are opponents in the early period of the religion of Muhammad (ﷺ) — may God fight them. This is the breaking of the argument of the disbelievers from their own position; it does not mean that we depended on the testimony of these people. Rather, the truth is clear in itself. And Quraysh had sent to the Jews of Yathrib, asking them and relying on them.

The Exalted's words ﴿with clear proofs﴾ are connected to an implied verb whose estimate is: "We sent them with clear proofs." Another group said that it is connected to "arsalna" at the beginning of the verse, and the meaning according to this is: "We did not send before you with clear proofs and scriptures except men." So in the verse there is inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir). "Al-zubur" are the written books; one says "zabarta wa dabbarta" when one writes. And "al-dhikr" in this verse is the Qur'an. The Exalted's words "li-tubayyina" (that you may explain) may mean: that you explain by reciting the text of the Qur'an what was sent down, and it may mean: that you explain through your interpretation of what is ambiguous (al-mujmal) and through clarifying what has become difficult of what was sent down. On this latter view, what the Sunnah (the prophetic practice and teachings) has clarified regarding the matters of the Sharia (divine law) is included. This is the view of Mujahid.

A group said: "al-hasanah" (the good place) is a promise of a noble spot, which the unseen revealed to be Madinah, and to it the phrase "hasanah" refers. Another group said: "al-hasanah" is the lasting good mention (lisan al-sidq) left for them throughout the ages. In the phrase "linubawwi'annahum" or "linuthwiyannahum," on this interpretation, there is a great deal of metaphorical extension (tajawwuz) and a distant metaphor (isti'arah). This is on the basis that "al-hasanah" is the life and the abode, and that the apparent verb is the governing element for it. Abu al-Fath said: he put it in the accusative on the meaning "We will treat them well in that, with good treatment," and "hasanah" was placed in the position of "ihsanan" (good treatment). A group held that "al-hasanah" is general, covering every praiseworthy matter that a human being attains. On this interpretation the aforementioned metaphor is concealed. This view includes what is reported from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, that he would give wealth at the time of distribution to a man from among the emigrants and say to him: "Take what God has promised you in this world, and the reward of the Hereafter is greater," and then he would recite this verse. This view also includes victory over the enemy, the conquest of lands, and every hope that the emigrants attained. "The reward of the Hereafter" here refers to Paradise. The pronoun in "ya'lamun" (they know) refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh. The response of "law" (if) is elided and omitted, and the object of "ya'lamun" is likewise omitted. There is scrutiny regarding this.

The Exalted's words ﴿Those who were patient﴾ are a description of the emigrants whom God promised. Patience (al-sabr) comprises restraint from desires, endurance of hardships for the sake of God Most High, and trust in God (al-tawakkul) with its detailed levels. Among those who trust there is one who excessively relies on this, and that is permissible and good, as long as it does not go to the extreme of causing destruction. And there is one who is moderate: he strives well and trusts, and this is in line with the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Tie it and trust [in God]." And there is one who falls short, and there is no benefit in his shortcoming, for he only has what has been decreed for him.

The Exalted's words ﴿We did not send before you﴾ and so on, are a response to the disbelievers of Quraysh, who considered it unlikely that a human being could be a messenger from God Most High. So God informed them, addressing Muhammad (ﷺ), that He had sent to the nations only men, and had not sent an angel or anything other than that. "Rijalan" (men) is in the accusative governed by "arsalna" (We sent), and "illa" (except) is affirmative. The majority read "yuha" (is revealed) with a damma on the yā' and a fatha on the ḥā'. A group read it with a damma on the yā' and a kasra on the ḥā'. 'Asim, by the transmission of Hafs alone, read "nuhi" with a nūn and a kasra on the ḥā'. This is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, Talhah ibn Musarrif, and Abu 'Abd al-Rahman. Then the Exalted said: "fas'alu" (so ask), that is, say to them: ask. And "ahl al-dhikr" (the People of the Reminder) here means the Jews and Christians, as stated by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and al-Hasan. Al-A'mash and Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah said that what is meant is those among them who embraced Islam. Abu Ja'far and Ibn Zayd said: "ahl al-dhikr" means the people of the Qur'an. Both of these views are weak, because there is no proof against the disbelievers in the report of believers about what was mentioned, since they would deny these fabrications. Al-Zajjaj said: "ahl al-dhikr" is general, covering everyone who is ascribed to knowledge.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

The most apparent of all of this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, that "ahl al-dhikr" here means the rabbis (ahbar) of the Jews and Christians who did not embrace Islam. In this particular case, they only inform that the messengers were human beings, and their reports are a proof against these people, for they have always confirmed them (the messengers), and they are not accused of testimony against us, because they are opponents in the early period of the religion of Muhammad (ﷺ) — may God fight them. This is the breaking of the argument of the disbelievers from their own position; it does not mean that we depended on the testimony of these people. Rather, the truth is clear in itself. And Quraysh had sent to the Jews of Yathrib, asking them and relying on them.

The Exalted's words ﴿with clear proofs﴾ are connected to an implied verb whose estimate is: "We sent them with clear proofs." Another group said that it is connected to "arsalna" at the beginning of the verse, and the meaning according to this is: "We did not send before you with clear proofs and scriptures except men." So in the verse there is inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir). "Al-zubur" are the written books; one says "zabarta wa dabbarta" when one writes. And "al-dhikr" in this verse is the Qur'an. The Exalted's words "li-tubayyina" (that you may explain) may mean: that you explain by reciting the text of the Qur'an what was sent down, and it may mean: that you explain through your interpretation of what is ambiguous (al-mujmal) and through clarifying what has become difficult of what was sent down. On this latter view, what the Sunnah (the prophetic practice and teachings) has clarified regarding the matters of the Sharia (divine law) is included. This is the view of Mujahid.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 16, verses 45–48:

The Exalted and Mighty said:

﴿Do those who devised evil schemes feel secure that God will cause the earth to swallow them, or that the punishment will come upon them from where they do not perceive?﴾ ﴿Or that He will seize them in their going back and forth, and they will not be able to escape?﴾ ﴿Or that He will seize them by gradual wasting? Indeed, your Lord is Most Kind and Merciful.﴾ ﴿Have they not considered the things God has created, whose shadows incline to the right and the left, prostrating to God while they are humbled?﴾

This verse is a warning to the people of Mecca, and they are the intended referent of "those" (alladhina) according to most scholars. Mujahid said the intended referent is Namrud ibn Ka'nan.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

The first view is more apparent. The word "evil deeds" (al-sayyi'at) in the accusative may be read in two ways. One is that it is governed by the verb in "Do those who..." (afa-amina alladhina), so that "evil deeds" here means the punishments that cause harm to those upon whom they descend, and "that He will cause the earth to swallow" (an yakhsifa) is in apposition to them. The second is that it is governed by "devised" (makaru). The verb "devised" is transitive because it carries the sense of "did" or "performed," and "evil deeds" here means sinful acts of disbelief and others, as Qatada said. Then He threatened them with what had befallen the nations before them of being swallowed up, which is that the earth swallows the one who is swallowed and he is pushed downward. Al-Naqqash reported on the authority of some scholars that a group in this community had the prayer established for them, and they quarrelled over leading it and boasted about it, and they continued in that state until they were swallowed up.

"Their going back and forth" (taqallubihim) means their travels and their attempts to make a living through travel, through pasturing, and other means. "Those who cannot be escaped" (al-mu'jiz) means one who escapes by flight, as if he has made his pursuer unable to catch him. As for His words "by gradual wasting" (ala takhawwuf), that is, in the manner of gradual wasting. Takhawwuf means diminishing. From it comes the line of the poet describing a she-camel:

"Her travelling gradually wore her down, a hump-backed, mangy camel, as the file (safan) gradually wears down the stick of nab'a wood."

So "safan" is the file. It is reported that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, did not understand the meaning of "takhawwuf" in this verse and he wrote to the regions asking about it, until he heard this line. It is also reported that a young Arab man came to him, and the meaning of the word takhawwuf was unclear to him. He said to him: "O Commander of the Faithful, my father is wearing down my wealth (yatakhawwafuni mali)." 'Umar, may God be pleased with him, said: "God is Greatest!" [and recited] "or that He will seize them by gradual wasting." From it is the saying of Tarafa:

"And a camel that wore down (kahawwafa) his camel... the driving of al-Mu'alla, the root and the lowest."

It is also reported as "from his own self" (min nafsihi). From it is the saying of another:

"I am blamed for satire, and every day there comes to meet me from the neighbours a ghoul... who wears down (yatakhawwafu) their enemies' wealth for me, and brings chains upon the necks that clink."

He means satires. From it is the saying of al-Nabigha:

"He wore them down until he humbled their chieftains, with a harmful thrust after the smiting of the blades."

This diminishing is to be understood as a threat in two senses. One is that He destroys them and takes their souls by gradual wasting, that is, one by one, diminishing them with one thing after another. No one claims to be safe from this. It seems that this threat refers to the punishment they will suffer after death, since otherwise all nations perish in this way. This is supported by His words "Indeed, your Lord is Most Kind and Merciful," meaning that this third level of threat contains kindness, mercy, and a reprieve so that the one who repents may repent and the one who returns may return. The other is what al-Dahhak said: that a group or a town is seized with punishment while another is left alone, and then in this way until all perish. Another group said that "takhawwuf" here comes from fear (khawf), meaning He seizes them after a fear that befalls them, so that He punishes them with it.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

In this there is some strain.

As for His words "Have they not considered the things God has created" to the end of the verse: Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, and Ibn 'Amir read "Have they not seen" (awa lam yaraw) with the letter ya', in the third-person form, and likewise in al-'Ankabut. This reading follows the preceding third-person verbs: "or that He will seize them" (aw ya'khudhahum), "or that the punishment will come upon them" (aw ya'tiyahum), and "from where they do not perceive" (la yash'urun). Al-Tabari preferred this reading. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "Have you not seen" (awa lam tarawa) with the letter ta' in the second-person form in both places, and this is the reading of al-Hasan, al-A'raj, and Abu 'Abd al-Rahman. This reading can carry two meanings. One is that it means: "Say to them, O Muhammad, have you not seen?" The second is that it is a general address to all creation, which began with the speech just before. 'Asim read it with the ta' in al-Nahl, and his reading differed in al-'Ankabut.

As for His words "of any thing" (min shay'), it is a general term for everything that the description in His words "whose shadows incline" requires, because that description applies to whatever is presented for consideration among all the bodies that have a shadow. The seeing here is the seeing of the heart, but consideration through the seeing of the heart applies only to things seen with the eye.

Abu 'Amr alone read "tatafayya'u" with the ta' in front, and this is the reading of 'Isa and Ya'qub. The majority read "yatafayya'u" with the ya'. Abu 'Ali said: when the verb is attributed to a plural noun of this kind, both the masculine and feminine forms are acceptable.

"Fa'a al-zill" means the shadow returned in the opposite direction to the decline, because from sunrise until midday the sun is only erasing the general shadow that existed before its rising. When it passes midday, the return of the general shadow begins, and it continues to grow until the sun sets, and then it covers everything. The shadow extended in Paradise is not called "fay'" by God, because it does not return after it has gone. Likewise is the saying of Humayd ibn Thawr:

"Neither can the shadow withstand the coolness of the forenoon, nor does the afternoon shade taste the coolness of the evening."

So this is the path. Likewise is the saying of 'Alqama ibn 'Abada:

"Following the afternoon shadows in the evening, on paths as if they were the silk threads (suyub)."

Likewise is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"The shadow returns upon them (yafi'u 'alayha al-zill)."

As for al-Nabigha al-Ja'di, he said:

"So the peace of God comes to them in the morning, and the shade of Paradise, its shadows, returns (fuyu'u al-Firdaws dhat al-zilal)."

He used "fay'" metaphorically to describe a state where there is no return. Ruba ibn al-'Ajjaj said: after midday it is called "fay'" and "zill," but before it is only called "zill." It is said "fa'a al-zill" when it returns from decrease to increase. The verb "fa'a" can be made transitive with the hamza, as in God's words, blessed and exalted: "what God has returned (afa'a) to His Messenger" (al-Hashr 59:7). It can also be made transitive with the doubling of the middle letter, so one says "af'aahu Allah" and "fayyaahu," and "tafayya'a" is the intransitive form of "fayya'a." "Fay'" is not used except after midday in the well-known usage of the Arabs. But in this verse the consideration is from the beginning of the day until its end. So it seems that in some interpretations the verse follows the figurative usage of Arabic and the requirement to put "tatafayya'u" in place of "tatanaqqalu" (shifts) and "tamilu" (leans). He attributed the shadows to a singular pronoun, in agreement with the wording "mā" or "shay'," which has a collective sense.

Al-Thaqafi read "zulalahu" with a fatha on the first lam, a damma on the second, and a damma on the zay.

As for His words, the Exalted: "to the right and to the left," He mentioned "the right" in the singular, though it is meant as a plural, so it is as if it were a generic term. The meaning is "to the rights and the lefts," as the poet said:

"The arrivals, and Tha'am on the heights of Saba, the hide of the buffaloes has bitten their necks."

Another said:

"Let the stone be in the mouths of the mockers, if the loss of the two cubs of a lion in the thickets has broken me."

What is intended for consideration in this verse is every person and body that has a shadow, such as mountains, trees, and others. What has rights and lefts in the true sense is only the human being. But the mention of rights and lefts here is by way of metaphor for other than humans. That is, you suppose it to have a right and a left, and you suppose it facing whatever direction you wish, then you look at its shadow and you see it leaning either to the right or to the left. This happens in all the regions of the world. This is one way that covers all the wording of the verse, and in it there is figurative extension and breadth. As for the one who holds that the right is from the morning until midday, and then from midday until sunset the shadow is on the left (this is the view of Qatada and Ibn Juraij), that only follows for him in what he supposes to be facing the south. In my view, the consideration in this verse is only with regard to facing the south. As for what some people have said, that "the right is the first movement of the shadow after midday, and then the other movement until sunset is toward the lefts, and that is why He used the plural for the lefts and the singular for the right," this is a confused statement that is refuted in several respects.

Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with both of them, said: When you pray the dawn prayer, everything between the rising of the sun and its setting is shadow. Then God sends the sun over it as a guide, and it pulls the shadow toward itself.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

According to this, the first peak of the sun's position, when the shadow is to the right, is facing the south. Then the deviation begins, and it is to the lefts, because these are many movements and fragmented shadows, so they are many lefts. The shadow on the right was a single, continuous, general shadow for everything. In this view there is figurative usage in "tafayya'a." According to what we have supposed of facing the south, the shadow is always moving away from the right until midday. When it moves after leaving the rights entirely, its movement is away from the lefts.

A group said: the "shadows" here are the bodies themselves, and it is their persons that are meant, and the Arabs sometimes express bodies by "shadow." From it is the saying of 'Abida ibn al-Tabib:

"When we alight, we set up the shade of tents, and the cooking-pots bubble with meat for the people."

It is the tents that are set up. From it is the saying of another:

"Following the afternoon shadows in the evening"

meaning the afternoon shadows of the bodies. All this is possible, but not explicit, although Abu 'Ali established it.

The interpreters differed about this prostration. One group said it is true prostration of worship. Al-Tabari reported from al-Dahhak that he said: when the sun passes midday, everything prostrates before the qibla, whether plant or tree, and for this reason the righteous used to prefer praying at that time. Mujahid said: only the shadows prostrate, not the bodies. Another group, among them al-Tabari, said: He expressed submission, obedience, and the inclining and turning of the shadows by the word "prostration," just as one says of someone who gestures with his head toward the ground in humility that he "prostrates." From it is the saying of the poet:

"Both of them fell, and her head bowed down, as a Christian woman bows and does not turn aside."

"Dakhir" means one who is abased and humble. From it is the saying of Dhu al-Rumma:

"Nothing remained but one who is humbled in an enclosure, and one who hides in a hole, not in your land, in a burrow."

The Exalted and Mighty said:

Al-Naqqash reported on the authority of some scholars that a group in this community had the prayer established for them, and they quarrelled over leading it and boasted about it, and they continued in that state until they were swallowed up.

"Their going back and forth" (taqallubihim) means their travels and their attempts to make a living through travel, through pasturing, and other means. "Those who cannot be escaped" (al-mu'jiz) means one who escapes by flight, as if he has made his pursuer unable to catch him. As for His words "by gradual wasting" (ala takhawwuf), that is, in the manner of gradual wasting. Takhawwuf means diminishing. From it comes the line of the poet describing a she-camel:

"Her travelling gradually wore her down, a hump-backed, mangy camel, as the file (safan) gradually wears down the stick of nab'a wood."

So "safan" is the file. It is also reported that a young Arab man came to him, and the meaning of the word takhawwuf was unclear to him. He said to him: "O Commander of the Faithful, my father is wearing down my wealth (yatakhawwafuni mali)." 'Umar, may God be pleased with him, said: "God is Greatest!" "And a camel that wore down (kahawwafa) his camel... the driving of al-Mu'alla, the root and the lowest."

It is also reported as "from his own self" (min nafsihi). From it is the saying of another:

"I am blamed for satire, and every day there comes to meet me from the neighbours a ghoul... who wears down (yatakhawwafu) their enemies' wealth for me, and brings chains upon the necks that clink."

He means satires. From it is the saying of al-Nabigha:

"He wore them down until he humbled their chieftains, with a harmful thrust after the smiting of the blades."

This diminishing is to be understood as a threat in two senses. One is that He destroys them and takes their souls by gradual wasting, that is, one by one, diminishing them with one thing after another. No one claims to be safe from this. Another group said that "takhawwuf" here comes from fear (khawf), meaning He seizes them after a fear that befalls them, so that He punishes them with it.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

In this there is some strain.

As for His words "Have they not considered the things God has created" to the end of the verse: Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, and Ibn 'Amir read "Have they not seen" (awa lam yaraw) with the letter ya', in the third-person form, and likewise in al-'Ankabut. This reading follows the preceding third-person verbs: "or that He will seize them" (aw ya'khudhahum), "or that the punishment will come upon them" (aw ya'tiyahum), and "from where they do not perceive" (la yash'urun). Al-Tabari preferred this reading. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "Have you not seen" (awa lam tarawa) with the letter ta' in the second-person form in both places, and this is the reading of al-Hasan, al-A'raj, and Abu 'Abd al-Rahman. The second is that it is a general address to all creation, which began with the speech just before. 'Asim read it with the ta' in al-Nahl, and his reading differed in al-'Ankabut.

As for the one who holds that the right is from the morning until midday, and then from midday until sunset the shadow is on the left (this is the view of Qatada and Ibn Juraij), that only follows for him in what he supposes to be facing the south. According to this, the first peak of the sun's position, when the shadow is to the right, is facing the south. According to what we have supposed of facing the south, the shadow is always moving away from the right until midday. When it moves after leaving the rights entirely, its movement is away from the lefts.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 16, verses 49–55:

(p-366) The words of the Exalted and Majestic:

﴿To Allah prostrates whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth of creatures, and the angels, and they are not arrogant.﴾ ﴿They fear their Lord above them, and they do what they are commanded.﴾ ﴿And Allah has said: Do not take two gods. He is but one God, so fear Me alone.﴾ ﴿And to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth, and to Him is religion, perpetual. Will you then fear other than Allah?﴾ ﴿And whatever blessing you have is from Allah. Then when harm touches you, to Him you cry for help.﴾ ﴿Then when He removes the harm from you, behold, a group of you associates others with their Lord.﴾ ﴿So that they deny what We have given them. So enjoy yourselves, for you will soon know.﴾

The word "mā" (what) in this verse is used for those who have intellect. Al-Zajjaj said: His saying, ﴿whatever is in the heavens﴾, encompasses the angels of the heaven, and whatever is in the clouds, and whatever living creatures are in the atmosphere. His saying, ﴿and whatever is on the earth of creatures﴾, is clear. Then he mentioned the angels of the earth in His saying, "and the angels."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is possible that His saying "and the angels" is what encompasses the angels of the heavens and the earth, and what precedes it does not include any angel; rather it is the animals altogether. His saying "above them" may have two meanings. One is the aboveness by which Allah, exalted is He, is described: it is the aboveness of power, greatness, dominance and sovereignty. The other is that His saying ﴿above them﴾ is connected to His saying "they fear", meaning: they fear the punishment of their Lord from above them, because the usual manner of Allah's punishment upon nations comes from above. As for His saying ﴿and they do what they are commanded﴾: as for the believers, it is according to the Law and obedience; as for other than them among the animals, it is by subjugation and the decree that drives them to what has preceded of the command of Allah, blessed and exalted is He.

His exalted saying ﴿And Allah has said: Do not take two gods﴾ is a prohibition from Allah, blessed and exalted is He, against associating partners with Him. Its meaning: Do not take two gods, or more, and this is made explicit by His saying ﴿He is but one God﴾. One group said: the first object of "take" is His saying "two gods", and His saying "two" is emphasis and specification by number. This is well known in the speech of the Arabs: to specify the counted thing by mentioning its number for emphasis. From this is His saying ﴿one God﴾, because the word "God" (ilah) implies singularity. Others among them said: the second object is omitted, its estimate being: singular, or worshipped, or obeyed, and similar. Another group said: (p-367) the first object is His saying "two", and the second is His saying "gods", and the sense of the speech is: Do not take two gods, and there is no need to excuse it by emphasis. The meaning of the verse is a reminder that a human being, in his great affairs and small, is in the blessing of Allah (p-369) and His favours; his existence and what follows it are included in that. Then He reminded them of the times of illness, because the ignorant human being feels in them the measure of his need for the gentleness of Allah, exalted is He. "Al-Durr", though it encompasses every disliked thing, most often comes as an expression for bodily afflictions. "Tajarun" means you raise your voices in supplication and humble entreaty; its root is in the bellowing of the bull and the cow and their crying out, which is at a hardship that befalls them, or in the trace of blood from cattle that are slaughtered; that outcry is likened to the wailing of the supplicant who calls upon Allah when he raises his voice. From this is the saying of al-A'sha:

"He alternates between the prayers of the king, at times prostration, at times bellowing."

Abu 'Ubayda recited:

"With Abil, whenever he prays, he bellows."

(p-370) Sounds generally come in the pattern "fi'al" or "fa'il". Al-Zuhri read "tajarun" with a fatha on the jim without hamza, its vowel having been dropped and placed upon the jim, as "tasaluna" (you ask) is lightened to "tasalun".

His exalted saying ﴿Then when He removes the harm from you﴾: the majority read "kashafa"; Qatada read "kashif", and its basis is that it is an active participle from a verb of one-root meaning "kashafa", and it is weak. "The group" here means the polytheists who believe that the idols have powers of healing the sick, bringing good and averting harm; so when Allah heals them, they glorify their idols and attribute that healing to them.

His exalted saying "li-yakfuru" (so that they may deny): the lam may be the lam of becoming, meaning: their affair became that they deny, though they did not intend by those actions that they should deny. It may also be the lam of command, in the sense of threat and warning, like His exalted saying ﴿Do what you will﴾ [Fussilat: 40]. Denial here may be the denial of disbelief in Allah and polytheism, and this is supported by His saying ﴿with their Lord they associate partners﴾; and it may be the denial of blessing, which is more apparent, given His saying ﴿so that they deny what﴾, meaning: what We have bestowed upon them. The majority read "fa-tamatta'u fa-sawfa ta'lamun" in the sense: say to them, O Muhammad. Abu Rafi' related from the Prophet (ﷺ): "fa-yumatta'u fa-sawfa ya'lamun" with a yā' below, dammed, and "fa-sawfa ya'lamun" in the sense of the third person, and likewise in al-Rum; this is the reading of Abu al-'Aliya. al-Hasan read "fa-tamatta'u" as the majority did, in the imperative, and "fa-sawfa ya'lamun" with yā' in the third person, like the reading of Abu Rafi'. So "yumatti'u" in Abu Rafi's reading is in the accusative position, coordinated with "yakfuru" if the lam is the lam of "kay", and in the accusative by the fa' answering the imperative if the lam is the lam of command. The meaning of "tamatta'" in this verse is: enjoyment of the worldly life, whose end is to perish and vanish.

**Commentary of Ibn ʿAṭiyya (al-Muḥarrar al-Wajīz) on Sūrah 16, verses 56–59:**

Allah's statement, the Exalted and Majestic:

﴿And they assign to what they do not know a portion of what We have provided them. By Allah, you will surely be questioned about what you used to fabricate.﴾ ﴿And they assign to Allah daughters—glory be to Him—while for themselves is what they desire.﴾ ﴿And when one of them is given good news of a female, his face becomes dark, and he is filled with suppressed grief.﴾ ﴿He hides himself from the people because of the ill of what he has been given good news of. Should he keep it in humiliation or bury it in the dust? Unquestionably, evil is what they judge.﴾

The pronoun in "yajʿalūna" (they assign) refers to the disbelievers. By "what they do not know" he means the idols, i.e., they do not know any proof or evidence concerning them. It is also possible that by "they know" (yaʿlamūna) he means the idols, i.e., they assign a portion to inanimate things that know nothing; the object is then omitted. Then He expressed them with the phrasing of those who have intellect, in accordance with the doctrine of the disbelievers who attribute to them what is attributed to those who have intellect, and in accordance with the fact that this is a negated attribution. All of this is weak. The "portion" referred to is that which the Arabs had established as their custom of slaughtering for their idols, offering to them, and setting aside a share of the crops for them.

Then Allah, blessed and exalted, commanded His Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace, to swear to them that they would be questioned about their fabrication, namely that those customs are the truth which Allah had commanded, as some of them said. "Al-fir'ah" (fabrication) is the invention of falsehood.

As for His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And they assign to Allah daughters﴾ (the verse). This is an enumeration of the ugliness of the disbelievers' saying: "The angels are the daughters of Allah." He refuted them in two respects: first, the attribution of offspring to Allah, exalted is He above that; and second, that they attributed to Him the lowest kind of offspring, the one they themselves found hateful. The "mā" in His statement ﴿what they desire﴾ is in the nominative case as the subject of the sentence, and the predicate lies in the prepositional phrase. Al-Farrāʾ permitted that it be in the accusative case in coordination with "al-banāt" (the daughters). The Basrans do not permit this verse under the pattern of "ḍaraba-nī" (he struck me), and according to them it would have had to be: "wa-li-anfusihim mā yashtahūn" (and for themselves what they desire). The intended meaning of ﴿what they desire﴾ is the males among the children.

As for His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And when one of them is given good news﴾ (the verse). Since the thing given as good news was explicitly stated, it is fitting to mention "good news" in it; otherwise, "good news" is unrestricted and occurs only with good. His statement ﴿his face becomes dark﴾ is an expression for the frowning and gloom that afflicts the distressed person, and blackness and foam may overspread the face of the distressed, and its brightness departs; therefore blackness is mentioned for him. "Kaẓīm" means "kāẓim" (one who suppresses), like "ʿalīm" and "ʿālim"; the meaning is that he conceals his face and his grief over the female.

As for His statement: ﴿He hides himself from the people﴾ (the verse). This hiding that Allah mentioned occurs only after the good news of a female. What is related about a man among them, that when his wife went into labor he would hide until he was informed of one of the two outcomes, is not the intended meaning of the verse. It seems that this was so that if he was informed of something pleasant he would emerge, and if he was informed of something bad he would remain in his concealment and would not need to bring it about. The meaning of "yatawārā" is "yataghayyab" (he hides himself away). The construction of the speech is: "yatawārā min al-qawm mudbiran" (he hides from the people, turning away), "a-yumsikuhu am yadussuhā?" (shall he keep it or bury it?). One group read "a-yumsikuhu" according to the wording of "mā" (what), and "am yadussuhā" according to the meaning of "the female." Al-Jaḥdarī read "a-yumsikuhā" and "am yadussuhā," both according to the meaning of "the female" in both places. The majority read "ʿalā hawnin" with a dammah on the "hāʾ," while one group read it with a fatḥah; ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar read "ʿalā hawānin," which is the reading of ʿĀṣim al-Jaḥdarī; and al-Aʿmash read "ʿalā sūʾin" (in evil). The meaning of the verse is: he deliberates—shall he keep this female in humiliation which he bears, and grief which abides with him, or shall he bury her alive in the ground? That is "al-dass fi al-turāb" (the burying in the dust). Then Allah, exalted, began the report about the evil of their deed and their judgment in this regard concerning their daughters, while the provision of all is upon Allah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 16, verses 60–62:

His the Exalted and Majestic's saying:

﴿For those who do not believe in the Hereafter is the evil description, and for Allah is the highest description. And He is the Mighty, the Wise.﴾ ﴿And if Allah were to take mankind to task for their wrongdoing, He would not leave upon it [the earth] a single moving creature. But He defers them to a specified term. So when their term comes, they will not remain behind it by an hour, nor will they precede it.﴾ ﴿And they attribute to Allah what they dislike, and their tongues describe falsehood, [claiming] that for them is the best. Undoubtedly, for them is the Fire, and they will be the first to be neglected.﴾

A group said: "mathal" (example, likeness) here means "ṣifah" (attribute). That is, for them is the attribute of evil, and for Allah is the highest attribute. This is not necessary, because it is a departure from the wording. Rather, His saying "mathal" remains as it is. This is because when they say "the daughters are for Allah," they have assigned to Him a likeness: the daughters are of mankind, and having many daughters is hateful and blameworthy in their view. So it is "the evil likeness" which Allah the Exalted informed was theirs, not only in the matter of daughters, but because they assigned it for themselves in the matter of daughters, He assigned it to them absolutely in every evil, and there is no limit beyond the torment of the Fire.

(p-373) His saying: ﴿And for Allah is the highest likeness﴾ is also absolute, that is, the established perfection. Qatadah said: "The highest likeness" is: there is no god but Allah. The rest of the verse is clear.

His the Exalted's saying: ﴿And if Allah were to take mankind...﴾ the verse. "Yu'ākhidh" is "yufā'il" from "akhadha," as if one of the two being taken to task takes from the other a "ma'khadh" (a seizing), as is the case regarding the right of Allah the Exalted, or by harm in the direction of created beings, so the one takes the other from the first by punishment and recompense. There are two dialects: "wākhadha" and "ākhadha." "Yu'ākhidh" may be from "ākhidh," and as for its being from "wākhadha," it is clear. The pronoun in "'alayhā" refers to the earth, and this is possible even though no mention of it has preceded, due to its fame. It is also possible to refer to it as Labid said about the sun:

"Until, when it cast a hand upon a disbeliever, and its darkness concealed the nether parts of the lands."

And from this is His saying: ﴿until it disappeared behind the veil﴾ [Ṣād: 32], though there has been no mention of the sun. His saying: ﴿from a moving creature﴾ — "min" (from) has entered to encompass the whole genus. The apparent meaning of the verse is that Allah the Exalted informed that if He were to take mankind to task with a punishment they deserve for their wrongdoing in their disbelief and their disobediences, that punishment would destroy from them every living thing that crawls upon the earth of animals. It is as if this were by drought or by some matter that befalls them from Allah the Exalted. Upon this interpretation some scholars said: "The dung beetle nearly perished because of the sins of the children of Adam," mentioned by al-Tabari. And it is narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: « "Indeed Allah the Exalted makes the fish in the water and the bird in the air grow lean because of the sins of the disobedient."» Abu Hurayrah heard a man saying: "Indeed the wrongdoer destroys only himself," so Abu Hurayrah said: "Indeed Allah destroys the bustard in its nests, lean, because of the sins of the oppressors." The Sharia has indeed spoken in its reports that Allah destroyed nations, both the righteous and the disobedient among them, because of the sins of the disobedient among them. A group said: His saying: ﴿from a moving creature﴾ means: from those oppressors only. What indicates this specification is that Allah the Exalted does not punish anyone for the sin of another, and they argued with His saying: ﴿and no bearer of burdens bears the burden of another﴾ [al-An'am: 164]. All of this has no proof in it, because Allah the Exalted does not make the punishment target anyone because of another's sinning. Rather, when He sends a punishment upon a disobedient nation, He does not enable the innocent to escape that punishment, so the punishment afflicts him not as a requital for him. Similar to this is His saying: ﴿And beware of a trial which will not strike exclusively those who have wronged among you﴾ [al-Anfal: 25]. «It was said to the Prophet ﷺ: "Will we be destroyed while the righteous are among us?" He said: "Yes, when wickedness increases."» Then there must be some connection of wrongdoing to the innocent; that is by not changing [the wrong], and by flattering the people of wrongdoing and constantly remaining in their neighborhood. And the "specified term" in this verse is according to a particular person who is identified. There are many implications in the meaning of the verse which I have left out for brevity and concision.

His the Exalted's saying: ﴿what they dislike﴾ means the daughters. "Mā" in this position is used for one who has intellect, insofar as it denotes a category. Al-Hasan recited "alsinatuhumu al-kadhiba" with a sukun on the nun, out of fear of consecutive vowels. This is not necessary, because it is a departure from the wording. Rather, His saying "mathal" remains as it is. This is because when they say "the daughters are for Allah," they have assigned to Him a likeness: the daughters are of mankind, and having many daughters is hateful and blameworthy in their view. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 16, verses 63–66:

(p-376) His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿By God, We certainly sent [messengers] to nations before you, but Satan made their deeds seem fair to them, so he is their guardian today, and theirs will be a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿And We have not sent down to you the Book except that you may make clear to them that about which they differ, and as guidance and mercy for a people who believe.﴾ ﴿And God sent down water from the sky and gave life thereby to the earth after its death. Indeed, in that is a sign for a people who listen.﴾ ﴿And indeed, in livestock there is a lesson for you. We give you to drink from what is in their bellies, from between digestive contents and blood, pure milk, palatable to the drinkers.﴾

This is a verse of parable-making for them concerning those who came before, and within it is a threat for them and a consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ). His saying "today" may mean the day this verse was revealed, after those mentioned nations had died, meaning: there is no guardian for them since they died and needed help except Satan. It may also mean the Day of Resurrection, and the alif and lam in it are for the known (al-'ahd), meaning: he is their guardian on the witnessed day, which is the time of need and judgment. It may also mean: he is their guardian for the duration of their lives, and his guardianship ended with their death, and He expressed this by His saying "today" as a figure for the addressees by the span of their lives, as you say to a young man whom you urge to seek knowledge: "O so-and-so, no one among people studies except today," meaning: at your age. So it is as if He said to these people: he is their guardian in a life like this life of yours, which was the life that belonged to them. The rest of the verse is a threat.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We have not sent down to you the Book﴾ means the Qur'an. His saying ﴿except that you may make clear﴾ is in the position of a causative object (maf'ul min ajlihi), and His saying ﴿and as guidance and mercy﴾ is coordinated with it, as if He said: "except for clarification," that is, for the sake of clarification. His saying ﴿that about which they differ﴾ is a general expression covering the various kinds of disbelief of the disbelievers: denial of God, the Last Day, prophethood, and other things. However, the reference in this verse is specifically to their denial of divine lordship (rububiyya) and their associating idols with God in divinity, and this is shown by His following this with the proofs of lessons indicating that livestock and all other actions come from God, exalted is He, and not from idols.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And God sent down water from the sky﴾, the verse. When He commanded clarification of what they differed about, He set out the lessons that lead to clarifying the matter of lordship. He began with the blessing of rain, which is the clearest of the lessons, the foundation of life, and wholly manifest, about which no rational person disagrees. The giving of life and death to the earth is a metaphor and a comparison with living beings: when it is dormant, dusty and unproductive, it is like the dead; when it sprouts, turns green, stirs and swells, it is like the living. His saying "they listen" indicates that this lesson is manifest in itself and its clarification, because it does not require reflection or insight of the heart; rather, the one being admonished only needs to hear the statement.

"Al-an'am" are the four kinds: camels, cattle, sheep and goats. "Al-'ibra" is the state in which one takes a lesson. Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim (in the transmission of Abu Bakr), Ibn Mas'ud (with variant), al-Hasan, and the people of Madina read "nasqikum" with a fatha on the nun, from asqa yasqi. The rest of the readers, and Hafs from 'Asim, read it with a damma on the nun, and this is the reading of the Kufans and the people of Makka. Some philologists said: they are two dialects with the same meaning. A group said: one says "saqaytuhu" to one whom one gives drink by the lip or once, and one says "asqaytuhu" to one whom one gives a continuous supply or grants a drink; and this is the view of those who read "nasqikum," because the milk of livestock is a continuous provision for humans. Those who said they are two dialects with the same meaning recited the verse of Labid:

"Saqa qawmi Banu Badrin wa-asqa / Numayran wa-l-qaba'ila min Hilali"

And that is necessary, because he does not pray for his people with what is little. Abu Raja' read "yasqikum" with ya', meaning God gives you to drink. A group read "tasqikum" with ta', and it is weak. Likewise the readers differed concerning the surah al-Mu'minun.

His saying ﴿from what is in their bellies﴾: the pronoun refers to the genus and to what was mentioned, as the poet said:

"Like the young birds whose crops have been plucked"

This is common, like His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Nay, indeed it is a reminder﴾ [Abasa: 11] ﴿so whoever wills may remember it﴾ [Abasa: 12]. It was also said: He said "buṭūnihi" because "al-an'am" and "al-na'am" are a singular collective, and the pronoun follows the meaning of "al-na'am." A group said: the pronoun refers to "the part," since males have no milk, so the lesson is in fact only in the females of livestock. "Al-farth" is what descends into the intestines. "Al-sa'igh" is that which is made easy to drink and pleasant. A group read "siyyighan" with the yā' doubled; 'Isa al-Thaqafi read "sayghan" with the yā' sukūn, and this is a lightening of "sayg," like mayyit and hayyin. Its measure is not fi'l, because the word is waw-rooted, so its fa'l form would be "sawgh." It is related that no one has ever choked on milk; this is related from the Prophet (ﷺ).

It is narrated from Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he would not complain of anything except that he treated it with honey, even rubbing it on boils and wounds, and reciting: ﴿in it is healing for mankind﴾.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This implies that he saw healing in it in general. Mujahid said: the pronoun refers to the Qur'an, meaning: in it is healing. Some people of ignorance (ahl al-jahala) went to the view that this verse is intended for the People of the House from the Banu Hashim, and that they are the bees, and that the drink is the Qur'an and wisdom. Some of them mentioned this in the assembly of al-Mansur Abu Ja'far al-'Abbasi, and a man from those present said to him: "May Allah make your food and drink that which comes out of the bellies of the Banu Hashim," so he made the attendees laugh and left the other one perplexed, and the frivolity of his statement became apparent. The rest of the verse is clear.

(p. 379) The words of the Exalted: ﴿And from the fruits of the date palms and grapevines you derive intoxicant and good provision. Indeed, in that is a sign for a people who reason.﴾ ﴿And your Lord inspired to the bee: "Take for yourself houses in the mountains, and in the trees, and in what they construct.﴾ ﴿Then eat from all the fruits and follow the ways of your Lord, made easy." From their bellies emerges a drink of varying colors, in which is healing for mankind. Indeed, in that is a sign for a people who give thought.﴾

Al-Tabari said: The implied meaning is: "And from the fruits of the date palms and grapevines [is] that which you derive." A group said: The implied meaning is: "And from the fruits of the date palms and grapevines [there is] something from which you derive." It is also permissible that His saying "and from the fruits" is a conjunction with "the livestock," meaning: "And for you, from the fruits of the date palms and the livestock, there is a lesson." It is also permissible that it is a conjunction with "of what," meaning: "And We also give you drinks from fruits."

"Al-sakar" (intoxicant) is that which intoxicates; this is the well-known meaning in the language. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: This verse was revealed before the prohibition of wine, and by "al-sakar" he meant wine, and by "good provision" he meant everything that is drunk or eaten, lawfully, from these two trees. Ibn Jubayr, Ibrahim [al-Nakha'i], al-Sha'bi, and Abu Razin also held this view. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: Allah mentioned His blessing in "al-sakar" before the prohibition of wine. Al-Sha'bi and Mujahid said: "Al-sakar" is the vinegar, syrup and nabidh (fermented date drink) derived from these two trees, and "good provision" is grapes and dates. Al-Tabari said: "Al-sakar" also, in the speech of the Arabs, means what is eaten, and al-Tabari preferred this view, and wine is not included in it, and nothing of the verse has been abrogated. Some of the group who considered "al-sakar" to be wine said that this verse is abrogated by the prohibition of wine. In this view there is a flaw, because abrogation (naskh) occurs only in an established, legislated ruling. It is narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Wine was prohibited in its very substance, and intoxicant from other than it." Thus it is narrated, but the sound narration is with a fatha on the sin and the kaf, meaning: everything that intoxicates from it is prohibited in the same manner as the prohibition of wine, its little and its much. The Iraqis narrated it with a damma on the sin and a sukun on the kaf, "al-sukr" (intoxication), and this is based on their jurisprudence that what intoxicates in its large quantity from other than grape wine is lawful in its small quantity. The rest of the verse is clear.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And your Lord inspired to the bee﴾ (the verse). "Wahy" (inspiration) in the speech of the Arabs is the casting of a meaning from the one who inspires to the one inspired, in concealment. From it is the inspiration to the prophets through the message of the Angel, and from it is the inspiration of dreams, and from it is the inspiration of instinct, which is what is meant here by agreement of the exegetes. "Wahy" also means command, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿that your Lord inspired to it﴾. Yahya ibn Wathhab read "ila al-nakhl" (to the palm) with a fatha on the ha. The "an" in His saying "an ittakhidhi" is explanatory (mufassira). Allah has made the bee's houses in these three: either in the mountains and their crevices, or in the hollows of trees, or in what the children of Adam construct of hives and walls and the like. "'Arasha" means: he prepared, and it is most often used for what is made by intertwining branches and wood and arranging their shade. From it is the "arish" (arbor) which was built for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ on the day of Badr, and from this is the word "al-'arsh" (throne). It is said: "'arasha" yaʿrishu and yaʿrushu, with a kasra and a damma on the ra. Ibn 'Amir read with the damma, and the rest with the kasra, and it varied from 'Asim, and the majority of people read with the kasra. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman and 'Ubayd ibn Nadla read with the damma. Ibn Zayd, regarding His saying "ya'rishun," said: "the vines." Al-Tabari said: "wa mimma ya'rishun" means: what they build of roofs.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This explanation from both of them is not well-founded.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Then eat from all the fruits﴾ (the verse). The meaning: then He inspired her that she should eat, so He conjoined "kulí" (eat) to "ittakhidhi" (take), and "min" is partitive, meaning: eat a part or some of all the fruits, because she only eats the blossoms of the trees. "Subul" means the paths, and they are her routes in flying and otherwise, and He attributed them to the Lord because they are His dominion and His creation, meaning: those which your Lord has made easy for you. His saying "dhululan" (made easy) may be a state (hal) of "al-nahl" (the bee), meaning: obedient and submissive to what has been made easy for it, as Qatada said. Ibn Zayd said: they go out with the bees seeking pasture, and the bees follow them. He recited: ﴿Do they not see that We have created for them, from what Our hands have made, livestock which they own?﴾ [Yasin: 71] up to His saying ﴿and they eat﴾ [Yasin: 72]. It may also be a state of "al-subul," meaning: facilitated and straight. Mujahid said: no path that it takes is difficult for it.

Then, Blessed and Exalted is He, mentioned, by way of enumerating the blessing and drawing attention to the lesson, the matter of honey in His saying: ﴿emerges from their bellies﴾. The majority of people hold that honey emerges from the mouths of the bees. It is reported from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said, in belittling the world: "The most noble garment of the children of Adam in it is the spittle of a worm, and the most noble of its drinks is the dung of a bee." The apparent meaning of this is that it comes from other than the mouth. The variation of colors in honey is according to the variation of the bees and the pastures, and its taste may vary according to the variation of the pastures. From this meaning is the statement of Zaynab to the Prophet ﷺ: "His bees graze on the 'urfut (a tree)," when she likened its smell to the smell of the maghafir (a sweet-smelling gum).
