Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 16, verse 70–72:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿And Allah created you, then He takes you in death; and among you is he who is returned to the most abject age, so that he knows nothing after having known. Indeed, Allah is Knowing, Competent.﴾ ﴿And Allah has favoured some of you over others in provision. Yet those who have been favoured do not give their provision to those whom their right hands possess, so that they are equal in it. Then do they deny the favour of Allah?﴾ ﴿And Allah has made for you spouses from yourselves, and made for you from your spouses sons and grandchildren, and provided for you of the good things. Then in falsehood do they believe, and in the favour of Allah do they disbelieve?﴾

This is a reminder to take heed of our bringing into existence after non-existence and our causing to die after that. Then he turns to those among people who are reduced to the lowest state, because they are a place of lesson. The phrase ﴿the most abject age﴾ means its last part, in which the senses decline and speech deteriorates. That is specified as the abject condition, although the state of childhood is similar in this respect, insofar as hope is attached to it, whereas childhood is only a beginning, and hope in it is firmly established. Some people said: the beginning of the most abject age is seventy-five years; this is related from ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is the general case, and it is not confined to a specific period; rather it varies from person to person. The meaning is: among you is he who is returned to the most abject age of his life. Many a person who is fifty years old is in his most abject age, and many a person who is a hundred or ninety years old is not in his most abject age. The lām in "li-kaylā" appears to be the lām of outcome (lām al-ṣayrūra), but this is not evident. The meaning is: so that his state, after knowledge of things, ends with his not knowing anything. This is an expression for the scarcity of his knowledge, not that he knows nothing at all. The "lā" does not intervene between "kay" and its governed element, because of its flexibility, and because it may be superfluous. Then, may He be blessed and exalted, affirmed His knowledge and His power, which do not change, are not altered by events, and are not transformed.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah has favoured some of you over others in provision﴾ is a report intended as a lesson, and it is only a principle upon which the parable is built. The parable is that those who are favoured cannot properly share with their slaves what they have been given, so that their conditions become equal. If this is so in the small matter, how do you, O disbelievers, attribute to Allah, exalted is He, that He permits idols and images to be associated in His divinity, when they are His creation, and other things that were worshipped, such as the angels and the prophets, who are His servants and creation? This is the interpretation of al-Ṭabarī, and he related it from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both. It is also related from him that the verse alludes to ʿĪsā, peace be upon him. The exegetes said: this verse is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He has struck for you a parable from yourselves﴾ [al-Rūm: 28], and so on. Then He made them confront their denial of the favour of Allah, by alerting them to such a place of reflection which leads to (p-383) faith. Al-Jumhūr, and Ḥafṣ from ʿĀṣim, read "yajḥadūn" with the yāʾ at the beginning; Abū Bakr from ʿĀṣim read it with the tāʾ, and this is the reading of Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān and al-Aʿraj (according to a variant from him). It carries the meaning: say to them, O Muḥammad. Qatādah said: denial occurs only after recognition.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah has made for you﴾ and so on, is a verse enumerating blessings. "Al-azwāj" means the spouses, and in this verse no categories or anything else are implied. His saying: ﴿from yourselves﴾ may mean that He created Ḥawwāʾ from the self and body of Ādam; since the two were the origin of all, the matter may be applied to all, until it is as if women were created from the selves of men. This is the saying of Qatādah. My own view, however, is that by His saying ﴿from yourselves﴾ He means: of your kind and of your nature, as He said: ﴿There has certainly come to you a Messenger from yourselves﴾ [al-Tawbah: 128], and so on. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and made for you from your spouses sons﴾ clearly enumerates the blessing of children. People differed regarding His saying "ḥafadah". Ibn ʿAbbās said: the ḥafadah are the children's children. al-Ḥasan said: they are your sons and your sons' sons. Ibn Masʿūd, Abū al-Ḍuḥā, Ibrāhīm and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: the ḥafadah are the in-laws, who are the wife's relatives. Mujāhid said: the ḥafadah are the helpers, the assistants and the servants. al-Zajjāj related that some of them said the ḥifdah are the daughters; al-Zahrāwī said: because they serve their parents, and because the word "banīn" (sons) does not refer to them. Do you not see that they are not included in the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted: ﴿Wealth and children are the adornment of the life of this world﴾ [al-Kahf: 46]? The adornment lies only in males. Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, also said: the ḥafadah are the children of a man's wife by another man. There is no disagreement that the meaning of "al-ḥafd" is service, dutifulness, and walking swiftly in obedience; and from it is the phrase in the qunūt: "and to You we hasten and serve (nuḥfid)". Al-ḥafadān is a trot above walking. From it is the saying of the poet, who is Jamīl ibn Muʿammar:

Serving maidens hasten among them, and the reins of the camels are given into their hands.

And from it is the saying of another:

I burdened her unknown [camel] with Yemeni she-camels, when the drivers hastened upon their saddles.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

These groups whose sayings I have mentioned are all built on the premise that each person is given sons and grandchildren from his spouses, and this is in the majority of cases and for most people. In my view it is possible that His saying ﴿from your spouses﴾ is general and inclusive, meaning: from the spouses of mankind Allah has made sons for them, and from among them He made servants. Whoever has no wife, Allah has made for him ḥafadah and he has obtained that blessing; and those ḥafadah are of the spouses. Thus the blessing that encompasses all the world is arranged, and the word "ḥafadah" remains in its linguistic course, since mankind as a whole cannot dispense with ḥafadah. A group said: the ḥafadah are the sons.

(p-385)The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is consistent if the waw is conjunctive, describing them, as if one said: We gave them sons and helpers, meaning: and they are helpers to them; so it is as if he said: and they are ḥafadah.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and provided for you of the good things﴾ means: the pleasant things among those things which are agreeable to whoever is provided with them. It is not restricted here to the lawful, because they are disbelievers who do not earn by any law. In this verse there is a refutation of those among the Muʿtazilah who said: "Provision is only what is lawful." They hold an argument based on the particle "min", since it indicates partiality, and they say: the provision enumerated for them is not all that is in their hands, but only what is lawful.

Al-Jumhūr read "yu'minūn" (with the alif, as "yu'minūn" in the sense of belief). On this reading the verse is a reproach to Muḥammad, peace and blessings be upon him, for their belief in falsehood and their disbelief in the favour of Allah. Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān read with the tāʾ from above, and it is also reported from ʿĀṣim, with the meaning: say to them, O Muḥammad. His saying after that: ﴿and in the favour of Allah do they disbelieve﴾ is then a plain report about them and a judgement upon them, not a reproach. It may also be possible that the reproach is present, though with less consistency in the wording.

If this is so in the small matter, how do you, O disbelievers, attribute to Allah, exalted is He, that He permits idols and images to be associated in His divinity, when they are His creation, and other things that were worshipped, such as the angels and the prophets, who are His servants and creation? This is the interpretation of al-Ṭabarī, and he related it from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both. It is also related from him that the verse alludes to ʿĪsā, peace be upon him. The exegetes said: this verse is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He has struck for you a parable from yourselves﴾ [al-Rūm: 28], and so on. Then He made them confront their denial of the favour of Allah, by alerting them to such a place of reflection which leads to (p-383) faith. Al-Jumhūr, and Ḥafṣ from ʿĀṣim, read "yajḥadūn" with the yāʾ at the beginning; Abū Bakr from ʿĀṣim read it with the tāʾ, and this is the reading of Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān and al-Aʿraj (according to a variant from him). It carries the meaning: say to them, O Muḥammad. Qatādah said: denial occurs only after recognition.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah has made for you﴾ and so on, is a verse enumerating blessings. "Al-azwāj" means the spouses, and in this verse no categories or anything else are implied. His saying: ﴿from yourselves﴾ may mean that He created Ḥawwāʾ from the self and body of Ādam; since the two were the origin of all, the matter may be applied to all, until it is as if women were created from the selves of men. This is the saying of Qatādah. My own view, however, is that by His saying ﴿from yourselves﴾ He means: of your kind and of your nature, as He said: ﴿There has certainly come to you a Messenger from yourselves﴾ [al-Tawbah: 128], and so on. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and made for you from your spouses sons﴾ clearly enumerates the blessing of children. People differed regarding His saying "ḥafadah". Ibn ʿAbbās said: the ḥafadah are the children's children. al-Ḥasan said: they are your sons and your sons' sons. Ibn Masʿūd, Abū al-Ḍuḥā, Ibrāhīm and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: the ḥafadah are the in-laws, who are the wife's relatives. Mujāhid said: the ḥafadah are the helpers, the assistants and the servants. al-Zajjāj related that some of them said the ḥifdah are the daughters; al-Zahrāwī said: because they serve their parents, and because the word "banīn" (sons) does not refer to them. Do you not see that they are not included in the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted: ﴿Wealth and children are the adornment of the life of this world﴾ [al-Kahf: 46]? The adornment lies only in males. Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, also said: the ḥafadah are the children of a man's wife by another man. There is no disagreement that the meaning of "al-ḥafd" is service, dutifulness, and walking swiftly in obedience; and from it is the phrase in the qunūt: "and to You we hasten and serve (nuḥfid)". Al-ḥafadān is a trot above walking. From it is the saying of the poet, who is Jamīl ibn Muʿammar:

Serving maidens hasten among them, and the reins of the camels are given into their hands.

And from it is the saying of another:

I burdened her unknown [camel] with Yemeni she-camels, when the drivers hastened upon their saddles.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

These groups whose sayings I have mentioned are all built on the premise that each person is given sons and grandchildren from his spouses, and this is in the majority of cases and for most people. In my view it is possible that His saying ﴿from your spouses﴾ is general and inclusive, meaning: from the spouses of mankind Allah has made sons for them, and from among them He made servants. Whoever has no wife, Allah has made for him ḥafadah and he has obtained that blessing; and those ḥafadah are of the spouses. Thus the blessing that encompasses all the world is arranged, and the word "ḥafadah" remains in its linguistic course, since mankind as a whole cannot dispense with ḥafadah. A group said: the ḥafadah are the sons.

(p-385)The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is consistent if the waw is conjunctive, describing them, as if one said: We gave them sons and helpers, meaning: and they are helpers to them; so it is as if he said: and they are ḥafadah.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and provided for you of the good things﴾ means: the pleasant things among those things which are agreeable to whoever is provided with them. It is not restricted here to the lawful, because they are disbelievers who do not earn by any law. In this verse there is a refutation of those among the Muʿtazilah who said: "Provision is only what is lawful." They hold an argument based on the particle "min", since it indicates partiality, and they say: the provision enumerated for them is not all that is in their hands, but only what is lawful.

Al-Jumhūr read "yu'minūn" (with the alif, as "yu'minūn" in the sense of belief). On this reading the verse is a reproach to Muḥammad, peace and blessings be upon him, for their belief in falsehood and their disbelief in the favour of Allah. Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān read with the tāʾ from above, and it is also reported from ʿĀṣim, with the meaning: say to them, O Muḥammad. His saying after that: ﴿and in the favour of Allah do they disbelieve﴾ is then a plain report about them and a judgement upon them, not a reproach. It may also be possible that the reproach is present, though with less consistency in the wording.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 16, verse 73–75:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿And they worship, besides Allah, that which possesses for them no provision from the heavens or the earth, nor are they able﴾ ﴿So do not set up comparisons for Allah. Indeed, Allah knows, and you do not know﴾ ﴿Allah presents an example: a slave owned, who has power over nothing, and one whom We have provided with good provision from Us, so he spends from it secretly and openly. Are they equal? Praise be to Allah! But most of them do not know﴾

This is a verse of reproach and rebuke for the disbelievers, and a demonstration of the corruption of their reasoning, and a placing before them of the idols in the very domain where people strive and direct their concerns, which is the seeking of provision. These idols do not possess the sending down of rain or the growing of any blessing, and, moreover, they do not possess, nor are they able even to attempt that, any part of the dominion of Allah, the Exalted. His saying "rizqan" (provision) is a verbal noun (maṣdar), and it is in the accusative as the object of "yamliku" (possesses).

As for His saying "shay'an" (anything), many of the grammarians hold that it is in the accusative as a substitute (badal) for "rizqan", and "rizqan" is a noun. The Kufans, and Abu 'Ali along with them, hold that it is in the accusative governed by the verbal noun in His saying "rizqan", and we do not take it as a noun. This is like His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Have We not made the earth a receptacle﴾ [al-Mursalat: 25] ﴿for the living and the dead?﴾ [al-Mursalat: 26], and from it His saying: ﴿or feeding on a day of hunger﴾ [al-Balad: 14] ﴿an orphan﴾ [al-Balad: 15], where "yatiman" (an orphan) is in the accusative governed by "it'am" (feeding). And from it is the saying of the poet:

﴿Had it not been for hope of victory from you and fear﴾ ∗∗∗ ﴿of your punishment, they would have become for us like watering-troughs.﴾

The verbal noun governs when it is in the genitive construct (idafa) by agreement, because it is in the sense of separation. It does not govern when the alif and lam (definite article) enter upon it, because it has become deeply rooted in the status of nouns and far removed from the status of the verb. The sense of separation in the construct form made its governing acceptable. It has come governing with the alif and lam in the saying of the poet:

﴿weak in inflicting harm on his enemies﴾

And his saying:

﴿from striking, hearing (one)﴾

As for His, the Exalted, saying "yamliku" (possesses), it is in agreement with the wording of "ma" (that which), and His saying "yastati'una" (they are able) is in agreement with its meaning, according to the disbelievers' belief that the idols understand. It is possible that the pronoun in "yastati'una" refers to those who worship, and the meaning is: they are not able to do that with any proof they might display or any argument they might make clear.

As for His saying ﴿fa-la tadribu﴾ (so do not set up), i.e., do not make likenesses for Allah. It is derived from your saying "darib hadha", i.e., its like, and "al-darb" means the kind; you say: animals are of various kinds (durub), and these two are of one kind. The rest of the verse is clear.

As for His, the Exalted, saying ﴿Allah presents an example﴾, the verse. The example in this verse is a slave with this attribute, owned, who has no power over any wealth or over his own affair; rather he is subjected and managed by the will of his master. It does not follow from the verse that all slaves are in this condition, as some of those who claim to be jurists have drawn out. He said in the second example: ﴿who has power over nothing﴾, so on this line of reasoning it would follow that the mute have nothing. Opposite the slave in the example is a man who is given wide means of wealth, so he disposes of it by his will. It does not follow from the example itself that he is a believer who spends in accordance with obedience; however, it is more noble that he be an example.

"Rizq" (provision) is that from which benefit is validly obtained. Abu Mansur said in his creed: "Rizq is that by which nourishment has occurred." This verse refutes this restriction, and likewise His, the Exalted, saying ﴿and from what We have provided them they spend﴾ [al-Baqara: 3] and ﴿spend from what We have provided you﴾ [al-Baqara: 254], and other than that, from the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "My provision has been placed in the shade of my spear," and his saying: "The provisions of my community are in the hooves of their horses and the points of their spears," so the entire spoil is provision. The correct view is that what is validly benefited from is provision, and it has degrees, the highest of which is that by which one is nourished. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) confined the aspects of benefit in his saying: "The son of Adam says: 'My wealth, my wealth.' Do you have any wealth other than what you have eaten and so consumed, or worn and so worn out, or given in charity and so sent ahead?" And within the meaning of clothing is included riding.

People differed about the one to whom this example refers. Qatada and Ibn 'Abbas said: it is the likeness of the disbeliever and the believer; as if the disbeliever is a owned slave, diverted from obedience, so he has no power over anything for that reason, and he resembles the slave mentioned.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The comparison, according to this interpretation, occurs only in respect of the disbeliever; an example is made for him, then he is paired with the believer who is provided for, unless the one provided for is not a believer, and he is merely an example for the believer, so the comparison occurs from two aspects.

Mujahid and al-Dahhak said: this example, and the other example after it, are only for Allah and the idols; thus those are like the owned slave who has no power over anything, while Allah, the Exalted, has power whose dominion is unopposed. Al-Zajjaj also interpreted it in a manner similar to Mujahid's.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This interpretation is more correct, because the verse fits with what precedes and follows it in clarifying the command of Allah, blessed and exalted, and refuting the idols. Al-Tabari mentioned from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: this verse was revealed concerning 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, may Allah be pleased with him, and a slave he had. Other than this has been reported, but its chain is not sound. The example does not need the specification of any individual. His saying ﴿Praise be to Allah﴾ is thanks for the clarification of the matter through this example, and for the opponent's acquiescence to it, just as you say to one who has conceded to you in an argument and accepted what your statement is built upon: "Allahu akbar," and "on this basis it is such-and-such." So when He said here ﴿Are they equal?﴾, it is as if the opponent said to Him: "No," so He said: "Praise be to Allah," the proof has become manifest. His saying ﴿But most of them do not know﴾ means they will never know, and faith will never enter them. On this interpretation the phrase "most of them" is well-grounded, because the fewer among the disbelievers are those of them who believed. Had He meant by ﴿do not know﴾ "now," the phrase "most of them" would have meant totality, since none of them knew His saying.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 16, verses 76–79:

His words, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿Allah sets forth a parable: two men, one of them mute, who has no power over anything and is a burden on his master. Wherever he directs him, he brings no good. Is he equal to one who enjoins justice and is upon a straight path?﴾

﴿To Allah belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth. The matter of the Hour is but as a glance of the eye, or it is nearer. Indeed Allah is over all things competent.﴾

﴿And Allah brought you out from the wombs of your mothers, knowing nothing, and made for you hearing, sight and hearts, that you may be grateful.﴾

﴿Have they not considered the birds, subjected in the atmosphere of the sky? None holds them up except Allah. Indeed in that are signs for a people who believe.﴾

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 16, verse 80–81:

(p-392) His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿And Allah has made for you, from your houses, a place of rest, and has made for you, from the hides of cattle, dwellings which you find light [to carry] on the day of your moving and the day of your settling, and from their wool, their fur and their hair [He has made] furnishings and provision for a time.﴾ ﴿And Allah has made for you, from what He has created, shades; and has made for you, from the mountains, refuges; and has made for you garments which protect you from the heat, and garments which protect you from your violence. Thus does He complete His favour upon you, that you may submit.﴾

This is a verse enumerating Allah's blessing upon people concerning houses. He first mentioned the houses of settled life (al-tamaddun), which are those for long-term residence, and they are the bulk of human dwellings, although the description "sakan" (a place of rest) encompasses all houses. "Sakan" is a verbal noun (maṣdar) that is applied as a description of the singular, and its meaning is: one dwells in it and toward it. Then Exalted is He mentioned the houses of travel and journeying.

His saying: ﴿and has made for you, from the hides of cattle, dwellings﴾ may be understood to include tents of leather (al-udum), tents of hair, and tents of wool, because these are made of hides by virtue of their being attached to them. Ibn Salam inclined to this view. And His saying: ﴿and from their wool﴾ would then be a new sentence, as if He had said: "He made furnishings," meaning garments and bedding and other things. It is also possible that by His saying: ﴿from the hides of cattle﴾ He means only leather tents, and that ﴿and from their wool﴾ is a conjunction with His saying ﴿from the hides of cattle﴾, meaning: He also made dwellings [from them]; and His saying "furnishings" would then be in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl). And "tastakhiffūnahā" means you find them light (khifāf). Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read "ẓa'anikum" with a fatha on the ʿayn; Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it with a sukun on the ʿayn. These are two dialects, and it is not a case of lightening (takhfif). "Ẓaʿana" means he journeyed (raḥala). "Al-aṣwāf" are for sheep, "al-awbār" for camels, and "al-ashʿār" for goats and cattle. Their lands were not lands of cotton and linen, which is why He limited Himself to this. It is possible that the mention of cotton, silk and linen was omitted out of disapproval of extravagance, since the clothing of the righteous servants of Allah is indeed wool. Moreover, cotton and linen have been alluded to in the word "sarābīl". "Al-athāth" is the household goods; its singular is "athātha". This is the statement of Abu Zayd al-Ansari, while others said: "al-athāth" is all kinds of property, and it has no singular from its own form.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Etymology supports this more general meaning, because a person's condition becomes "athītha" (abundant) through property. One says: "shaʿrun athīthun, wa nabātun athīthun" (thick hair, and thick vegetation) when it becomes abundant and dense. His saying: ﴿until a time﴾ means by it an unspecified time, which differs for each person, either by his death or by the loss of those things which are furnishings. (p-393) From this word is the saying of the poet:

؎ Did the caravans stir you on the day they departed, with the fine adornment of household goods?

His, Exalted is He, saying: ﴿And Allah has made for you, from what He has created, shades﴾, etc. These are blessings which He enumerated to them according to their conditions and lands, and they are the things directly present to them, because their land is so hot and scorched by the sun that shade has great benefit and clear utility. His saying: ﴿from what He has created﴾ includes all the shaded objects. "Al-akনān" is the plural of "kinn", which is that which protects from rain, wind and other things. "Al-sarābīl" is everything worn over the whole body, such as the shirt, the qarqal, the mujul, the armour, the jawshan, the ḥiffatān and the like. He mentioned protection from heat, since it is the prevalent condition in those lands as we have mentioned, while cold there is absent for the most part; and when winter comes, they protect themselves with what is thicker than the sirbāl from the furnishings mentioned earlier. Thus the sarābīl remain to protect only from heat. This was said by al-Tabari, from ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurasani. Do you not see that Allah, Exalted is He, alerted them to the lesson in the cold but did not mention snow to them, because it is not in their lands? Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "Snow is a white thing that descends from the sky; I have never seen it at all." Moreover, mentioning one of them indicates the other. From this is the saying of the poet:

؎ And I do not know, when I head toward a land, desiring good, which of the two will befall me?

(p-394) These that we have mentioned are the lands of the Hijaz; otherwise, in the lands of the Arabs there is intense cold, and from this is the saying of Mutammim:

؎ When the hide, from the cold of winter, rattled.

And from it is the saying of another:

؎ On a night of Jumada, full of dews.

The two lines, and other than these. The sarābīl which protect from violence are the armour, and from it is the saying of Ka'b ibn Zuhayr:

؎ Lofty of noses, champions whose garments are of the weaving of Dawud in battle, are sarābīl.

(p-395) And Aws ibn Hajar said:

؎ And excellent is the padding of the armour and the sirbāl.

So this is meant as the shirt.

"Al-ba's" is the touching of iron in war. The majority read "yutimmu niʿmatahu" (He completes His favour); Ibn ʿAbbas read "tatimmu niʿmatuhu" (His favour is completed), taking the favour as the thing that is completed; it is also narrated from him "tatimmu niʿamuhu" in the plural. The majority read "tuslimūn" from Islam (islām); Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, read "taslamūn" from safety (salāma), so the word is specific to the violence of war. And what is in "laʿalla" of hoping and expectation belongs to the realm of the addressed humans; that is, if an observer considered this condition, he would hope from it that they submit (islām).

Then Exalted is He mentioned the houses of travel and journeying.

Their lands were not lands of cotton and linen, which is why He limited Himself to this. This is the statement of Abu Zayd al-Ansari, while others said: "al-athāth" is all kinds of property, and it has no singular from its own form.

The Exalted and Majestic says:

﴿But if they turn away, then upon you is only the clear conveyance.﴾ ﴿They recognize the favor of God, then they deny it, and most of them are disbelievers.﴾ ﴿And on the Day We raise up from every nation a witness, then permission will not be given to those who disbelieved, nor will they be asked to make amends.﴾ ﴿And when those who did wrong see the punishment, it will not be lightened for them, nor will they be reprieved.﴾

This verse contains a *muwada'a* (a temporary truce), which was abrogated (*naskh*) by the verse of the sword (*ayat al-sayf*). The meaning is: if they turn away, you are not able to create faith in their hearts. Your duty is only to make clear and convey the command and prohibition of God. Then He rebuked and reproached them, saying that they recognize God's favor in the things mentioned, and say that they come from Him, and then they disbelieve in Him, may He be exalted. That is the act of one who denies a blessing and rejects it. This is the statement of Mujahid, who called them "deniers of the blessing" by way of *tajawwuz* (figurative usage), since they did the actions of deniers, namely disbelief in the Lord of the blessings, and because they associated the idols with the blessings in some way, attributing to the idols the acts of benefit and harm that they believed the idols performed.

Al-Suddi said: "The blessing here is Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him." He described them, blessed and exalted is He, as recognizing (p-396) his miracles and the signs of his prophethood, and denying them by rejecting them. Al-Tabari preferred this view. Then He judged most of them to be disbelievers, and they were the people of Makkah, because among them were those who had already entered Islam and those who embraced Islam afterwards.

God's words: ﴿And on the Day We raise up from every nation a witness﴾ are a threat. The implied sense is: "Remember the Day when We raise up and send a witness against their disbelief and their belief." Here *shahid* carries the meaning of *shahid* (the active participle, "witness"). Al-Tabari mentioned that the meaning is: "Then they deny it today, and on the Day We raise up, that is, they deny their disbelief, and the witness refutes them." His words: ﴿then permission will not be given﴾ mean that permission is not given to those who disbelieved to offer an excuse. This applies to one station and not another, because the Qur'an states that every soul comes disputing on its own behalf, and it follows that every soul will come arguing. When their statements have been completed, God raises up witnesses from the nations, and they refute the disbelievers, so the liars are not then permitted to offer an excuse. ﴿Nor will they be asked to make amends﴾ means: they will not be asked to be pleased (*yu'tabun*). You say "*'ataba al-rajul*" (I pleased the man) when you remove from him what displeased him, just as you say "*ashkaytu-hu ma shaka*" (I removed from him what he complained of). It is as if He said: nor will they be relieved of what displeases them and what is hard for them. The Arabs use *istaf'ala* in the sense of *af'ala*: you say "*adnaytu al-rajul*" and "*istadnaytu-hu*" (I brought the man near). Some people said: they will not ask to return to what they were upon in the world.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: This is *isti'tab* (seeking to be pleased), meaning the request to have their displeasure removed. Al-Tabari said: its meaning is that they seek to return to the world, but they are not granted this, so no repentance through action takes place from them.

God's words: ﴿And when those who did wrong see the punishment﴾: in this verse God, Exalted is He, informs us that these disbelieving wrongdoers, in their disbelief, when God shows them the punishment of the Fire, approach it and realize the reality of its severity, that this terrible matter that befalls them will not be lightened in any way, nor postponed for them. The purpose of the verse is to distinguish between what befalls them and the calamities of the world. A person does not expect a matter of the world's misfortunes without hoping that it will be delayed, or that it will come in the lightest form he imagines. Likewise, when it befalls him, he hopes that it will be lighter. This often happens with the world's misfortunes. God, Exalted is He, therefore informs us that the punishment of the Hereafter, when the disbeliever witnesses it, has no hope of lightening or postponement.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 16, verses 86–89:**

The Most High said:

﴿When those who associated partners with God see their partners, they will say, "Our Lord, these are our partners whom we used to call upon besides You." But they will throw the word back at them: "You are indeed liars."﴾ ﴿And on that day they will offer submission to God, and what they used to fabricate will vanish from them.﴾ ﴿As for those who disbelieved and barred others from the way of God, We will increase their punishment upon punishment, because of their corruption.﴾ ﴿On the Day when We raise up in every nation a witness against them from among themselves, and We bring you as a witness against these people. We have sent down to you the Book as an explanation of all things, a guidance, a mercy, and good tidings for those who submit.﴾

He, glorified and exalted, informs that on the Day of Resurrection, when they see with their eyes the idols, the images, and every object of worship besides God (because they will be gathered with them as a rebuke to them before all witnesses), they will point to them and say: "These are the ones we used to worship besides God." It seems they intended by this to make the objects of worship culpable and to draw them into sin. They attributed the partners to themselves, since they are the ones who made them partners. This is like a man who describes another person as good, and you say to him, "What has become of your good man?" You attribute him to him, because he is the one who described him with that quality. The pronoun in "the word" (al-qawl) refers to the partners. Whoever among the worshipped ones was a human being cast the known word with his tongue. Whatever was inanimate spoke by the power of God, denying the polytheists' description of them as gods and partners of God. In this, the lie occurred, not in the worship itself. Al-Tabari said: the meaning is, "Indeed, you are liars; we did not call you to worship us."

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: So they denied to them their having made them culpable.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 16, verses 90–91:**

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿Indeed, Allah commands justice (al-'adl) and excellence (al-ihsan), and giving to relatives, and forbids indecency, wrongdoing, and oppression. He admonishes you that you may remember.﴾ ﴿And fulfill the covenant of Allah when you have made it, and do not break oaths after their confirmation, and you have already made Allah your surety. Indeed, Allah knows what you do.﴾

'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "The most comprehensive verse in the Book of Allah is the verse in Surat an-Nahl," and he recited this verse. It is also narrated from 'Uthman ibn Maz'un, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "When this verse was revealed, I recited it to 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, and he was amazed and said: 'O family of Ghalib, follow him and you will prosper. By Allah, Allah sent him to you to command noble character.'" Al-Naqqash related: "It was said: 'The zakat of justice is excellence, the zakat of power is pardon, the zakat of wealth is kindness, and the zakat of status is that a man writes to his brothers.'"

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Justice (al-'adl) is the performance of every obligation, whether of beliefs or of laws, and conduct with people in the discharge of trusts, abstaining from wrongdoing, fairness, and giving what is due. Excellence (al-ihsan) is the performance of every recommended act. Among things, some are wholly recommended, and some are obligatory; but the minimum of what suffices (hadd al-ijza') falls within justice, and the perfecting addition beyond the minimum of sufficiency falls within excellence. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said, as related by al-Tabari: "Justice is: there is no god but Allah, and excellence is: performing the obligatory duties."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

In this last statement there is room for consideration, because performing the obligatory duties is Islam as the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) explained it in the hadith of Jibril's (peace be upon him) questioning. That is justice. Excellence is rather the perfecting additions and what is recommended, as the Prophet's (ﷺ) explanation of Jibril's (peace be upon him) question requires, in his saying: "That you worship Allah as if you see Him, and if you do not see Him, indeed He sees you." If this is authentically reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, then he meant the performance of obligatory duties in their perfected form.

﴿And giving to relatives﴾: the wording requires maintaining ties of kinship (silat al-rahim), and it encompasses every kind of conferring good upon relatives. Leaving it unspecified is more eloquent, because whoever reaches a limit in this matter, however high, sees himself as falling short. This meaning commanded regarding relatives falls within justice and excellence, but Allah, the Exalted, singled it out for mention, showing concern for it and making it binding.

"Al-fahsha'" (indecency) is fornication (al-zina), as Ibn 'Abbas said, and other sins whose ugliness is evident and whose doer always conceals them. It seems they specified it with matters of the private parts. "Al-munkar" (wrongdoing) is more general than it, because it encompasses all sins, vices, and harms in their various kinds. "Al-baghy" (oppression) is initiating injustice against a person and working toward it. It falls within wrongdoing, but Allah, the Exalted, singled it out for mention, showing concern for it because of the severity of its harm to people. The Prayer and peace of Allah be upon him said: "No sin is quicker in punishment than oppression," and he (ﷺ) said: "The oppressor is overthrown." Allah has promised victory to whoever is oppressed. In some of the revealed books: "If one mountain oppressed another mountain, Allah would make the oppressor of them both crumble to dust."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Changing wrongdoing is obligatory upon the rulers, but the one who changes it should not pursue those who conceal themselves, should not act on suspicion, should not spy, and should change only what is openly displayed, and his command and prohibition should be with kindness. All this applies more strongly to non-rulers, and it is an obligation upon Muslims in general, as long as the one who changes it does not fear harm or humiliation. The believer should not change it with his hand if he finds no authority, but if such authority is absent, he changes it with his hand. However, he does not reach the point of taking up fighting, confrontation, or wielding weapons except under leadership and a followed imam. It is fitting for people that every one of them should change wrongdoing, the pious and the non-pious alike. If only the pious changed it, wrongdoing would for the most part not be changed. Allah, the Exalted, censured a people for not forbidding one another from it. Every wrongdoing that involves room for analysis (ijtihad) is not entered by anyone except the bearers of knowledge. This is a summary of discourse on changing wrongdoing, which contains eight conditions. It is related that a group of the Companions lodged a complaint against their governor with Abu Ja'far al-Mansur, but the governor argued against them and prevailed, since they had not established against him any great injustice or tyranny in anything. Then a young man from the group stood up and said: "O Commander of the Faithful, indeed Allah commanded justice and excellence, and he has been just but has not been excellent." He said: "Abu Ja'far was amazed at his accuracy and dismissed the governor."

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And fulfill the covenant of Allah when you have made it﴾ — the verse. It includes, through His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah commands justice and excellence﴾, the previous verse, as if it said: "Do this and abstain from that." So He conjoined to that implied sense His saying "and fulfill." "The covenant of Allah" is a term for everything that is contracted by the tongue and binds a person, such as a sale, a tie of kinship, or a pact in a matter that agrees with the religion. His saying ﴿and do not break oaths after their confirmation﴾ singled out in this verse the familiar expressions with which oaths are joined, emphasizing them and drawing attention to them.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

All this applies where persisting in the oath is obedience to Allah, the Exalted, whereas where turning away from it is more correct in truth, this is what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) spoke of when he said: "Whoever swears an oath and then sees something else as better than it, let him make expiation for his oath and do what is better." It is said: "tawkid" and "ta'kid," and "wakkada" and "akkada," both being dialects. Al-Zajjaj said: "The hamza is substituted from a waw."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is not clear, because there is nothing in the morphological forms of the word that indicates this.

"Kafilan" means: one who takes responsibility for your fulfilling (of the covenant). The rest of the verse is a warning within the form of a report about Allah's knowledge of His servants' deeds. A group said: this verse was revealed concerning those who pledged allegiance to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) upon Islam; Abu Layla related it from Buraydah. Qatada, Mujahid, and Ibn Zayd said: it was revealed concerning the alliances of the Jahiliyya in matters of commanding good or forbidding wrong, which Islam made stronger.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

As the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "There is no alliance in Islam, and whatever alliance existed in the Jahiliyya, Islam only strengthened." This is a hadith in meaning. And even if the occasion of revelation was some of these matters, the wording of the verse is general, addressed to all the worlds.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Justice (al-'adl) is the performance of every obligation, whether of beliefs or of laws, and conduct with people in the discharge of trusts, abstaining from wrongdoing, fairness, and giving what is due. Excellence (al-ihsan) is the performance of every recommended act. Among things, some are wholly recommended, and some are obligatory; but the minimum of what suffices (hadd al-ijza') falls within justice, and the perfecting addition beyond the minimum of sufficiency falls within excellence. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said, as related by al-Tabari: "Justice is: there is no god but Allah, and excellence is: performing the obligatory duties."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

In this last statement there is room for consideration, because performing the obligatory duties is Islam as the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) explained it in the hadith of Jibril's (peace be upon him) questioning. That is justice. Excellence is rather the perfecting additions and what is recommended, as the Prophet's (ﷺ) explanation of Jibril's (peace be upon him) question requires, in his saying: "That you worship Allah as if you see Him, and if you do not see Him, indeed He sees you." If this is authentically reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, then he meant the performance of obligatory duties in their perfected form.

﴿And giving to relatives﴾: the wording requires maintaining ties of kinship (silat al-rahim), and it encompasses every kind of conferring good upon relatives. Leaving it unspecified is more eloquent, because whoever reaches a limit in this matter, however high, sees himself as falling short. This meaning commanded regarding relatives falls within justice and excellence, but Allah, the Exalted, singled it out for mention, showing concern for it and making it binding.

"Al-fahsha'" (indecency) is fornication (al-zina), as Ibn 'Abbas said, and other sins whose ugliness is evident and whose doer always conceals them. It seems they specified it with matters of the private parts. "Al-munkar" (wrongdoing) is more general than it, because it encompasses all sins, vices, and harms in their various kinds. "Al-baghy" (oppression) is initiating injustice against a person and working toward it. It falls within wrongdoing, but Allah, the Exalted, singled it out for mention, showing concern for it because of the severity of its harm to people. The Prayer and peace of Allah be upon him said: "No sin is quicker in punishment than oppression," and he (ﷺ) said: "The oppressor is overthrown." Allah has promised victory to whoever is oppressed. In some of the revealed books: "If one mountain oppressed another mountain, Allah would make the oppressor of them both crumble to dust."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Changing wrongdoing is obligatory upon the rulers, but the one who changes it should not pursue those who conceal themselves, should not act on suspicion, should not spy, and should change only what is openly displayed, and his command and prohibition should be with kindness. All this applies more strongly to non-rulers, and it is an obligation upon Muslims in general, as long as the one who changes it does not fear harm or humiliation. The believer should not change it with his hand if he finds no authority, but if such authority is absent, he changes it with his hand. However, he does not reach the point of taking up fighting, confrontation, or wielding weapons except under leadership and a followed imam. It is fitting for people that every one of them should change wrongdoing, the pious and the non-pious alike. If only the pious changed it, wrongdoing would for the most part not be changed. Allah, the Exalted, censured a people for not forbidding one another from it. Every wrongdoing that involves room for analysis (ijtihad) is not entered by anyone except the bearers of knowledge. This is a summary of discourse on changing wrongdoing, which contains eight conditions. It is related that a group of the Companions lodged a complaint against their governor with Abu Ja'far al-Mansur, but the governor argued against them and prevailed, since they had not established against him any great injustice or tyranny in anything. Then a young man from the group stood up and said: "O Commander of the Faithful, indeed Allah commanded justice and excellence, and he has been just but has not been excellent." He said: "Abu Ja'far was amazed at his accuracy and dismissed the governor."

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And fulfill the covenant of Allah when you have made it﴾ — the verse. It includes, through His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah commands justice and excellence﴾, the previous verse, as if it said: "Do this and abstain from that." So He conjoined to that implied sense His saying "and fulfill." "The covenant of Allah" is a term for everything that is contracted by the tongue and binds a person, such as a sale, a tie of kinship, or a pact in a matter that agrees with the religion. His saying ﴿and do not break oaths after their confirmation﴾ singled out in this verse the familiar expressions with which oaths are joined, emphasizing them and drawing attention to them.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

All this applies where persisting in the oath is obedience to Allah, the Exalted, whereas where turning away from it is more correct in truth, this is what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) spoke of when he said: "Whoever swears an oath and then sees something else as better than it, let him make expiation for his oath and do what is better." It is said: "tawkid" and "ta'kid," and "wakkada" and "akkada," both being dialects. Al-Zajjaj said: "The hamza is substituted from a waw."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is not clear, because there is nothing in the morphological forms of the word that indicates this.

"Kafilan" means: one who takes responsibility for your fulfilling (of the covenant). The rest of the verse is a warning within the form of a report about Allah's knowledge of His servants' deeds. A group said: this verse was revealed concerning those who pledged allegiance to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) upon Islam; Abu Layla related it from Buraydah. Qatada, Mujahid, and Ibn Zayd said: it was revealed concerning the alliances of the Jahiliyya in matters of commanding good or forbidding wrong, which Islam made stronger.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

As the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "There is no alliance in Islam, and whatever alliance existed in the Jahiliyya, Islam only strengthened." This is a hadith in meaning. And even if the occasion of revelation was some of these matters, the wording of the verse is general, addressed to all the worlds.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 16, verse 92–93:

His saying, Exalted is He:

﴿And do not be like her who unravels her thread after it has been made strong, into pieces, taking your oaths as deception between you, lest one community should be more numerous than another. Allah only tests you thereby, and He will surely make clear to you on the Day of Resurrection that over which you used to differ.﴾ ﴿And had Allah willed, He would have made you one community, but He leads astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills. And you will surely be questioned about what you used to do.﴾

This verse likens the one who swears an oath, or makes a covenant, or confirms his contract, to the woman who spins her thread and twists it firmly, and it likens the one who breaks his covenant after its confirmation to that spinstress when she unravels the strong thread after having tightened it. It is related that a foolish woman in Makkah called Rayta bint Sa'd used to do this, and the comparison was made with her; this was said by 'Abdullah ibn Kathir and al-Suddi, and they did not name the woman. It was also said: there was a woman afflicted with obsessive whisperings called Khittiyya who would spin near the Hijr and do this. Mujahid and Qatada said: this is a parable, not about a specific woman.

"Ankathan" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl). Naks (نكث) means to undo. "Quwwa" (قوة) in the language is the singular of the strands (quwā) of yarn, rope and other things that are plaited, and from it is the verse of al-Aghlab the rajaz poet:

"The rope of an old woman who twisted seven strands."

It appears to me that what is meant by "quwwa" in the verse is the strength that arises from the combination of the strands of the yarn. If we took it to mean a single strand, nothing would remain with it that could be unravelled into pieces, and the Arabs say: "the rope unravelled (intakatha)" when its strength is undone. As for if the yarn is understood as a single strand but has parts, as if it were many strands, Mujahid said: the meaning is "after the passing of a strand (quwwa)."

"Dakhal" (الدخل) is the same as "dagal" (الدغل), namely the means to deceit and treachery. This is because the one to whom the oath is sworn is reassured, so the one who swears can harm him by whatever he wills.

As for His saying, ﴿lest one community should be more numerous than another﴾, the commentators said: this verse was revealed concerning the Arabs, among whom a tribe, when it made an alliance with another, and then a larger, stronger tribe came and entered into alliance with the first, would betray the first, break its covenant, and return to this greater one. So Allah, Exalted is He, said: do not break the covenants for the sake of one tribe being greater than another in number and strength. "Ribā" (الربا) means increase. It is possible that (p-404) the saying means: do not break the oaths for the sake of your being more increased in good than others, i.e., more excellent; so the meaning is: do not seek increase of some of you over others by breaking covenants. "Yabluwakum" (يبلوكم) means He tests you. The pronoun in "bihi" may refer to the fulfilment that Allah commanded, and it may refer to ribā. That is, Allah tests His servants with envy and with some of them seeking dominance over others, and He tests them thereby in order to see who strives against his own soul among those who follow its desire. The remainder of the verse is a clear warning of the Day of Resurrection.

As for His saying, ﴿hiya arbā﴾, the position of "arbā" according to the Basrians is nominative, and according to the Kufans is accusative, and "hiya" is a pronoun of separation (ʿimād). The ʿimād is not permitted here according to the Basrians, because it does not occur with an indefinite noun, and "ummah" is indefinite. The argument of the Kufans is that "ummah" and what runs in its course of generic nouns are close to definiteness in their indefiniteness; do you not see that putting the definite article on them does not greatly specify them? In this there is room for consideration.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And had Allah willed, He would have made you one community﴾, the verse. Allah, Exalted is He, informs in this verse that He tests His servants with commands and prohibitions so that each one goes to what is made easy for him, and this is from Him, Exalted is He, by right of dominion, and He is not questioned about what He does. Had He willed, all people would have been on one path, either in guidance or in misguidance, but He, Exalted is He, willed to differentiate among them, and to single out a people with felicity and a people with wretchedness. "Yudill" (يضل) and "yahdi" (يهدي) mean: "He creates that in the hearts," contrary to the saying of the Mu'tazila. Then at the end of the verse He threatens that everyone will be questioned on the Day of Resurrection about his deeds, and this is a questioning of rebuke, not a questioning of inquiry; and that is the negated kind in (other) verses.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 16, verses 94–97:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿And do not take your oaths as a means of deception among yourselves, lest a foot slip after being firmly planted, and you taste evil for having averted [others] from the way of Allah, and there will be for you a great punishment.﴾ ﴿And do not sell the covenant of Allah for a small price. Indeed, what is with Allah is best for you, if you only knew.﴾ ﴿What is with you will end, but what is with Allah remains. And We will surely reward those who were patient with the best of what they used to do.﴾ ﴿Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while he is a believer – We will surely cause him to live a good life, and We will surely reward them with the best of what they used to do.﴾

He repeated the prohibition against taking oaths as a means of deception, emphasizing it and intensifying the prohibition against it because of the gravity of its position in the religion and its recurrence in people's dealings. And "al-dakhal" (deceit, hidden corruption), as we have said, means the hazards. His saying, ﴿lest a foot slip after being firmly planted﴾, is a metaphor for one who was upright in his condition and then falls into a great evil and collapses into it, because when a foot slips it moves a person from a state of good to a state of evil. From this meaning is the saying of Kuthayyir:

"So when we met, I stood firm, and it slipped."

That is, it moved from one state to another, so he used "slipping" for it. From this comes the saying about one who errs in a matter: "zalla fihi" (he slipped in it). Then He threatened, after that, with punishment in this world and a great punishment in the Hereafter. His saying, ﴿for having averted [others] from the way of Allah﴾, indicates that the verse concerns those who pledged allegiance to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And do not sell the covenant of Allah for a small price﴾ – the verse. This is a verse prohibiting bribery and taking wealth in exchange for doing what the taker is obligated to abandon, or abandoning what he is obligated to do. These are the matters in which Allah has bound His servants by covenant. Whoever takes money for that has given away the covenant of Allah and taken a small amount of this world. Then He, blessed and exalted, informed that what is with Him of the bliss of Paradise and the gifts of the Hereafter is better for those who fear Allah, know, and are guided. Then He explained the difference between the state of this world and the state of the Hereafter: that this one ends and passes away from a person, or he passes away from it, while the Hereafter is lasting and eternal.

Ibn Kathir and 'Asim read "wa-lanajziyanna" with the nun, while the rest read "wa-liyajziyanna" with the ya'. They did not differ regarding His saying "wa-lanajziyannahum" that it is with the nun. Thus said Abu 'Ali. Abu Hatim said that Nafi' was narrated from as reading "wa-liyajziyannahum" with the ya'.

"Sabaru" (they were patient) means: patient regarding desires and upon the hardships of obedience. This is an indication of patience against the desire for acquiring wealth by the ways mentioned. His saying, "bi-ahsan" means: according to the measure of the best of what they used to do.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Whoever does righteousness﴾ encompasses all acts of obedience. Then He restricted it by faith. People differed regarding "al-hayat al-tayyiba" (the good life). Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak said: it is lawful provision. al-Hasan and 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, said: it is contentment, and this is the best life of this world. Ibn 'Abbas also said: it is happiness. al-Hasan al-Basri said: the good life is the life of the Hereafter and the bliss of Paradise.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

There, it is good in the absolute sense, but the apparent meaning of this promise is that it is in this world. What I say is: the good life that is necessary for the righteous is only by the vigor of their souls, their attainment, and the strength of their hope. Hope for the soul is a pleasurable matter, and by this their lives become good. And by their having despised this world, its worries have left them. If lawful wealth and health are added to this, or contentment, then that is perfection. Otherwise, the good in what we have mentioned is constant.

His saying, ﴿So We will surely cause him to live a good life﴾, came in the wording of "man" (whoever), and His saying "wa-lanajziyannahum" came in its meaning. This promises the bliss of Paradise. The rest of the verse is clear.

Al-Tabari reported from Abu Salih that he said: this verse was revealed concerning a group of people from among the adherents of the religions who boasted, and each of them said: "My religion is superior." So Allah, Exalted is He, informed them in this verse of the best of the religions.

**Commentary of Ibn ʿAtiyya (al-Muḥarrar al-Wajīz) on Surah 16, verses 98–103**

The Almighty's saying:

﴿So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan.﴾ ﴿Indeed, he has no authority over those who believe and put their trust in their Lord.﴾ ﴿His authority is only over those who take him as a protector and those who associate others with Him through him.﴾ ﴿And when We substitute one verse in place of another—and God knows best what He sends down—they say, "You are only a fabricator." But most of them do not know.﴾ ﴿Say, "The Holy Spirit has brought it down from your Lord in truth, to make firm those who believe, and as guidance and good tidings for the Muslims."﴾ ﴿And We certainly know that they say, "It is only a human who teaches him." The tongue of the one they point to is foreign, while this is a clear Arabic tongue.﴾

The *fāʾ* in *"fa-idhā"* (so when) connects the two statements. The Arabs use it in such contexts. The implied meaning of the verse is: "So when you begin to recite the Qur'an," just as God says: ﴿O you who believe, when you rise up to …﴾ [al-Māʾida: 6], and as you say to a man: "When you eat, say: In the name of God." Seeking refuge (*al-istiʿādha*) is recommended (*nadb*) according to all scholars. Al-Naqqāsh reported from ʿAṭāʾ that seeking refuge is obligatory (*wājib*). The wording *al-istiʿādha* is in the same order as the verse. I have mentioned the scholarly disagreement on this matter at the beginning of this book. *"Al-Rajīm"* means the one stoned with the curse, and this is Iblīs (Satan).

Then God, blessed and exalted, informed that Iblīs has no dominion (*malaka*) or leadership (*riyāsa*). In my view, this is the apparent meaning of *"sulṭān"* in this verse. If we take *sulṭān* to mean proof (*ḥujja*), then he has no proof in this world against anyone, neither believer nor unbeliever. The exception would be if an interpreter takes it as: "He has no authority on the Day of Resurrection," in which case it may be understood to mean proof, because Iblīs does have a proof against the unbelievers: that he called them without evidence, and they responded to him of their own accord. Those over whom Iblīs has no authority or leadership are all the believers, because God has not given him authority except over the polytheists who take him as a protector. *Sulṭān* is negated here in the case of associating partners with God, since he does have a certain dominion over them in sins. These are the ones about whom God said: ﴿Indeed, My servants—you have no authority over them﴾ [al-Ḥijr: 42], and they are the ones about whom Iblīs said: ﴿except Your sincere servants among them﴾ [al-Ḥijr: 40].

*"Yatawallawnahu"* means: they make him a protector (*walī*). The pronoun in *"bihi"* may refer to the name of God, but the apparent reference is to the name of Iblīs, with the meaning: "because of him and on account of him." This is as when you say to your teacher: "I am knowledgeable because of you." So it is as if He said: "And those who, because of him, associate others with God." This statement that Satan has no authority over the believers, placed right after the command to seek refuge, implies that seeking refuge turns away his plotting, as if it includes reliance upon God and turning exclusively to Him.

As for God's saying: ﴿And when We substitute one verse in place of another﴾: when God abrogated the wording of a verse by replacing it with another wording while the meaning remained (even if its wording remained, since all of this falls under substitution), the Meccan unbelievers would say: "If this were from God, it would not change. It is only the fabrication of Muḥammad. He retracts from an error that appears to him to a correction he sees afterward." So God informed that He knows best what is suitable for His servants for a period of time, and then (p-408) what is suitable for them after that, and that they do not know this. Al-Jumhūr read *"yunazzilu"* with a fatḥa on the *nūn* and a shadda on the *zāy*. Abū ʿAmr read it with a sukūn on the *nūn* and a light *zāy*. He used the word *"aktharuhum"* (most of them), taking into account that a few of them were in a state of standing back, with less exaggeration in denial, and in a state of doubt. It is possible that this wording establishes that a few of them knew, yet disbelieved out of rebellion and obstinacy.

God commanded His Prophet to inform them that the Qur'an, along with its abrogating and abrogated verses, was sent down only by Gabriel, peace be upon him, who is the Holy Spirit. There is no disagreement about this. *"Al-Qudus"* means the purified place, as if Gabriel was attributed to the purified matter absolutely. He was called "spirit" either because he is a living being from among the spirit of God that He breathed into His creation, and he was singled out with this name, or because he flows with guidance and messages, and also among the angels, in the manner that the spirit flows through bodies, because of his nobility and status. Ibn Kathīr read *"al-Qudsi"* with a sukūn on the *dāl*, and the rest read it with a ḍamma. As for His saying *"bil-ḥaqq"* (in truth): it means with the truth in His commands, prohibitions, rulings, interests, and reports. It is possible that *"bil-ḥaqq"* means *ḥaqqan* (truly). It is also possible that it means: "in truth in that it descends." On this last possibility there are objections raised by the theologians regarding the principles of religion. The rest of the verse is clear.

As for God's saying: ﴿And We certainly know that they say﴾: Ibn ʿAbbās, may God be pleased with him and his father, said: In Mecca there was a foreign boy belonging to one of the Quraysh called Bilʿām. The Messenger of God, peace be upon him, used to speak with him, teach him Islam, and seek to influence him. So the Quraysh said: "This one teaches Muḥammad from the side of the foreigners," and the verse was revealed concerning him. ʿIkrima and Sufyān said: the boy's name was Yaʿīsh. ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muslim al-Ḥaḍramī said: In Mecca there were two boys, one named Jabr and the other Yasār. They used to recite in Roman (Greek), and the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, used to sit with them. The Quraysh said this, and the verse was revealed. Ibn Isḥāq said: the reference is to Jabr. al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: the reference is to Salmān al-Fārisī, but this is weak, because Salmān only embraced Islam after the Hijra, not in Mecca.

A group read *"lisānu alladhī"* (the tongue of the one who). al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī read *"al-lisānu alladhī"* with the definite article and without tanwīn on the *rāʾ* of *"basharu."* Nāfiʿ and Ibn Kathīr read *"yulḥidūna"* with a ḍamma on the *yāʾ*, from *"alḥada"*, meaning to incline. This is the reading of Abū ʿAmr, ʿĀṣim, Ibn ʿĀmir, and Abū Jaʿfar ibn al-Qaʿqāʿ. Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read *"yalḥadūna"* with a fatḥa on the *yāʾ* and the *ḥāʾ*, from *"laḥada"*. This is the reading of ʿAbd Allāh, Ṭalḥa, Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, al-Aʿmash, and Mujāhid. Both have the same meaning, and from it is the poet's saying:

*"Enough of me regarding the victory of the two Khubayybs, my beloved (?)*
*My commander is not stingy or inclining (to his own interest)."*

He means: one who turns away from generosity and from the state of leadership.

His saying *"aʿjamiyy"* is an attribution to *aʿjam* (non-Arab), because he used to say *"ʿajamiyy"*. The *aʿjam* is the one who does not speak Arabic, whereas the *ʿajamiyy* may speak Arabic, and his attribution remains valid. His saying *"wa-hādhā"* (and this) refers to the Qur'an, and the implied meaning is: "and this is the sequence of a tongue, or the utterance of a tongue," so there is an omitted *muḍāf* (a word elided before it). This is if we take *lisān* here to mean the organ of speech. In the speech of the Arabs, *lisān* means language. It is possible that this is intended here, and *lisān* means report, from which is the saying of al-Aʿshā:

*"Indeed, a report has come to me that is not false."*

And from it is the saying of another:

*"The evil report brings it to us, and you came back, and I did not think that you would come back."*

(p-410) Al-Ṭabarī reported from Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib that the reference in their saying "a human" is to a scribe who used to write for the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him. The Messenger would say to him at the end of verses: "Hearing, Knowing," and he would write "Mighty, Wise" or something similar. Then he would be occupied with listening to the revelation and would change it to "Forgiving, Merciful" or something similar. The Prophet said to him, peace be upon him, concerning some verses: "It is as you have written." He was then tempted and said: "I teach Muḥammad," and he apostatized and joined Mecca, and the verse was revealed.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This was a Christian who embraced Islam, wrote, then apostatized and died, and the earth rejected him. Otherwise, this report is weak, because the well-known scribe who apostatized for this reason and similar ones is ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Sarḥ al-ʿĀmirī, and his tongue was not foreign. So reflect.
