These are the ones about whom God said: ﴿Indeed, My servants—you have no authority over them﴾ [al-Ḥijr: 42], and they are the ones about whom Iblīs said: ﴿except Your sincere servants among them﴾ [al-Ḥijr: 40].

*"Yatawallawnahu"* means: they make him a protector (*walī*). The pronoun in *"bihi"* may refer to the name of God, but the apparent reference is to the name of Iblīs, with the meaning: "because of him and on account of him." This is as when you say to your teacher: "I am knowledgeable because of you." So it is as if He said: "And those who, because of him, associate others with God." This statement that Satan has no authority over the believers, placed right after the command to seek refuge, implies that seeking refuge turns away his plotting, as if it includes reliance upon God and turning exclusively to Him.

As for God's saying: ﴿And when We substitute one verse in place of another﴾: when God abrogated the wording of a verse by replacing it with another wording while the meaning remained (even if its wording remained, since all of this falls under substitution), the Meccan unbelievers would say: "If this were from God, it would not change. It is only the fabrication of Muḥammad. He retracts from an error that appears to him to a correction he sees afterward." So God informed that He knows best what is suitable for His servants for a period of time, and then (p-408) what is suitable for them after that, and that they do not know this. Al-Jumhūr read *"yunazzilu"* with a fatḥa on the *nūn* and a shadda on the *zāy*. Abū ʿAmr read it with a sukūn on the *nūn* and a light *zāy*. He used the word *"aktharuhum"* (most of them), taking into account that a few of them were in a state of standing back, with less exaggeration in denial, and in a state of doubt. It is possible that this wording establishes that a few of them knew, yet disbelieved out of rebellion and obstinacy.

God commanded His Prophet to inform them that the Qur'an, along with its abrogating and abrogated verses, was sent down only by Gabriel, peace be upon him, who is the Holy Spirit. There is no disagreement about this. *"Al-Qudus"* means the purified place, as if Gabriel was attributed to the purified matter absolutely. He was called "spirit" either because he is a living being from among the spirit of God that He breathed into His creation, and he was singled out with this name, or because he flows with guidance and messages, and also among the angels, in the manner that the spirit flows through bodies, because of his nobility and status. Ibn Kathīr read *"al-Qudsi"* with a sukūn on the *dāl*, and the rest read it with a ḍamma. As for His saying *"bil-ḥaqq"* (in truth): it means with the truth in His commands, prohibitions, rulings, interests, and reports. It is possible that *"bil-ḥaqq"* means *ḥaqqan* (truly). It is also possible that it means: "in truth in that it descends." On this last possibility there are objections raised by the theologians regarding the principles of religion. The rest of the verse is clear.

As for God's saying: ﴿And We certainly know that they say﴾: Ibn ʿAbbās, may God be pleased with him and his father, said: In Mecca there was a foreign boy belonging to one of the Quraysh called Bilʿām. The Messenger of God, peace be upon him, used to speak with him, teach him Islam, and seek to influence him. So the Quraysh said: "This one teaches Muḥammad from the side of the foreigners," and the verse was revealed concerning him. ʿIkrima and Sufyān said: the boy's name was Yaʿīsh. ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muslim al-Ḥaḍramī said: In Mecca there were two boys, one named Jabr and the other Yasār. They used to recite in Roman (Greek), and the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, used to sit with them. The Quraysh said this, and the verse was revealed. Ibn Isḥāq said: the reference is to Jabr. al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: the reference is to Salmān al-Fārisī, but this is weak, because Salmān only embraced Islam after the Hijra, not in Mecca.

A group read *"lisānu alladhī"* (the tongue of the one who). al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī read *"al-lisānu alladhī"* with the definite article and without tanwīn on the *rāʾ* of *"basharu."* Nāfiʿ and Ibn Kathīr read *"yulḥidūna"* with a ḍamma on the *yāʾ*, from *"alḥada"*, meaning to incline. This is the reading of Abū ʿAmr, ʿĀṣim, Ibn ʿĀmir, and Abū Jaʿfar ibn al-Qaʿqāʿ. Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read *"yalḥadūna"* with a fatḥa on the *yāʾ* and the *ḥāʾ*, from *"laḥada"*. This is the reading of ʿAbd Allāh, Ṭalḥa, Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, al-Aʿmash, and Mujāhid. Both have the same meaning, and from it is the poet's saying:

*"Enough of me regarding the victory of the two Khubayybs, my beloved (?)*
*My commander is not stingy or inclining (to his own interest)."*

He means: one who turns away from generosity and from the state of leadership.

His saying *"aʿjamiyy"* is an attribution to *aʿjam* (non-Arab), because he used to say *"ʿajamiyy"*. The *aʿjam* is the one who does not speak Arabic, whereas the *ʿajamiyy* may speak Arabic, and his attribution remains valid. His saying *"wa-hādhā"* (and this) refers to the Qur'an, and the implied meaning is: "and this is the sequence of a tongue, or the utterance of a tongue," so there is an omitted *muḍāf* (a word elided before it). This is if we take *lisān* here to mean the organ of speech. In the speech of the Arabs, *lisān* means language. It is possible that this is intended here, and *lisān* means report, from which is the saying of al-Aʿshā:

*"Indeed, a report has come to me that is not false."*

And from it is the saying of another:

*"The evil report brings it to us, and you came back, and I did not think that you would come back."*

(p-410) Al-Ṭabarī reported from Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib that the reference in their saying "a human" is to a scribe who used to write for the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him. The Messenger would say to him at the end of verses: "Hearing, Knowing," and he would write "Mighty, Wise" or something similar. Then he would be occupied with listening to the revelation and would change it to "Forgiving, Merciful" or something similar. The Prophet said to him, peace be upon him, concerning some verses: "It is as you have written." He was then tempted and said: "I teach Muḥammad," and he apostatized and joined Mecca, and the verse was revealed.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This was a Christian who embraced Islam, wrote, then apostatized and died, and the earth rejected him. Otherwise, this report is weak, because the well-known scribe who apostatized for this reason and similar ones is ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Sarḥ al-ʿĀmirī, and his tongue was not foreign. So reflect.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 16, verses 104–106:

The Exalted said:

﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the signs of Allah, Allah will not guide them, and for them is a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿It is only those who do not believe in the signs of Allah who invent falsehood, and it is they who are the liars.﴾ ﴿Whoever disbelieves in Allah after his belief—except one who is compelled while his heart remains firm in faith—but whoever opens his breast to disbelief, upon them is wrath from Allah, and for them is a great punishment.﴾

What is understood from the wording is that those whom Allah does not guide are those who do not believe in His signs. However, He placed the clause in this order and delayed the other, to emphasize the ugliness of their action and to censure their speech. This is like His saying: ﴿So when they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate﴾ [al-Saff: 5]. The meaning is what we have mentioned, as if He had said: "Indeed, those who did not believe, Allah did not guide them."

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿It is only those who invent falsehood﴾, it means: "It is only those who lie." This is a rebuttal of those who said to Muhammad (ﷺ): "You are only a fabricator." The particle "innama" (only, exclusively) is always restrictive, but the nature of its restriction varies according to the meanings in which it occurs. Sometimes the meaning requires that its restriction be literal, as in His saying: ﴿Allah is only one God﴾ [al-Nisa': 171]. And sometimes the meaning requires that its restriction be figurative and hyperbolic, as in your saying: "The brave one is only 'Antara." And so it is in this verse. Al-Zajjaj said: "This category invents falsehood, because when they see the signs which none can produce except Allah, they deny them, and this is the most abominable of lies."

He repeated the meaning in His saying: ﴿and it is they who are the liars﴾, for the benefit of attaching the attribute of lying to them, since describing a thing by an attribute is more emphatic than informing about it, because an attribute implies permanence more than a statement does. Thus He began in this verse with the statement and then confirmed it with the attribute. Makki objected to this view, but his objection is not strong.

The "man" (whoever) in His saying: ﴿Whoever disbelieves﴾ is a substitute (badal) for His saying: "the liars." Al-Zajjaj permitted no other interpretation than this, because he saw that the sentence up to the end of the exception was incomplete, so he linked it to what preceded it. But what al-Zajjaj rejected is permissible according to what I shall now present, if Allah wills.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This is reinforced by what has been narrated: that His saying ﴿and it is they who are the liars﴾ refers to 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Sarh, Maqis ibn Subaba, and others like them, who had believed in the Messenger of Allah and then apostatized (irtadda). When He explained in this verse the matter of the liars, that they are those who disbelieved after believing, He excluded from this description the believing people who were tortured in Makka: Bilal, 'Ammar, his mother Sumayya, Khabbab, Suhayb, and those like them. This is because the disbelievers of Makka, in the early period of Islam, used to harm those among them who had embraced Islam, because of their weakness, and torture them so that they would renounce it. Some of them would indulge the disbelievers by saying what they wanted to hear. It is narrated that 'Ammar ibn Yasir did this, so Allah made an exception for him in this verse, and the concession remained general in the matter after him. Then He began the statement that whoever opens his breast to disbelief, upon them [is wrath], and this pronoun is according to the meaning of "man" and not its wording.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

Among the objections to this is that the case of Ibn Abi Sarh and those like him occurred while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was in Madina, whereas the apparent evidence of this verse is that it is Meccan.

A group said: "Whoever" (man) in His saying ﴿Whoever disbelieves﴾ is an opening statement, and His saying ﴿but whoever opens his breast﴾ is a specification of it. The exception entered for the reason we have mentioned, namely the exclusion of 'Ammar and those like him. Close to the first exception is the resumptive "but" (lakin). His saying "upon them" is the predicate for the first and second "man," since they are one in meaning, because the statement in His saying "it is only" was intended for the category that opens its breast to disbelief. Thus "صَدْرًا" (sadran, "breast") is in the accusative as a specifier (tamyiz). His saying ﴿opens with disbelief a breast﴾ means: he expands his breast to disbelief by his own choice.

It is narrated that 'Ammar ibn Yasir complained to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about what had been done to him of torture and of what he had been made to say, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "How do you find your heart?" He said: "I find it firm in faith." He said: "Then answer them with your tongue, for it will not harm you, and if they return to it, then return to it."

Connected to this verse are some matters of compulsion (ikrah). As for one whom a capable disbeliever tortures so that he disbelieves with his tongue, and the torture would lead to his death, then for him the answer with the tongue is permitted, by unanimous opinion as far as I know. But if the one who compels him demands an answer by an act, such as prostrating to an idol or the like, then there is a difference of opinion about this. One group, which is the majority, said: he answers according to the degree of taqiyya (dissimulation under compulsion). Another group said: he does not answer, and surrenders himself. Another group said: if the idol is toward the qibla, he may answer, and he intends prostration to Allah.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

How fitting it is that he should prostrate to Allah at that time wherever he turns, and this is permitted during travel because of the hardship of dismounting from the mount while moving about. So how much more so in this case?

A group relied on the distinction in prohibition with the statement of Ibn Mas'ud: "There is no speech by which I may ward off from myself two lashes from a ruler except that I would speak it." So he restricted the concession to speech, excluding action.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This is not a proof, because it is possible that he made speech an example while intending that action is under the same ruling.

As for compulsion in sale, divorce, manumission, breaking the fast in Ramadan, drinking wine, and similar sins that are between the servant and Allah, Blessed and Exalted, nothing of that is binding upon the one compelled. This was said by Mutarrif, who narrated it from Malik, and it was said by Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam and Asbagh, and they narrated it from Ibn al-Qasim from Malik. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) distinguished between those among them which are statements, such as manumission and divorce, and allowed taqiyya in them, and he said: "There is no taqiyya in what is an action, such as drinking wine and breaking the fast in Ramadan, and its doing is not lawful for the one compelled."

As for the oppressed person who is pressed until he sells his goods, that is a sale which is not valid against him, and he has more right to his goods, taking them back without price, and the buyer sells them for the price to that oppressor. If the goods are lost, he recovers their price or their value, whichever is greater, from the oppressor, if the buyer did not know of his oppression. Mutarrif said: whoever among the buyers knows the condition of the one compelled, he is liable for what he purchased of his slaves and goods, like a usurper (ghasib). As for one who does not know, he is not liable for the goods and the animals, and he is liable only for what was destroyed through his cause, such as food he ate or a garment he wore. And the produce (ghalla), whether he knew or did not know, is in no way his, but he is liable for it, like a usurper. This was said by Asbagh and Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam.

Mutarrif said: whatever the buyer has done with it, of manumission, or assignment of ownership (tadbir), or endowment (tahbis), it is not binding upon the one compelled, and he may take back his goods.

As for compulsion to kill a Muslim, or to beat him, or to take his property, or to sell his goods, there is no excuse in it, and there is no compulsion in committing a sin that violates another's rights, such as adultery, killing, or the like. Mutarrif, Asbagh, and Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam said: no one should do that even if he is killed for not doing it, and if he does it, he is sinful, and the prescribed punishment (hadd) and retaliation (qawad) are binding upon him.

Malik said: shackles are compulsion, imprisonment is compulsion, and a frightening threat is compulsion even if it is not carried out, when the oppression of that aggressor and his execution of what he threatens are established. In my view, compulsion is measured according to the resolve of the one compelled and his standing in religion, and according to the value of the thing to which he is compelled. Beating may be compulsion in one matter and not in another. Thus for these incidents there is a jurisprudence of the situation.

As for the oath of the one compelled, as we have said, it is not binding. Ibn al-Majishun said: it is the same whether he swears regarding something which is an act of obedience or disobedience to Allah, Blessed and Exalted, when he is compelled to the oath. This was said by Asbagh.

Mutarrif said: if he is compelled to swear regarding what is disobedience to Allah Exalted, or regarding what in its doing is neither obedience nor disobedience, then the oath in it is void. If he is compelled to swear regarding what is obedience, such as when the governor seizes a dissolute man and compels him to swear by divorce that he will not drink wine, or will not commit immorality, or will not cheat in his work; or when a father makes his child swear in such a matter for the sake of discipline, then the oath is binding, even if the one compelled erred in what he undertook of that. Ibn Habib said likewise.

As for a man who is compelled to swear, or else money will be taken from him—like tax collectors, oppressive collectors, and aggressors—Mutarrif said: there is no taqiyya in that, for a person only wards off by his oath for his body, not for his wealth. Ibn al-Majishun said: he does not break the oath (lit. does not become a violator) even if he warded off for his wealth and did not fear for his body. Ibn al-Qasim said in accordance with Mutarrif's view, and he narrated it from Malik (may Allah have mercy on him). It was also said by Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam, Asbagh, and Ibn Habib.

Mutarrif and Ibn al-Majishun said: if the swearer hastens with his oath to the oppressive governor before he is asked, in order to ward off by it what he feared for his body and property, and he swears to him, then it is binding upon him. This was said by Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam and Asbagh. Ibn al-Majishun also said, concerning one whom an oppressor seized and who swore to him by an unconditional divorce without being made to swear, and he left him while he was lying, and he only swore out of fear of being beaten or killed or having his property taken: if he swore out of overwhelming fear and hope for deliverance from his oppression, then he has entered into compulsion and there is nothing upon him. But if he did not swear with hope of deliverance, then he is a violator.

When a governor accuses someone of doing a matter and says to him: "You must be punished unless you swear to me," then if that matter is one which the compelled person may do, whether it is an act of obedience or neither obedience nor disobedience, then taqiyya applies in this. But if the matter is one which is not lawful for him to do, and the governor's prohibition in it is correct, then there is no taqiyya in the oath, and he is a violator. This was said by Malik and Ibn al-Majishun.

This is a summary of matters of compulsion.

Ibn al-Majishun said: he does not break the oath (lit. does not become a violator) even if he warded off for his wealth and did not fear for his body. Ibn al-Qasim said in accordance with Mutarrif's view, and he narrated it from Malik (may Allah have mercy on him). It was also said by Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam, Asbagh, and Ibn Habib.

Mutarrif and Ibn al-Majishun said: if the swearer hastens with his oath to the oppressive governor before he is asked, in order to ward off by it what he feared for his body and property, and he swears to him, then it is binding upon him. This was said by Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam and Asbagh. Ibn al-Majishun also said, concerning one whom an oppressor seized and who swore to him by an unconditional divorce without being made to swear, and he left him while he was lying, and he only swore out of fear of being beaten or killed or having his property taken: if he swore out of overwhelming fear and hope for deliverance from his oppression, then he has entered into compulsion and there is nothing upon him. But if he did not swear with hope of deliverance, then he is a violator.

When a governor accuses someone of doing a matter and says to him: "You must be punished unless you swear to me," then if that matter is one which the compelled person may do, whether it is an act of obedience or neither obedience nor disobedience, then taqiyya applies in this. But if the matter is one which is not lawful for him to do, and the governor's prohibition in it is correct, then there is no taqiyya in the oath, and he is a violator. This was said by Malik and Ibn al-Majishun.

This is a summary of matters of compulsion.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 16, verses 104–106:

The Exalted said:

﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the signs of Allah, Allah will not guide them, and for them is a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿It is only those who do not believe in the signs of Allah who invent falsehood, and it is they who are the liars.﴾ ﴿Whoever disbelieves in Allah after his belief—except one who is compelled while his heart remains firm in faith—but whoever opens his breast to disbelief, upon them is wrath from Allah, and for them is a great punishment.﴾

What is understood from the wording is that those whom Allah does not guide are those who do not believe in His signs. However, He placed the clause in this order and delayed the other, to emphasize the ugliness of their action and to censure their speech. This is like His saying: ﴿So when they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate﴾ [al-Saff: 5]. The meaning is what we have mentioned, as if He had said: "Indeed, those who did not believe, Allah did not guide them."

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿It is only those who invent falsehood﴾, it means: "It is only those who lie." This is a rebuttal of those who said to Muhammad (ﷺ): "You are only a fabricator." The particle "innama" (only, exclusively) is always restrictive, but the nature of its restriction varies according to the meanings in which it occurs. Sometimes the meaning requires that its restriction be literal, as in His saying: ﴿Allah is only one God﴾ [al-Nisa': 171]. And sometimes the meaning requires that its restriction be figurative and hyperbolic, as in your saying: "The brave one is only 'Antara." And so it is in this verse. Al-Zajjaj said: "This category invents falsehood, because when they see the signs which none can produce except Allah, they deny them, and this is the most abominable of lies."

He repeated the meaning in His saying: ﴿and it is they who are the liars﴾, for the benefit of attaching the attribute of lying to them, since describing a thing by an attribute is more emphatic than informing about it, because an attribute implies permanence more than a statement does. Thus He began in this verse with the statement and then confirmed it with the attribute. Makki objected to this view, but his objection is not strong.

The "man" (whoever) in His saying: ﴿Whoever disbelieves﴾ is a substitute (badal) for His saying: "the liars." Al-Zajjaj permitted no other interpretation than this, because he saw that the sentence up to the end of the exception was incomplete, so he linked it to what preceded it. But what al-Zajjaj rejected is permissible according to what I shall now present, if Allah wills.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This is reinforced by what has been narrated: that His saying ﴿and it is they who are the liars﴾ refers to 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Sarh, Maqis ibn Subaba, and others like them, who had believed in the Messenger of Allah and then apostatized (irtadda). When He explained in this verse the matter of the liars, that they are those who disbelieved after believing, He excluded from this description the believing people who were tortured in Makka: Bilal, 'Ammar, his mother Sumayya, Khabbab, Suhayb, and those like them. This is because the disbelievers of Makka, in the early period of Islam, used to harm those among them who had embraced Islam, because of their weakness, and torture them so that they would renounce it. Some of them would indulge the disbelievers by saying what they wanted to hear. It is narrated that 'Ammar ibn Yasir did this, so Allah made an exception for him in this verse, and the concession remained general in the matter after him. Then He began the statement that whoever opens his breast to disbelief, upon them [is wrath], and this pronoun is according to the meaning of "man" and not its wording.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

Among the objections to this is that the case of Ibn Abi Sarh and those like him occurred while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was in Madina, whereas the apparent evidence of this verse is that it is Meccan.

A group said: "Whoever" (man) in His saying ﴿Whoever disbelieves﴾ is an opening statement, and His saying ﴿but whoever opens his breast﴾ is a specification of it. The exception entered for the reason we have mentioned, namely the exclusion of 'Ammar and those like him. Close to the first exception is the resumptive "but" (lakin). His saying "upon them" is the predicate for the first and second "man," since they are one in meaning, because the statement in His saying "it is only" was intended for the category that opens its breast to disbelief. Thus "صَدْرًا" (sadran, "breast") is in the accusative as a specifier (tamyiz). His saying ﴿opens with disbelief a breast﴾ means: he expands his breast to disbelief by his own choice.

It is narrated that 'Ammar ibn Yasir complained to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about what had been done to him of torture and of what he had been made to say, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "How do you find your heart?" He said: "I find it firm in faith." He said: "Then answer them with your tongue, for it will not harm you, and if they return to it, then return to it."

Connected to this verse are some matters of compulsion (ikrah). As for one whom a capable disbeliever tortures so that he disbelieves with his tongue, and the torture would lead to his death, then for him the answer with the tongue is permitted, by unanimous opinion as far as I know. But if the one who compels him demands an answer by an act, such as prostrating to an idol or the like, then there is a difference of opinion about this. One group, which is the majority, said: he answers according to the degree of taqiyya (dissimulation under compulsion). Another group said: he does not answer, and surrenders himself. Another group said: if the idol is toward the qibla, he may answer, and he intends prostration to Allah.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

How fitting it is that he should prostrate to Allah at that time wherever he turns, and this is permitted during travel because of the hardship of dismounting from the mount while moving about. So how much more so in this case?

A group relied on the distinction in prohibition with the statement of Ibn Mas'ud: "There is no speech by which I may ward off from myself two lashes from a ruler except that I would speak it." So he restricted the concession to speech, excluding action.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This is not a proof, because it is possible that he made speech an example while intending that action is under the same ruling.

As for compulsion in sale, divorce, manumission, breaking the fast in Ramadan, drinking wine, and similar sins that are between the servant and Allah, Blessed and Exalted, nothing of that is binding upon the one compelled. This was said by Mutarrif, who narrated it from Malik, and it was said by Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam and Asbagh, and they narrated it from Ibn al-Qasim from Malik. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) distinguished between those among them which are statements, such as manumission and divorce, and allowed taqiyya in them, and he said: "There is no taqiyya in what is an action, such as drinking wine and breaking the fast in Ramadan, and its doing is not lawful for the one compelled."

As for the oppressed person who is pressed until he sells his goods, that is a sale which is not valid against him, and he has more right to his goods, taking them back without price, and the buyer sells them for the price to that oppressor. If the goods are lost, he recovers their price or their value, whichever is greater, from the oppressor, if the buyer did not know of his oppression. Mutarrif said: whoever among the buyers knows the condition of the one compelled, he is liable for what he purchased of his slaves and goods, like a usurper (ghasib). As for one who does not know, he is not liable for the goods and the animals, and he is liable only for what was destroyed through his cause, such as food he ate or a garment he wore. And the produce (ghalla), whether he knew or did not know, is in no way his, but he is liable for it, like a usurper. This was said by Asbagh and Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam.

Mutarrif said: whatever the buyer has done with it, of manumission, or assignment of ownership (tadbir), or endowment (tahbis), it is not binding upon the one compelled, and he may take back his goods.

Mutarrif, Asbagh, and Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam said: no one should do that even if he is killed for not doing it, and if he does it, he is sinful, and the prescribed punishment (hadd) and retaliation (qawad) are binding upon him.

Malik said: shackles are compulsion, imprisonment is compulsion, and a frightening threat is compulsion even if it is not carried out, when the oppression of that aggressor and his execution of what he threatens are established. In my view, compulsion is measured according to the resolve of the one compelled and his standing in religion, and according to the value of the thing to which he is compelled. Beating may be compulsion in one matter and not in another. Thus for these incidents there is a jurisprudence of the situation.

Mutarrif said: if he is compelled to swear regarding what is disobedience to Allah Exalted, or regarding what in its doing is neither obedience nor disobedience, then the oath in it is void. Ibn Habib said likewise.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 16, verses 107–111:**

His, may He be exalted and glorified, saying:

﴿That is because they preferred the worldly life to the Hereafter, and because Allah does not guide the disbelieving people.﴾ ﴿Those are the ones upon whose hearts and hearing and sight Allah has set a seal, and those are the heedless.﴾ ﴿Undoubtedly, in the Hereafter they are the losers.﴾ ﴿Then indeed your Lord, for those who emigrated after they had been tried and then struggled and endured patiently, indeed your Lord, after that, is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ ﴿On the Day when every soul comes pleading for itself, and every soul is paid in full for what it did, and they will not be wronged.﴾

"That" (dhalika) is a reference to the anger and the punishment that was threatened before this verse. The pronoun in "annahum" (that they) refers to those who opened their breast to disbelief. When they did the act of one who prefers (the worldly life), they were held accountable for that, even though they did not believe in the Hereafter. Yet the matter in itself is clear, so because they turned away from considering it, they were like one who preferred something other than it. In this verse, the punishment is linked to their acquiring (taksib), because their preference for the adornment of this world and the pleasures of disbelief is the acquisition.

His saying: ﴿And that Allah does not guide the disbelieving people﴾ indicates that Allah, exalted is He, originates disbelief in their hearts. There is no doubt that the disbelief of the disbeliever for which punishment is due is only by origination from Allah, exalted is He, and acquisition from the disbeliever. So the verse combines the two matters, and the creed of the People of the Sunna (Ahl al-Sunna, the Sunni community, the followers of the prophetic tradition) has proceeded on this basis. His saying: ﴿does not guide the disbelieving people﴾ is a general statement meaning that He does not guide them in respect of being disbelievers, in the very essence of their disbelief; or it is a general statement by which particularity is intended, concerning those who die in that state.

His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿Those are the ones upon whose hearts Allah has set a seal﴾ (the verse), is an expression of Allah diverting them from the path of guidance, originating dark disbelief in their hearts, and making turning away prevail over their consideration. It is as if by that He blocked the avenues of these senses so that they are not benefited by them in reflection and contemplation. The statement and the mention of the disagreement regarding sealing and stamping (al-tab' wa'l-khatm), and whether it is literal or metaphorical, has already been mentioned in Surat al-Baqara. "Al-sam'" (hearing) is a noun of genus (ism jins), and it is originally a verbal noun (masdar); for this reason it is in the singular. He drew attention to their acquisition of turning away from consideration, and therefore described them as heedless. The explanation of "la jaram" (undoubtedly) has already preceded in this surah.

His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿Then indeed your Lord, for those who emigrated after they had been tried﴾ (the verse). Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: There was a group from the people of Makka who had embraced Islam, and they were treating Islam lightly. The polytheists took them out with them on the Day of Badr, and some of them were struck down. The Muslims said: "These companions of ours were Muslims and they were coerced; so ask forgiveness for them." Then this was revealed: ﴿Indeed, those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves﴾ [al-Nisa': 97] to the end of the verse. He said: It was written with it to those of the Muslims who remained in Makka, that they had no excuse. So they went out, and the polytheists caught up with them and inflicted the trial upon them. Then this was revealed concerning them: ﴿And among the people is one who says, "We believe in Allah"﴾ [al-Baqara: 8] to the end of the verse. So the Muslims wrote to them with that, and they went out and despaired of every good. Then this was revealed concerning them: ﴿Then indeed your Lord, for those who emigrated after they had been tried﴾. So they wrote to them with that, that Allah has made an exit for you. Then the polytheists caught up with them and fought them, until whoever was saved was saved and whoever was killed was killed.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The narration came in this form: that after the revelation of the verse they went out, so the struggle (jihad) mentioned in the verse is their struggle alongside the Messenger of Allah ﷺ for Islam. But a group related that they went out, and those who followed them went out and struggled with those who followed them, so whoever was killed was killed and whoever was saved was saved, and then the verse was revealed at that time. Thus the meaning of the struggle mentioned is their struggle against those who followed them.

Ibn Ishaq said: This verse was revealed concerning 'Ammar ibn Yasir, 'Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'a, and al-Walid ibn al-Walid.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

In my view, the mention of 'Ammar in this is not sound, for he is of a higher rank than these people. Rather, these are those who repented from among those who had opened their breast to disbelief, and Allah opened for them the door of repentance at the end of the verse.

'Ikrima and al-Hasan said: This verse was revealed concerning 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Sarh and those like him. So it is as if he said: "after the Satan had tried them." This verse is Medinan, and I know of no disagreement about that; and if any is found, it is weak.

al-Jumhur (the majority) read: "min ba'di ma futinu" with a damma on the fa' and a kasra on the ta', while Ibn 'Amir alone read it with a fatha on it. If the pronoun refers to those who were tormented, then it carries the meaning: they tried themselves by what they gave to the polytheists of speech, as 'Ammar ibn Yasir did. As for the reading of the majority, if the pronoun refers to those who were tormented, then it has the meaning: "after the polytheists had tried them"; and if the pronoun refers to the polytheists, then it has the meaning: "after the Satan had tried them." The pronoun in "ba'dihā" (after it) refers to the trial, or to the deed, or to the emigration, or to the repentance; and the context implies it, even though there is no explicit mention of it.

His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿On the Day when every soul comes pleading﴾: the meaning is: "Indeed He is Forgiving, Merciful, on the Day..." And His saying: ﴿every soul﴾ means "every possessor of a soul" (kullu dhī nafs). Then the verb was made to agree with the mentioned genitive noun, so the feminine marker was used; the first "nafs" is the well-known soul, and the second is in the sense of the essence (dhat), as you say: "nafs al-shay'" and "ayn al-shay'," meaning its essence. ﴿And every soul is paid in full﴾ means it is recompensed: everyone who did good is recompensed for his good, and everyone who did evil is recompensed for his evil.

The apparent meaning of the verse is that every soul comes pleading, whether believing or disbelieving. When the disbelievers plead with their lies and their denial of disbelief, their limbs and the messengers and others testify against them according to the categories. At that point they will not speak, ﴿nor will they be permitted to offer an excuse﴾ [al-Mursalat: 36]. Thus the verses of the Qur'an are reconciled by the differing situations. A group said: the saying of every individual among the prophets and others will be: "myself, myself," and this is not pleading or argumentation; it is merely a desire.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 16, verses 112–114:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿And Allah presents a parable: a town that was secure and tranquil, its provision coming to it abundantly from every place. But it denied the favours of Allah, so Allah made it taste the garment of hunger and fear for what they used to do.﴾ ﴿And there had certainly come to them a Messenger from among themselves, but they denied him, so the punishment seized them while they were wrongdoers.﴾ ﴿So eat of what Allah has provided for you, lawful and good, and be grateful for the favour of Allah, if it is Him that you worship.﴾

Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Ibn Zayd and Qatada said: The town whose parable is struck is Makkah, which had this description that Allah mentioned, because it was not raided and no one attacked it, and provisions were brought to it. Allah bestowed favour upon it through His Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. The intended referent of all these pronouns is the people of the town, who denied the favours of Allah in that and in the whole of the Law and guidance. So there befell them the years of famine, fear, and the rest of the expeditions (sarayا, singular sariyya: detachments) and military campaigns (ghazawat, singular ghazwa) of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. This is if the verse is Madani. If it is Makki, then the hunger of the years and the fear of the punishment from Allah are in proportion to the denial.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

And if it is [Madina] that was struck as a parable, then it was struck for others that come after it, so that one may beware of falling into what it fell into. Al-Tabari related from Hafsa, Mother of the Believers, may Allah be pleased with her, that during the siege of 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, may Allah be pleased with him, she used to ask: "What have the people done?" She was returning from Hajj from Makkah, and it was said to her: "He has been killed." She said: "By the One in whose hand is my soul, it is indeed the town, meaning Madina, of which Allah said: ﴿And Allah presents a parable﴾, the verse."

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Al-Tabari included this to argue that Hafsa said the verse was revealed about Madina and that it is the town that was struck as a parable. In my view the matter is not so. Rather, she meant that Madina had come to be in the feared situation of the parable, and what befell the town made into a parable had befallen it. Similarly, it appears to me that the verse intends an unspecified town made into a parable, but in the sense of warning its people and others from the towns until the Day of Resurrection.

"Raghadan" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl). "An'um" is the plural of ni'ma, like shidda and ashudd. So said Sibawayh. Qutrub said: "An'um" is the plural of nu'm, which means comfort (na'im), as one says: "These are days of nu'm and ṭu'm."

Allah's saying ﴿so Allah made it taste the garment of hunger and fear﴾ is a metaphor: when that afflicted them it became like a garment. This is like the saying of al-A'sha:

When the bedfellow bends her neck, she bends upon him and becomes a garment.

Similar to it is Allah's saying: ﴿They are a garment for you and you are a garment for them﴾ [al-Baqara: 187]. And from it is the saying of the poet:

After al-Zubayr, Mujashi' has worn the garments of her who menstruates and did not wash the blood.

As if the shame, when it afflicted them and clung to them, made them wear it.

His saying "adhaqa-ha" (made her taste) is like Allah's saying: ﴿Taste, indeed you are the mighty, the noble﴾ [al-Dukhan: 49], and like the saying of the poet:

Yours is what you have committed, so fear and taste.

The majority read "wal-khawf" (and the fear) in the genitive, as a conjunction to "al-ju'" (hunger). Abu 'Amr (with a variant transmitted from him) read "wal-khawfa" in the accusative, as a conjunction to "libasa" (garment). In the Mushaf of Ubayy ibn Ka'b, may Allah be pleased with him, it is "libas al-khawf wal-ju'" (the garment of fear and hunger). Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, read: "fa-adhaqaha Allahu al-khawf wal-ju'" without mentioning "libas."

The pronoun in "jaa'a-hum" refers to the people of Makkah, and the Messenger is Muhammad, upon him be blessings and peace. The "adhab" (punishment) is hunger, the affair of Badr, and the like, if the parable is about Makkah and the verse is Madani. If it is Makki, then it is hunger alone. Al-Tabari mentioned that it was killing at Badr, and this requires that the verse was revealed in Madina. If the parable is about an unspecified ancient town, then the pronoun in "jaa'a-hum" may refer to the people of that town, and this would be among what happened to them, like the town of Shu'ayb and others. It may also be that the pronoun refers to the people of Makkah. So reflect.

His saying: ﴿So eat of what Allah has provided for you﴾, the verse, is the beginning of another speech and a ruling. The fa' in His saying "fa-kuluu" serves to connect the speech and the coherence of the sentences. It has moved from mention of the disbelievers and the parable about them to commanding the believers with a legal ruling, so the speech was joined with fa', and the meanings are not connected. This is one view. But what appears correct to me is that the speech is connected in meaning: that is, you, O believers, are not like this town, so eat and thank Allah for the difference of your state from the state of the disbelievers. This verse is occasioned by the fact that the disbelievers had instituted practices concerning livestock, permitting some and forbidding some, so Allah commanded the believers to eat of all the livestock which Allah has provided to His servants.

The scholars differed concerning His saying "tayyiban" (good). The sound view is that it means "mustaladhdhan" (pleasant, delightful), after His saying "halalan" (lawful). The text in this is upon the delightful, since in it appears the manifestation of blessing, which is the greatness of blessings, although the lawful may sometimes be not delightful. It is possible that "tayyib" has the meaning of "halal," and He repeated it for emphasis and affirmation. The rest of the verse is clear.

His saying: ﴿if it is Him that you worship﴾ is an establishing of the souls, as you say to a man: "If you are a man, then do such-and-such," meaning to establish his self. Al-Tabari related that some people said: this verse was revealed as an address to the disbelievers concerning food which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had sent to them during their hunger. Al-Tabari rejected this view, and indeed it is corrupt in several respects.

Al-Tabari related from Hafsa, Mother of the Believers, may Allah be pleased with her, that during the siege of 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, may Allah be pleased with him, she used to ask: "What have the people done?" She was returning from Hajj from Makkah, and it was said to her: "He has been killed." She said: "By the One in whose hand is my soul, it is indeed the town, meaning Madina, of which Allah said: ﴿And Allah presents a parable﴾, the verse."

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Al-Tabari included this to argue that Hafsa said the verse was revealed about Madina and that it is the town that was struck as a parable. In my view the matter is not so. Rather, she meant that Madina had come to be in the feared situation of the parable, and what befell the town made into a parable had befallen it. Similarly, it appears to me that the verse intends an unspecified town made into a parable, but in the sense of warning its people and others from the towns until the Day of Resurrection.

"Raghadan" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl). "An'um" is the plural of ni'ma, like shidda and ashudd. So said Sibawayh. Qutrub said: "An'um" is the plural of nu'm, which means comfort (na'im), as one says: "These are days of nu'm and ṭu'm."

Allah's saying ﴿so Allah made it taste the garment of hunger and fear﴾ is a metaphor: when that afflicted them it became like a garment. This is like the saying of al-A'sha:

When the bedfellow bends her neck, she bends upon him and becomes a garment.

Similar to it is Allah's saying: ﴿They are a garment for you and you are a garment for them﴾ [al-Baqara: 187]. And from it is the saying of the poet:

After al-Zubayr, Mujashi' has worn the garments of her who menstruates and did not wash the blood.

As if the shame, when it afflicted them and clung to them, made them wear it.

His saying "adhaqa-ha" (made her taste) is like Allah's saying: ﴿Taste, indeed you are the mighty, the noble﴾ [al-Dukhan: 49], and like the saying of the poet:

Yours is what you have committed, so fear and taste.

The majority read "wal-khawf" (and the fear) in the genitive, as a conjunction to "al-ju'" (hunger). Abu 'Amr (with a variant transmitted from him) read "wal-khawfa" in the accusative, as a conjunction to "libasa" (garment). In the Mushaf of Ubayy ibn Ka'b, may Allah be pleased with him, it is "libas al-khawf wal-ju'" (the garment of fear and hunger). Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, read: "fa-adhaqaha Allahu al-khawf wal-ju'" without mentioning "libas."

The pronoun in "jaa'a-hum" refers to the people of Makkah, and the Messenger is Muhammad, upon him be blessings and peace. The "adhab" (punishment) is hunger, the affair of Badr, and the like, if the parable is about Makkah and the verse is Madani. If it is Makki, then it is hunger alone. Al-Tabari mentioned that it was killing at Badr, and this requires that the verse was revealed in Madina. If the parable is about an unspecified ancient town, then the pronoun in "jaa'a-hum" may refer to the people of that town, and this would be among what happened to them, like the town of Shu'ayb and others. It may also be that the pronoun refers to the people of Makkah. So reflect.

His saying: ﴿So eat of what Allah has provided for you﴾, the verse, is the beginning of another speech and a ruling. The fa' in His saying "fa-kuluu" serves to connect the speech and the coherence of the sentences. It has moved from mention of the disbelievers and the parable about them to commanding the believers with a legal ruling, so the speech was joined with fa', and the meanings are not connected. This is one view. But what appears correct to me is that the speech is connected in meaning: that is, you, O believers, are not like this town, so eat and thank Allah for the difference of your state from the state of the disbelievers. This verse is occasioned by the fact that the disbelievers had instituted practices concerning livestock, permitting some and forbidding some, so Allah commanded the believers to eat of all the livestock which Allah has provided to His servants.

The scholars differed concerning His saying "tayyiban" (good). The sound view is that it means "mustaladhdhan" (pleasant, delightful), after His saying "halalan" (lawful). The text in this is upon the delightful, since in it appears the manifestation of blessing, which is the greatness of blessings, although the lawful may sometimes be not delightful. It is possible that "tayyib" has the meaning of "halal," and He repeated it for emphasis and affirmation. The rest of the verse is clear.

His saying: ﴿if it is Him that you worship﴾ is an establishing of the souls, as you say to a man: "If you are a man, then do such-and-such," meaning to establish his self. Al-Tabari related that some people said: this verse was revealed as an address to the disbelievers concerning food which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had sent to them during their hunger. Al-Tabari rejected this view, and indeed it is corrupt in several respects.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 16, verses 112–114:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿And Allah presents a parable: a town that was secure and tranquil, its provision coming to it abundantly from every place. But it denied the favours of Allah, so Allah made it taste the garment of hunger and fear for what they used to do.﴾ ﴿And there had certainly come to them a Messenger from among themselves, but they denied him, so the punishment seized them while they were wrongdoers.﴾ ﴿So eat of what Allah has provided for you, lawful and good, and be grateful for the favour of Allah, if it is Him that you worship.﴾

Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Ibn Zayd and Qatada said: The town whose parable is struck is Makkah, which had this description that Allah mentioned, because it was not raided and no one attacked it, and provisions were brought to it. Allah bestowed favour upon it through His Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. The intended referent of all these pronouns is the people of the town, who denied the favours of Allah in that and in the whole of the Law and guidance. (p-421) The Exalted's saying:

﴿Indeed, He has forbidden you only carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and that over which other than Allah has been invoked. But whoever is compelled [to it], neither desiring nor transgressing, then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

The word "innama" (only) here restricts these prohibited things to the time of the revelation of the verse; then prohibitions were revealed after that. The majority of readers recited "al-maytata" (carrion) with a light (unshaddated) ta', but Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa' recited it with a shadda, and that is the original form, the lightening being a later development upon it. The governing element in its accusative case is "harrama" (forbade). A group recited "al-maytatu" with a raised vowel (damma), taking "ma" to mean "alladhi" (that which).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

That "ma" is joined to "inna" weakens this reading and rules that it is restrictive and "ma" is a detaching particle (kafffa). If it means "alladhi," it must be separate, and that contradicts the orthography of the Mushaf. The majority recited "harrama" according to the meaning "Allah forbade." A group recited "hurrima" in the passive voice, and in this case "al-maytatu" must be raised, without exception.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Forbidden carrion is that which dies of the land animals that have flowing blood, dying of its own accord (hatf anfihi). As for what does not have flowing blood, such as locusts, flies, fleas, fig worms, bean creatures, and fish that die of their own accord and float on the water, there are two opinions within the school. And what dies of its own accord among animals that live both in water and on land, such as turtles and the like, there are two opinions; the prohibition here is more apparent, unless the predominant life of the animal is in water.

Forbidden blood is that which pours forth and flows if left alone. As for blood that mixes with the flesh and settles in it, cooking that meat with it is permissible, and no one is burdened with searching it out. The blood of fish is disputed as to its lawfulness, though it does pour forth if left alone.

The flesh of swine refers mainly to it, and the most apparent intent is this; therefore it was singled out for mention. The community has agreed on the prohibition of its fat and its cartilage. From this singling out, a group derived permission to benefit from its hide when tanned and to wear it. The preferable view is its total prohibition. As for its hair, benefiting from it is permitted, while another group said that this is not permissible; the first view is more preponderant.

(p-422) ﴿And that over which other than Allah has been invoked﴾: it means everything slaughtered with an intention other than seeking nearness to Allah, and drawing near to something else. It is the same whether one speaks that over the slaughtered animal or does not speak; but the expression came through "uhilla" (invoked), and its meaning is correct according to the custom of the Arabs, and it was intended as a reproach. That is because when they drove an animal to an idol, they would loudly proclaim the name of that idol and shout it out.

As for His saying ﴿fa-man id-turra (whoever is compelled)﴾: a group said its meaning is "ukriha (forced)," while the majority said its meaning is that hunger and need have compelled him (idtarrahuju'un wa-ihtiyaj). A group read "fa-manu" with a damma on the nun and "idturra" with a damma on the ta', and a group read "fa-mani" with a kasra on the nun and "idtirra" with a kasra on the ta', on the basis that the original form is "idturira," so the vowel of the ra' was transferred to the ta' and the first ra' was assimilated into the second. As for His saying ﴿ghayra baghin (neither desiring)﴾: a group said it refers to one who seeks rebellion against the ruler, or who commits highway robbery, and in general one who journeys in sin; and "al-'adi (transgressing)" has the same meaning in that it intends disobedience. The majority said: ﴿ghayra baghin﴾ means not using these prohibited things while other things are available, and ﴿wa-la 'adin (nor transgressing)﴾ means not exceeding the limits of Allah in this matter.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This view is more preponderant and more general in the concession.

A group said: "baghin" and "'adin" refer to excess in satisfying hunger and in taking provision. People differed over the manner of eating carrion: one group said that what is permitted is only that which keeps the throat moist (yumsiku al-ramaq) alone; another group said rather that full satiety is permitted; and another group, among them Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said: satiety and taking provision are permitted. Some grammarians said regarding His saying "'adin": it is inverted from "'a'id," so it is like "shakin al-silah" and like "yawmun rah," and like the saying of the poet:

Lathin bihi al-ashaa wal-'Ubriyy (wrapped about with the thorny shrub and the 'Ubri tree)

(p-423) His saying ﴿Indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ requires from Him permissibility for the one compelled. The permissibility came in these expressions with restraint and constriction regarding the matter, so that the speech would indicate the great gravity of these prohibited things. So the ultimate end for this one granted the concession is Allah's forgiveness of him and the removal from him of the sin that would have attached to him had it not been for his necessity. This explanation that we have mentioned is understood by the eloquent from the wording, and there is nothing of it in the meaning beyond that; it is only an allusion. Likewise, in another place He made its ultimate end that there is no sin upon him; and although "there is no sin upon him" and "it is permissible for him" return to one meaning, there is a difference in the form of the two expressions.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 16, verses 116–119:

His Exalted and Majestic saying:

﴿And do not say, concerning what your tongues describe as lies, "This is lawful and this is unlawful," to fabricate lies against Allah. Indeed, those who fabricate lies against Allah will not succeed.﴾ ﴿A little enjoyment, and for them is a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿And to those who were Jews We prohibited what We have related to you before. And We did not wrong them, but they were wronging themselves.﴾ ﴿Then indeed your Lord, for those who did evil in ignorance and then repented after that and reformed – indeed, your Lord thereafter is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

This is an address to the disbelievers who made forbidden the baheerah (a she-camel whose ear was slit) and the saibah (a freed animal), and who made lawful what is in the bellies of livestock even if it was dead. The evidence for this is His saying, relating about them: ﴿And if it is dead, they are partners in it﴾ [al-An'am: 139]. The verse entails every permission and prohibition they had, for all of it is fabrication on their part, and among it is what they did concerning the months.

The Seven Readers and the majority of people read "al-kadhiba" (الكَذِبَ) with a fatha on the kaf and the ba and a kasra on the dhal, with "ma" being a verbal-masdariyyah (ma as a verbal noun marker), so it is as if He said: "for the description of your tongues." Al-A'raj, Talhah, Abu Ma'mar, and al-Hasan read "al-kadhibi" (الكَذِبِ) with a kasra on the ba, as a substitute (badal) for "ma." Some of the people of Syria, Mu'adh ibn Jabal, and Ibn Abi 'Abla read "al-kudhubu" (الكُذُبُ) with damma on the kaf, dhal, and ba, as an adjective of "al-alsina" (the tongues). Muslima ibn Muharib read "al-kudhuba" (الكُذُبَ) with a fatha on the ba, as the plural of "kidhab," like "kutub" and "kitab."

His saying: ﴿This is lawful﴾ refers to the dead meat of the bellies of livestock and everything else they made lawful; His saying: ﴿And this is unlawful﴾ refers to the baheerah and the saibah and everything else they made unlawful; and His saying: "to fabricate lies against Allah" refers to their saying about their indecencies, of which this is one: ﴿We found our fathers upon it, and Allah has commanded us with it﴾ [al-A'raf: 28].

It is possible that He intends that their legislation was by following customs which Allah does not approve, a fabrication against Him, because whoever legislates a matter is as if he says to his followers: "This is the truth, and this is the intention of Allah." Then Allah informed them that those who fabricate lies against Allah do not reach their hope. Success (falah) is reaching one's hope, and sometimes it occurs in remaining (survival), as the poet said:

"And the evening and the morning have no remaining with it."

It seems that this verse is in this meaning, and His saying ﴿A little enjoyment﴾ strengthens this. It may also be in the attainment of one's aims, and from it is the saying of 'Ubayd:

"Succeed with whatever you wish, for one may be reached through weakness, and the shrewd may be deceived."

His saying ﴿A little enjoyment﴾ refers to their living in this world, and ﴿for them is a painful punishment﴾ after that in the Hereafter.

(p-425) As for His exalted saying: ﴿And to those who were Jews﴾ – the verse – when He, blessed and exalted, related to the believers what He prohibited for them, He also informed them of what He prohibited for the Jews, to clarify their alteration of the law concerning what they made lawful from that and what they made unlawful of their own accord. His saying ﴿what We have related to you﴾ refers to what is in Surat al-An'am concerning animals with claws and the fats. His saying ﴿And We did not wrong them﴾ means: We did not place the punishment upon them by prohibiting those things upon them in other than their proper place; rather, they brought it upon themselves, and their clinging to sins necessitated that.

His exalted saying: ﴿Then indeed your Lord, for those who did evil in ignorance﴾ – the verse. This is a verse of comfort for the whole world; Allah, exalted, informs in it that He forgives the one who repents. The verse refers to the disbelievers who fabricated against Allah and committed the aforementioned deeds; if they repent from their disbelief by faith and reform by the deeds of Islam, Allah forgives them. This verse – after that – encompasses every person falling under its wording, whether disbeliever or disobedient. A group said: "Jahalah" is deliberate action. But in my view, "jahalah" in this context is not the opposite of knowledge; rather it is transgressing the limit and recklessness, and from it is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Or be ignorant or be treated ignorantly toward me," and it is the one in the poet's words:

"Unquestionably, let no one act with ignorance toward us, lest we act with ignorance above the ignorance of the ignorant."

The jahalah which is the opposite of knowledge often accompanies this other sense, but the deliberate one is excluded from it, and it is the more common; and it is rarely found among the disobedient that one did not previously have knowledge of the prohibition of the sin being committed. The pronoun in "ba'dihā" refers back to the repentance.

(p. 426) Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says:

﴿Indeed, Abraham was a nation, devoutly obedient to Allah, upright, and he was not of the polytheists.﴾ ﴿Grateful for His blessings. He chose him and guided him to a straight path.﴾ ﴿And We gave him good in this world, and indeed he is in the Hereafter among the righteous.﴾ ﴿Then We revealed to you: follow the religion of Abraham, upright, and he was not of the polytheists.﴾ ﴿The Sabbath was only prescribed for those who differed concerning it. Indeed your Lord will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning that about which they used to differ.﴾

When Allah exposed the act of the Jews and their arbitrariness in their law by mentioning what He prohibited for them, He wished to show their distance from the law of Abraham and their false claim to it. So He describes the state of Abraham to make clear the difference between their state and the state of the Quraysh as well.

The word ummah (community, nation) in the language is a homonym (mushtarakah), used for goodness, for the common people, and for a large group of people. Then a learned man, a king, or a person who stands alone in a way (of his own) is likened to a large crowd of people and is called an ummah. In this sense Abraham, peace be upon him, was called an ummah. Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "The ummah is the teacher of good." At another time he said: "Mu'adh ibn Jabal, may Allah be pleased with him, was an ummah, devoutly obedient." Abu Qurrah al-Kindi, or Farwah ibn Nawfal, said to him: "That is not so; rather it is Abraham who was an ummah, devoutly obedient." He said: "Do you know what the ummah is? It is the teacher of good. And Mu'adh was like that: he taught good and obeyed Allah and His Messenger." Mujahid said: "Abraham was named an ummah because he stood alone in faith in his time for a period."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

In al-Bukhari it is reported that he said to Sarah: "There is no believer on earth today other than me and you." Some of the grammarians—I think it is Abu al-Hasan al-Akhfash—said: "Ummah is on the pattern fi'lah from amma yaummu, so it is like al-hamzah and al-dihkah (forms of intensity), meaning: one who is followed (yu'tamm bihi)."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

According to this view, "ummatan" is a descriptive adjective (sifah); according to the first view, it is a noun, not an adjective. "Al-qanit" is one who obeys and constantly persists in worship. "Al-hanif" is one who inclines toward good and reform. The Arabs used to say "hanifan" of one who was circumcised and performed the pilgrimage to the House. The deletion of the nun in "lam yaku" is due to frequent usage, like their deletion in "la ubali" and "wa la adri." It is also because the nun, when it is sukun (unvocalized), resembles the letters of prolongation (huruf al-'illah) in its nasality and lightness, and in that it may serve as a sign and otherwise. So "lam" here appears to have entered upon "yakun" in the state of jazm (apocopation), (p. 427) and the nun is not deleted when it is not sakin, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those who disbelieved did not...﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 1]. It is not deleted in such a case except in poetry, where it has come deleted. His saying ﴿of the polytheists﴾ points to Abraham's disassociation from the state of the polytheist Arabs and the polytheist Jews, since all of them claimed him, and polytheism is implicated for the Jews by their anthropomorphism (tajsim).

"Shakiran" is an adjective for Abraham, following what preceded. "Al-an'um" is the plural of ni'mah (blessing). "Ijtabahu" means: He chose him. The rest of the verse is clear.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We gave him good in this world﴾, the "good" (hasanah) is the tongue of truthfulness and his leadership over all creation. This is the view of all the exegetes, because every community that follows a law acknowledges that its faith is the faith of Abraham, that he is its exemplar, and that he was upon the right course. His saying ﴿among the righteous﴾ means: those on whom He has bestowed favor, i.e., among the righteous in their states and ranks; or it means that in the Hereafter he is among those who are judged with the judgment of the righteous in this world. This is on the basis that the verse describes his state in both abodes. It may also be that the meaning is: in works of the Hereafter; in that case it describes his state in worldly and otherworldly deeds.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then We revealed to you﴾ (the verse). The revelation to Muhammad (ﷺ) with this is among the good that Allah gave Abraham, peace be upon him. Ibn Fawrak said: "The command of the superior to follow the inferior, since it came before (him), is toward the right and acting upon it." The "an" in His saying ﴿an ittabi'﴾ is explanatory (mufassirah), and it may be a object-clause (maf'ulah). "Al-millah" is the path in the tenets of the law. "Hanifan" is a circumstantial accusative (hal), and its governing element is the verbal sense in His saying ﴿the religion of Abraham﴾. It may also be a circumstantial accusative from the pronoun (damir) of the subject in "ittabi'." Makki said: "It cannot be a circumstantial accusative from Abraham, because it is a genitive complement (mudaf ilayhi)." This is not as he said, because a circumstance may be governed by prepositions (huruf al-khafd) when they govern the one who has the circumstance, as in your saying: "I passed by Zayd standing."

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The Sabbath was only prescribed﴾, i.e., it was not from the religion of Abraham. Allah made it an obligation as a punishment with which He afflicted the people who differed about it, as Ibn Zayd said. That is because Moses, peace be upon him, commanded the Children of Israel to make a day of the week specifically for worship, and he commanded that it be Friday. Most of them said: "Rather let it be Saturday, because Allah finished the creation of His creatures on it." Others said: "Rather we accept what Allah commanded Moses, peace be upon him." The majority argued with them, and the others followed them. So Allah imposed Saturday upon them with a strong imposition as a punishment from Him for them. Then there was no steadfastness among them; rather they disobeyed in it, transgressed, and so they were destroyed.

Al-A'mash recited: "Innama unzila al-sabtu" (indeed the Sabbath was only sent down), and this is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud. Abu Haywah recited: "ju'ila" with a fatha on the jim and the ayn. It is reported in a hadith that the Jews and the Christians differed about the day that is specific to the week: these took Saturday, and those took Sunday, and Allah guided us to Friday. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "This is their day about which they differed." So the difference mentioned in the verse is not the difference in the hadith. The rest of the verse is a clear warning.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 16, verses 125–128:

The words of the Most High:

﴿Invite to the way of your Lord with wisdom and good admonition, and argue with them in the best manner. Indeed your Lord is most knowing of who has strayed from His way, and He is most knowing of those who are guided.﴾ ﴿And if you punish, then punish with the like of what you were punished with. But if you are patient, it is indeed better for those who are patient.﴾ ﴿And be patient, and your patience is not except by God. And do not grieve over them, and do not be in distress because of what they plan.﴾ ﴿Indeed God is with those who fear Him and those who are doers of good.﴾

It was revealed in Mecca at the time when he was commanded to make a truce with the polytheists. God the Exalted commanded him to invite to God and His law with gentleness, which means that the one invited hears his ruling, and it is the right speech, close to the soul, falling in the most beautiful position. "Good admonition" means warning, guidance, and gentleness towards the person, by honouring him, encouraging him, and making him appear as one who accepts virtues. This is the condition of the one who is invited. As for the condition of the one who is argued with, it is without harshness, so that the truth prevails over him without fighting. The speech indicates that your striving, your concern and your toil will not avail, because God has known who among them will believe and be guided, and He has known who will go astray. So the overall meaning is: follow this path and do not resort to harshness, for it is ineffective, since God's knowledge has already preceded regarding the guided among them and the misguided.

A group said: this verse is abrogated (mansukh) by the verse of fighting. Another group said: it is muhkam (not abrogated).

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

What appears to me is that restriction to this condition, and that one should not exceed it with the disbelievers whenever harshness becomes necessary, is indeed abrogated without doubt. As for those disbelievers with whom these conditions are effective, and whose faith is hoped for through them without fighting, then the verse is muhkam concerning them until the Day of Resurrection. Also, it is muhkam in regard to the disobedient. Thus, in this manner, the Muslims should be admonished until the Day of Resurrection.

As for His saying, "And if you punish, then punish," the verse: the people of tafsir unanimously agreed that this verse is Medinan, and that it was revealed concerning the mutilation of Hamza, may God be pleased with him, on the day of Uhud. This is recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari and in the books of the biographies (al-Siyar). Al-Nahhas, however, held that it is Meccan.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

The meaning is connected with what precedes it from the Meccan portion in a fine connection, for the ranks progress from the one who is invited and admonished, to the one who is argued with, to the one who is repaid for his action. But what the majority narrated is more firmly established. Also, His saying, "And if you are patient, it is indeed better," is connected to the meaning of the verse according to what the majority narrated: "When the disbelievers of Quraysh mutilated Hamza, may God be pleased with him, this came from the Messenger of God ﷺ himself, and he said: 'If God gives me victory over them, I will mutilate thirty of them' (and in the book of al-Nahhas and others: 'seventy' of them). Then the people said: 'If we gain the upper hand, we will certainly do so and so,' and then this verse was revealed."

Then He emphatically commanded the Messenger of God ﷺ to be patient in the following verse, and in this verse He named the injuries "punishment," whereas punishment in its true sense is only the second. He did this so that the two expressions would be equal and the phrasing of the speech would be harmonious. This is the reverse of His saying, "And they plotted, and God plotted" [Al 'Imran: 54], and His saying, "God mocks them" [al-Baqarah: 15], for the second is figurative and the first is literal. Ibn Sirin recited: "And if you retaliate, then retaliate."

Al-Tabari related from a group that they said: this verse was only revealed concerning one who has suffered an injustice, that he should not take from his oppressors, when he is able, except the equivalent of his injustice, and he should not exceed it to others. The scholars differed concerning a man who wronged another by taking his property, and then the wrongdoer was entrusted by the wronged person with property. Is it permissible for him to betray him in the amount by which he wronged him? A group said: "It is permissible for him," among them Ibn Sirin, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, Sufyan and Mujahid, and they argued with this verse and the generality of its wording. Malik, may God have mercy on him, and a group with him said: "It is not permissible for him." They argued with the saying of the Messenger of God ﷺ: "Return the trust to the one who entrusted you, and do not betray the one who betrayed you." It occurs in the Musnad of Ibn Ishaq that this hadith was narrated concerning a man who committed adultery with the wife of another, and then the other man gained access to the wife of the second by leaving her with him while he travelled. So the man consulted the Messenger of God ﷺ about the matter, and he said to him this [hadith].

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

In the matter of property, the view of Malik, may God have mercy on him, is strengthened, because betrayal attaches to that, and it is a vice from which there is no escape, and a person should not emulate others in vices, but rather should avoid them for himself. As for a man who wrongs another in property, and then gains the ability to take redress without being entrusted, it seems that this is permissible for him, since he sees that God has judged in his favour, just as if he had gained it by a judgment from a judge.

His saying, the Most High, "And be patient, and your patience is not except by God," this is an emphatic command to the Messenger of God ﷺ to be patient in the face of retaliation for the mutilation of the slain. Ibn Zayd said: this verse is abrogated by fighting, but the majority of people hold that it is muhkam. It is narrated that the Messenger of God ﷺ said to his companions: "As for me, I will be patient as I have been commanded; what will you do?" They said: "We will be patient, O Messenger of God, as we have been urged." "And your patience is not except by God" means: by the help of God and His support for you in that. The pronoun in "over them" (ʿalayhim) is said by some to refer to the disbelievers, i.e., do not grieve that they did not submit. But a group said: rather it refers to the slain, Hamza and his companions, may the good pleasure of God be upon them, over whom the Messenger of God ﷺ grieved. The first view is the more correct, since the pronouns then refer to one single category.

The majority read "fi dayqin" (in distress) with a fatha on the dad. Ibn Kathir read "fi diqin" with a kasra on it. It is also narrated from Nafi', but this is an error by the one who narrated it. Some of the linguists said: the kasra and the fatha on the dad are two dialectal forms of the verbal noun. Abu 'Ubayda said: "al-diq" is a verbal noun, and "al-dayq" is a lightened form of "dayyiq," like "mayt" and "mayyit," and "hayn" and "hayyin." Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: the correct view is that "al-dayq" is a dialectal form of the verbal noun, because if it were a lightened form of "dayyiq," it would necessitate that the adjective stand in place of the noun it qualifies, and this is not the place for that.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

An adjective stands in place of the noun it qualifies only when the qualified noun is specified by the adjective itself, as when you say, "I saw a laughing one" (ḍāḥikan), for the laughing one specifies the person. But if you said, "I saw a cold one" (bāridan), it would not be good. Sibawayh, may God have mercy on him, gave the example of "bārid." And "dayyiq" does not specify the qualified noun.

Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Zayd said: what is in this verse of the command to be patient is abrogated.

His saying, "with those who fear Him," means: with help, support and assistance. "Those who fear Him" means: they refrain from disobedience. "Doers of good" means: they increase in what they have been urged to do of good deeds.

The tafsir of Surah al-Nahl is finished, and all praise is due to God, Lord of the worlds, and blessings and peace be upon our master Muhammad, and upon his family and companions, and peace.
